title: Google releases officially refurbished Pixel 9 devices starting at $499 with an extra perk
snippet: After outing its Pixel 7 series in recent weeks, Google has just quietly released the Pixel 9 series to its Certified Refurbished program with prices starting at $499. more…
fullText:
After outing its Pixel 7 series in recent weeks, Google has just quietly released the Pixel 9 series to its Certified Refurbished program with prices starting at $499. 

Released in 2024, the Pixel 9 series introduced the updated design language we see today in Google Pixel phones, as well as continuing to improve the Tensor chipset inside. This generation also saw new camera sensors and the introduction of two Pro-tier devices – Pixel 9 Pro as a smaller 6.3-inch device, and Pixel 9 Pro XL as a bigger 6.8-inch device.

Pricing originally started at $799, but is now down to $499 as a part of Google’s Certified Refurbished program.

Google kicked off this program in late 2024 and has since shuffled around its offerings to include newer devices and remove ones that are outdated and nearing their end-of-life status for software updates. The most recent removal, as mentioned, was the Pixel 7 series in early September 2026.

	

Today sees Google releasing the Pixel 9 series (minus the Fold) to its Certified Refurbished portal on the Google Store. 

Pixel 9: $499 (Obsidian)

Pixel 9 Pro: $649 (Obsidian & Hazel)

Pixel 9 Pro XL: $699 (Obsidian & Hazel)

The base Pixel 9 is currently out of stock, but Pro and Pro XL configurations are available. Google is also throwing in a 6-month AI Plus subscription for buyers of these refurbished Pixel 9 devices:

Purchase a refurbished Pixel Pro and receive a 6-month trial of Google AI Plus with 2TB of secure storage. Smart AI and extra savings. New subscribers only, subscription voided if returned, ends 4/4/2027, terms apply.

Google’s Certified Refurbished program for Pixel phones includes a “multi-point test,” a one-year warranty, repairs using authentic Google parts, and a fully unlocked device capable of using any carrier.

Meanwhile, Pixel 8 series prices have been adjusted to the following:

Pixel 8a: $339

Pixel 8: $389

Pixel 8 Pro: $549

title: Apple announces HomePod mini 2: Siri AI, new colors, Sound Glow, more
snippet: Apple has officially announced the new HomePod mini 2 smart speaker. The new product was announced by Apple today alongside the new HomeView smart display and fourth-gen Apple TV 4K. more…
fullText:
Apple has officially announced the new HomePod mini 2 smart speaker. The new product was announced by Apple today alongside the new HomeView smart display and fourth-gen Apple TV 4K.

HomePod mini 2 now available to pre-order

HomePod mini 2 features the same design as the original version. It comes in a variety of refreshed and returning color options: green, pink, blue, midnight, and white. It replaces the dated S5 chip with a new S10 chip to deliver new features and experiences.

Siri AI and Sound Glow are new to HomePod mini 2

Apple says the new HomePod mini 2 will work with Siri AI, Apple’s upgraded version of the personal assistant that debuted with iOS 27.

Powered by an entirely new architecture built on the latest generation of Apple Foundation Models, Siri AI transforms the HomePod mini experience and helps users get more done than ever before.

When paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, HomePod mini can tap into a user’s personal context to help them find what they need in the moment. 

HomePod mini 2 also includes a new hardware feature called Sound Glow:

With Sound Glow, the top of HomePod mini transforms into a visual canvas that glows and pulses in sync with the music, reacting in real time to bass and treble. The song’s album artwork from Now Playing generates a color-matched light experience that’s unique to every song, and users can pick a soundscape like rain to trigger bespoke animations for a soothing atmosphere.

HomePod mini 2 can create a home theater experience

When paired with the new Apple TV 4K (fourth-gen), a pair of HomePod mini 2 speakers and a pair of full-size HomePod 2 speakers can create a new home theater experience as well:

HomePod mini delivers rich 360-degree sound from its compact footprint, whether it’s used as a single speaker, in a stereo pair, or as part of a multiroom audio setup. Powered by the Apple S10 chip and advanced computational audio, it analyzes music in real time to optimize dynamic range, loudness, and acoustic performance. For the first time, users can create a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K (4th generation) and HomePod mini 2. Together, the four speakers and the new Apple TV 4K intelligently recognize each speaker’s position in the room, so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space.

Price and availability

Pre-orders start today ahead of the launch on October 30. The price is $149. Apple says it will run “HomePod software 27.2.” Apple adds that Siri AI will come in a future software update, suggesting it may not be available at launch.

The original HomePod mini was released in November 2020 for $99. Apple increased the price to $129 earlier this year.

title: Apple rolls out new AirPods beta firmware for several models, including AirPods Pro 3
snippet: In addition to the rollout of developer beta 4 for macOS 27.2, iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, and more, Apple also rolled out developer and public firmware betas for several AirPods models. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In addition to the rollout of developer beta 4 for macOS 27.2, iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, and more, Apple also rolled out developer and public firmware betas for several AirPods models. Here are the details.

Firmware betas also available for AirPods 5

Today has been quite a busy day in Cupertino. In a matter of hours, Apple unveiled the new Apple TV 4K, the new HomePod mini, the new $299 HomeView smart display, the Apple Home Collection, and multiple OS betas.

That includes macOS 27.2 Golden Gate developer beta 4, and its counterparts for iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Apple Vision Pro.

On top of all that, Apple is also rolling out public and developer firmware betas for several AirPods models, including:

AirPods Pro 3

AirPods 5

AirPods 5 (Wireless Charging Case)

AirPods Pro 2 (Lightning)

AirPods Pro 2 (USB-C)

AirPods Max 2

AirPods 4

AirPods 4 (ANC)

All firmware updates carry build number 9B5043a. Apple has yet to detail what is included in the new firmware.

If you’d like to join the public AirPods beta, you can do that by enabling that option from the AirPods settings screen on your iPhone.

Here are Apple’s official instructions to update AirPods and AirPods Pro firmware

Make sure that your iPhone, iPad, or Mac is updated to the latest version of iOS, iPadOS, or macOS, and that Bluetooth is on.

Make sure that your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Connect your iPhone, iPad, or Mac to Wi-Fi.

Connect your charging case to power.

Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to update.

Open the lid of the charging case to reconnect your AirPods to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Check the firmware version again.

If you still can’t update your firmware, reset your AirPods, then try to update your firmware again.

And here is Apple’s step-by-step guide to update AirPods Max firmware.

Make sure that your iPhone, iPad, or Mac is updated to the latest version of iOS, iPadOS, or macOS, and that Bluetooth is on.

Make sure that your AirPods Max are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Connect your iPhone, iPad, or Mac to Wi-Fi.

Plug the charging cable into the bottom-right earphone, then plug the other end of the cable into a USB charger or port.

Keep your AirPods Max in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad, or Mac, and wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to update.

Reconnect your AirPods Max to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.

Check the firmware version again.

If you still can’t update your firmware, reset your AirPods Max, then try to update your firmware again.

title: Pixel Watch 4 update adds Google’s AI watch face generator, more
snippet: One of the Pixel Watch 5’s quietly powerful features has landed on the Pixel Watch 4. The AI watch face generator that launched last year is currently rolling out to Pixel Watch 4 models. more…
fullText:
One of the Pixel Watch 5’s quietly powerful features has landed on the Pixel Watch 4. The AI watch face generator that launched last year is currently rolling out to Pixel Watch 4 models.

The Pixel Watch 5 wasn’t a massive shakeup as much as another refinement. The Pixel Watch 4 brought arguably more to the table when it launched last year, but if the newest model did anything new, it was to add a few enhancements under the hood. The majority of which were focused on AI performance.

One good byproduct of that push is an AI watch face generator; it’s a tool that makes creating custom watch faces a little easier, especially if you’re the type to pick a different one for each day of the week.

According to a few users on Reddit, a recent Pixel Watch 4 update added the AI watch face generator to their device. It looks like the update is packaged in version 4.2.12.989940186 and includes Pixel Watch 5 stock watch faces – Weave, Modular, Reveal, and Chronograph – and even the specialized Steph Curry dial. 

	

The custom face generator is straightforward. You can access the prompt section through the Pixel Watch app when you try to create a new look. Instead of picking from a template gallery, explain what you’re looking to generate, and Gemini Intelligence should come up with something close.

It has its limitations, of course, but it’s a great tool that Google didn’t really play up for the Pixel Watch 5. That made this Pixel Watch 4 update somewhat expected, but it’s a nice surprise nonetheless.

The Pixel Watch 4 update looks to be actively rolling out, so it might take some time for it to show up.

title: Googlebook OS review: A post-smartphone PC, if Google can keep it
snippet: All attempts to bring the lessons and benefits of the touch era to PCs have failed, from Windows 8 to the era after the iPad when the Mac gained fullscreen apps. From an experience perspective, the iPad came closest because it was built on iOS, but it still failed due to the locked-down limitations at its core. After using Googlebook OS for over a week, I think Google has the beginnings of a desktop OS for the Android smartphone generation, but the inherent strategy reset makes for a rough first take. more…
fullText:
All attempts to bring the lessons and benefits of the touch era to PCs have failed, from Windows 8 to the era after the iPad when the Mac gained fullscreen apps. From an experience perspective, the iPad came closest because it was built on iOS, but it still failed due to the locked-down limitations at its core.

After using Googlebook OS for over a week, I think Google has the beginnings of a desktop OS for the Android smartphone generation, but the inherent strategy reset makes for a rough first take.

System

Googlebook OS looks like ChromeOS on the surface but feels like Android. However, it is more optimized than any large-screen iteration of Android to date, including foldables and especially tablets. This is infinitely better than other desktop Android experiences, especially plugging your Pixel into an external display.

There is a level of nativeness here that I always thought was missing from Chromebooks. ChromeOS from the very start felt like an extension of the web and never outgrew that in my opinion. Googlebook OS does not have that issue.

	

As a Pixel user, I quickly adjusted to the Googlebook UI and UX, with the only real learning curve being keyboard shortcuts. I think that will be true for any proficient user of Android smartphones, and that immediate familiarity could be very appealing for both the average and more advanced users.

In the top-right corner, you’ll find familiar Android status icons. A tap opens Quick Settings that are identical to the Pixel experience save for a volume slider. The bell icon opens notifications with access to notification history in the bottom-left corner.

A shortcut that activates Magic Pointer is next, useful if you don’t want to enable the “cursor wiggle” gesture. There’s also a Live Update for any currently playing media. This tiny pill shows the responsible app and track name. Hovering over the icon lets you quickly play/pause and a tap brings up full media controls, which are also available in the notification shade. On other desktop OSes, pausing media always requires two clicks, with Googlebook’s implementation a really nice touch that takes advantage of having a cursor.

The top-left corner is home to time, day, and date, with a tap opening a useful calendar, like on ChromeOS.

On the HP Googlebook 14, the F1 key is Android’s back button and a genuinely useful hardware shortcut for quickly navigating apps. F2 is a Home button that takes you to the desktop, while F3 is Recents. F4 full-screens windows and F5 is for partial screen captures. F6 and F7 let you adjust screen brightness, while F8 lets you control the keyboard backlight. F9 is a microphone mute switch that works in conjunction with the Quick Settings Tile. F10, F11, and F12 are for volume, with F13 physically letting you start voice typing with Rambler. The icons could use some revamping, especially the fullscreen and screenshot symbols as both are too similar to the Recents key and too vague for glanceability. These rely on prior knowledge and are not designed intuitively.

The Quick Insert key that’s physically shared with Caps Lock opens a floating window that lets you quickly add emoji, access copied text, recent screenshots, and tabs. Carried over from Chromebook Plus, it’s deeply integrated with Gboard from Emoji Kitchen to GIFs and Stickers. You can also access the Gboard Clipboard Manager found on phones (and leave it open as a floating window), as well as invoke voice transcription. It’s pretty useful for surfacing common functionality for those who don’t remember or expertly use keyboard shortcuts, and more than worthy of being a physical key. The capability I’m missing from my Mac workflow is a text expander for macros.

The stylized ‘G’ or Action key opens the floating app launcher. This is basically Pixel Launcher device and web search, and I wish there was Gemini integration here. You will use this key in combination with a host of other shortcuts.

The Settings app is identical to the Pixel experience, with a dual-column layout. Controls you’d expect on a desktop OS appear first with “Device & accessories.” This lets you adjust the Touchpad, Keyboard, Display, Sound, and Glowbar. You can remap Modifier keys like Caps lock, Ctrl, Action (G), and Alt.

I greatly enjoy having Android widgets on my desktop (officially the “Home screen”). The first few times I saw them on this bigger screen, I had to do a double-take. It’s amusing to see the widgets, with Dynamic Color on full display, you see all the time on your phone, but now on your desktop. The larger size makes it a great surface for passive information throughout the day. For example, I use the Google Health widget to remind me to move and quickly log water consumption. You can also place app icons and folders, as well as folders and files for quick access.

Corner shortcuts (like on Mac) are great, and let you move your cursor to any of the four corners to trigger shortcuts like “Peek/unpeek desktop” or show notifications. My favorite is a Note-taking hot corner that opens my current Google Keep note. There’s also a Quick Settings Tile shortcut for that.

Multi-touch and text selection are all solid and feel like a desktop OS. Touchpad gestures include swiping three fingers up to get a zoomed-out Recents view of all open windows. Meanwhile, my external keyboard works normally on Googlebooks.

That said, there are some very annoying interfaces that come directly from smartphones and just enlarged for desktops. Taking fullscreen screenshots (G + S) results in a fullscreen flash that is okay on phones but incredibly distracting on a big laptop screen. I also find the copied text pop-up, which matches mobile Android, in the bottom-right corner to be equally distracting and would like an option to disable it. Similarly, the Tap & click sounds enabled by default are very annoying.

I haven’t really found myself using Cross-device services. Notification sync that shows all your phone alerts is a straightforward capability, but I always have my phone with me when I’m working on the laptop.

I used Cast My Apps, which has a prominent access point in the Taskbar, primarily for Google Messages over the PWA (more on that later). Otherwise, I would just install any Android apps I needed directly on the Googlebook. “Continue on” is something I haven’t really used, with Google intending the feature to pick up an activity from my phone on the bigger screen.

After first setting up the device, it might take some time for these Cross-device features to become available. That in itself is a bad first impression, but worse is how Googlebooks launched without day one support for the biggest player: Samsung.

Finally, I want to genuinely applaud Google for controlling the update process, like it did with Chromebooks before, rather than allowing OEMs to do so. Manufacturer customization is limited to preloaded OEM apps, like Acer’s that provides product registration, warranty information, and system stats. 

Chrome

Under-the-hood, Chrome on Googlebooks is built upon the Android version. Functionality added to the mobile browser includes extensions support, vertical tabs, and the full Gemini in Chrome side panel.

The browser delivers desktop-class performance that has not caused any website compatibility issues for me this past week.

However, the page reloads you’re familiar with on phones are definitely on our 16GB Googlebooks. There are also annoyances like Chrome Settings opening as a fullscreen interface that replaces all your other browser windows. Another is how right-click desktop menu items you expect are not available. Opening a new window (including Incognito) also won’t let you type until you tap the URL bar, unlike Chrome on every other desktop platform. For this initial release, Google did not port over all functionality and the result is an experience that feels barebones.

The browser is fine for 1.0, but I very much want Google to bring over all desktop functionality and every behavior — no matter how small — to this version. Chrome is truly a constant in most people’s desktop computing history and there is so much muscle memory built over years of use that any regression feels painful.

AI

Magic Pointer is fine and basically the Gemini overlay on phones. The cursor “wiggle” gesture is fundamentally intuitive, while the persistent shortcut in the top right lets you start it without the shake. I would not mind the ability to disable the corner icon from a visual standpoint.

That said, in what feels like a prime example of shipping your org chart, both Magic Pointer and Circle to Search are available on Googlebooks. The latter, invoked by G + A, is billed as Contextual Search and arguably convenient for OCR copying, while Magic Pointer is more for taking action on information. However, it feels wild for there to be two similar features in the OS.

On Googlebook, Gemini is powered by the Google (Search) app, with the large-screen interface looking quite nice. My preferred way of accessing it is via the actual Gemini overlay, launched using G + Space bar.

The obvious and more useful AI feature is Rambler. I’ve never really used voice dictation on a desktop until Googlebook OS. It’s surprisingly hard to remember that it’s available given the full hardware keyboard in front of you, but the F13 key that starts voice input helps.

The less apparent feature is Create My Widget. Generative UI where you specify what information you want to see is the future of computing. Google is starting with a friendly widget creator that gets the point across. I’ve been using this to keep track of how the Dodgers and Yankees are progressing through the playoffs, while a flight countdown is another widget of mine. 

Apps

From life to work, I can get everything I need done in a web browser. My MacBook Air is a glorified Chromebook in that regard. 

I’ve resized most of the native Android apps I frequently use to a phone-sized window. It makes for an even more familiar experience and lets me fit more onto each screen. That said, most of Google’s large-screen layouts are pretty good at this point. 

All the Google Workspace “apps” installed on Googlebooks are Trusted Web Activities (TWAs). These are essentially Progressive Web Apps (PWAs), but support homescreen widgets. For example, Google Calendar opens calendar.google.com in a window, but you can add the schedule widget you’re familiar with from your phone.

I think Googlebooks would have been an excellent opportunity to mandate that Gmail for Android and other Workspace apps have full feature parity with their web versions, but Google’s strategy of letting developers choose whether to use the web or Android is the right call to boost adoption and support. I have not felt the need to change any of the Workspace TWAs to the Android version.

Google Keep and Tasks use their Android versions, which are better than keep.google.com and tasks.google.com, respectively. I wrote most of this review on Keep for Android.

When I reviewed the Pixel Tablet in 2023, one of my complaints was that its Google Messages app was essentially just messages.google.com/web. That has frustratingly not changed on Googlebooks. Google desperately needs to offer a native experience that would ideally just be the large-screen interface found on foldables with a sync system. 

Other Android apps I’ve been using include Pixel Weather, Recorder, and Journal (marking the first time I’ve journaled with a full-size keyboard). As a Pixel user, I’m immensely glad that these three experiences are available on Googlebooks. 

On the media front, YouTube and YouTube Music both open their websites rather than the Android apps. I’m enjoying Apple Music’s in-beta Liquid Glass redesign for the tablet interface. It’s basically the iPad app with top tabs and a floating Now Playing bar.

A big annoyance I immediately noticed in Android apps is that the primary text field is often not active and requires a tap/click. This is so annoying that I’ve found myself tapping the touchscreen rather than using the trackpad. It’s almost second nature. The issue is particularly pronounced in the Gemini app, though a new Chrome tab always selects the address bar.

In terms of native apps:

The Files app is carried over from ChromeOS with a nice, modern icon. AI file summaries that are generated locally are pretty convenient when quickly browsing.

The Text app is code-oriented with a modern Material 3 Expressive design.

The Viewer app is basic compared to macOS Preview.

The “My Googlebook” app is strangely responsible for an “Up next” widget that shows data from Google Calendar, Drive, and Keep.

Of course, there’s also the elephant in the room. For the most part, Googlebooks haven’t fixed the app gap that Chromebooks have faced for over a decade. While there have been some expansions and Android as a whole delivers more of a foundation for desktop-class apps than ChromeOS did, Google hasn’t made the partnerships or the push to actually fix the problem. Those who, like me, can already do most things from a browser will be happy, but demanding that users adopt a new platform in 2026 without staples of the desktop ecosystem — Adobe’s suite sticks out like a sore thumb — is a tough ask.

Hardware 

I’ve been using Googlebook OS full-time this past week across the Acer Googlebook 14 and HP Googlebook 14.

On the lid, the primary branding is the manufacturer’s logo followed by the Glowbar. Once open, there’s a logo beneath the screen and “Googlebook” on the left palm rest. 

The Glowbar is additive, with the battery indicator proving useful when plugging in to charge. However, I would have liked a double-tap/knock gesture to invoke it at any time to see the charge level. In public, having a strip of light facing the world feels somewhat loud. Fortunately, you can turn it off in Settings.

Face unlock has worked as expected on the HP Googlebook 14. The setup experience is identical to what’s found on Pixel phones, and I wonder if the exact same recognition algorithms are leveraged. 

This could be an edge case tied to how I use “Tap to click,” but the trackpad might be too wide on the HP as I keep unintentionally activating it with the sides of my thumbs when typing. Most times the cursor just briefly appears and then disappears. However, there are occasions when moving a hand to reach the number row registers a tap and very disruptively moves my position on the page. Disabling the option, and thus getting the benefit of the haptic trackpad, negates the latter annoyance.

For being a 2-in-1, the Acer Googlebook 14 is incredibly light with a fairly solid build. USI stylus support is nice, especially on such a large canvas.

Between Acer’s Intel chip and Snapdragon on the HP, I have to give the clear advantage to ARM. I’d say the latter runs a bit smoother, while I’ve seen fewer webpage reloads as well when over a dozen tabs/windows and several Android apps are open. 

We’ll be reviewing all five Googlebooks in the coming weeks, so stay tuned to 9to5Google.

Conclusion

	

In going all-in on Googlebook OS for the past eight days, it’s clear that Google put the work in to design a native desktop experience for Android. My biggest fear in the lead-up to using Googlebooks was that the company just stretched out Android as seen on the Pixel Tablet and the Android (16+) desktop mode. That is not the case, with a number of well-thought-out power user features and customizations.

The switch from Chromebooks to Googlebooks gives Google a solid foundation to grow. But, at the same time, it’s hard to ignore that Googlebook OS on day one has taken some clear steps back from ChromeOS. A handful of issues are expected in a strategy reset like this, but missing features (e.g., Linux app support) and other shortcomings are hard to accept when this is Google’s replacement for an OS that’s been around for over a decade now. There are no fatal flaws for the general user, but there are plenty of “death by a thousand cuts” examples that will keep even Chromebook switchers away from Googlebooks for the time being. That said, I don’t think Googlebook OS has any foundational issues that can’t be remedied in future updates.

I think I’m fairly representative of the average user in that everything I use has web-based equivalents. As such, I can use Googlebook OS for everything I do on macOS. However, the Mac has a level of system polish that I appreciate and some native applications that upgrade the workflows I have. This is my barrier to switching. 

That polish and charm are not fully there yet on Googlebook OS, but there are a number of good UI and UX ideas here. The familiarity offered by sharing the Android OS and apps from your phone is a real competitive advantage. If you know how to use an Android phone, the jump to a Googlebook will be immediate. Personally, that similarity is motivating me to add a Googlebook to my daily driver lineup. Google just needs to continue iterating and updating quickly.

title: Meta’s Audio-Only Glasses Are Nicely Made. They Don’t Solve the Deeper Problems
snippet: Meta Ray-Ban Audio glasses are sleek and offer long battery life, but where will their AI go next?
fullText:
I’ve started feeling self-conscious when I wear camera-equipped smart glasses out and about. It’s not hard to imagine why. Public opinion of smart glasses seems lower than it’s ever, driven by a combination of AI fatigue, privacy concerns and a general lack of awareness of what smart glasses can do or why anyone would want to wear them. Some places are also starting to ban them.

Meta’s addressed one concern, at least, with its new camera-free line of Ray-Ban smart glasses. Getting rid of the camera completely on the Meta Ray-Ban Audio means they’re smaller and lighter, and have better battery life, too. But they’re not as cheap as I’d have expected. The two models that are available starting this week, the Clubmaster and Burbank, run from $349 to $429 — just for the frames, depending on whether they have transitions lenses or not. Meta has more affordable self-branded smart glasses staring at $249, but those have cameras onboard.

		

			

I’m not sure why Meta didn’t make self-branded, camera-free glasses, too, which could have helped bring the cost down. I’m sure those are coming in the future, but in the meantime, skipping the camera seems to be more about design, privacy and extending audio battery life.

Are they a worthwhile addition to Meta’s lineup? Here’s what I think of them so far.

They look absolutely normal and feel good: Meta’s glasses design has come a long way.Scott Stein/CNET

Wearing them: Lighter, for sure

I’ve been wearing a pair of the Clubmaster glasses, but without my prescription. That means perching them over my regular glasses or wearing them around the house without being able to see much. After all, the main thing that’s “new” here is the lack of a camera.

These glasses are definitely lighter and easier to wear, and the arms are a little smaller. They weigh between 43 and 47 grams, compared with a little over 50 grams for other Meta Ray-Bans. The front of the frames is a lot smaller on the Clubmaster model, but the half-metal design isn’t exactly my style.

Meta says battery life for constant audio playback is around six hours, a couple of hours more than the four I get from my Meta Ray-Ban Gen 2 and Scriber Optics glasses. For general wear, Meta gives the fuzzier estimate of “up to 12 hours,” versus eight hours for the others, which is harder to map out. Not using the glasses’ audio obviously makes the battery last longer.

The glasses work the same as other Meta smart glasses, with a touchpad on the right arm for tapping to start or stop playback and swiping to control the volume. I still activate it accidentally too often. A button on top activates Meta AI or can be set to launch music.

Audio is your only input and output with the Ray-Ban Audio glasses. Microphones and speakers are onboard.Scott Stein/CNET

What you can do with them

Now, what would I use these for? I already find the audio quality on Meta’s latest glasses surprisingly good, and the microphones are excellent for phone calls. The audio seems a bit louder on the Clubmaster model, although the overall quality is similar. It’s still prone to being washed out in noisy areas because of the open design, which angles the speaker audio from the temples.

Obviously, I’m not taking any photos with these. That also means the glasses can’t perform any visually aware AI tricks or provide visual assistance.

Beyond music, phone calls and anything else you’d use headphones for, Meta AI is the necessary conduit for everything these glasses can do. They still need to be paired with the Meta AI phone app, too.

Meta’s FDA-cleared hearing enhancement mode, which lets the glasses function as a type of hearing aid for mild hearing loss, costs an extra $149 or comes with a Meta One subscription. I tried the technology as best I could at Meta’s developer conference last month, but I still don’t know how well it’ll compare with hearing assistance options such as Apple’s AirPods Pro. The audio glasses should, however, support hearing enhancement for longer on a single charge.

Meta Ray-Ban Audio glasses on top of Ray-Ban Scriber Optics. One pair has a camera; the other doesn’t.Scott Stein/CNET

Why now?

Meta was clearly working on camera-free glasses before this year’s wave of backlash against its camera-enabled eyewear, though concerns about wearing camera-equipped glasses in public have been bubbling for a while.

But I also wonder what these particular models mean for Meta — and for its eyewear partner, EssilorLuxottica. The company has tons of eyewear stores worldwide and already makes a pair of assistance-focused audio glasses called Nuance.

The fact that these glasses are Ray-Ban branded rather than Meta branded lingers in my mind. I think they’re part of Essilor’s expanding range of more acceptable smart eyewear and likely aimed at customers who only want audio assistance.

But they feel a bit removed from the rest of Meta’s future-forward vision, which also includes display-equipped glasses and wearable neural bands. It could open up a path to display-enabled, camera-free glasses in Meta’s future lineup. It’s also likely an effort by Meta to find more acceptable ways to bring its AI to people’s faces, with or without cameras.

The charging case can rapid-charge the glasses much like other Meta glasses models, and it protects them nicely.Scott Stein/CNET

You’re still locked into Meta AI

Meta’s current Muse Spark-based AI on the glasses responds quickly and can provide live language translation and turn-by-turn navigation, set timers and serve as a general conversational research companion. But Meta’s support for connecting other services remains limited, and the privacy improvements promised for the company’s AI services in September haven’t arrived yet.

Fully agentic Muse AI is arriving on Meta’s glasses in the next year, but it’s unclear when. Muse already has an entire connected ecosystem of services, many of which require connecting other accounts to it. Some of Meta’s higher-powered AI models are now requiring extra subscription costs.

What this all means for Meta’s AI glasses over the next year is still a little unclear. They’ll increasingly become tools for tapping into those agents, perhaps to do work or monitor parts of your life. Currently, I don’t use Meta AI for much beyond short conversations about things I want to know on the fly.

Will Meta also explore always-recording “audio memories” in the future, capturing or summarizing conversations as companies like Apple and many others are already doing or promising? And if so, how will that be handled?

What I guess this means is that camera-free Meta glasses could gain acceptance in places where camera-enabled glasses are increasingly being banned. They could also offer a more reassuring option for people who want audio AI glasses but don’t want cameras. Still, most of the glasses Meta sells have cameras, and its AI is advancing so quickly that the shape of future smart glasses could change just as rapidly. They’re solid as wearable audio, but with Google’s glasses and a host of other audio glasses on their way in the next year, Ray-Bans are far from your only option.

title: Here’s how much it costs to repair the new Apple HomeView
snippet: Apple has published the estimated service costs for its new HomeView smart home display, including how much customers can expect to pay with and without AppleCare coverage. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple has published the estimated service costs for its new HomeView smart home display, including how much customers can expect to pay with and without AppleCare coverage. Here are the details.

Out-of-warranty repairs could cost nearly as much as a new unit

Apple unveiled the HomeView today, a 7-inch smart display that is currently available for pre-order, with shipments beginning November 13.

Users can choose between two models: Apple HomeView and Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted). Both cost $299, but the wall-mounted model doesn’t come with a wall mount or power adapter. Those need to be purchased separately.

The standard HomeView, meanwhile, comes attached to a base with a more powerful built-in speaker system.

Following the announcement, Apple has now published the service and repair costs for the devices, both with and without AppleCare coverage.

According to Apple, the estimated service cost for either model is $279, listed under a single category: “Other damage.” There’s currently no breakdown for specific issues, such as a cracked screen or a faulty speaker on the standard model, suggesting that Apple may replace entire units rather than repair individual components.

Apple HomeView service costs withouh AppleCare on the left, with AppleCare on the right

Similarly, for units covered by AppleCare, the accidental damage service fee is currently listed at $39, regardless of whether the device is the standard or wall-mounted model, or the type of accidental damage. For AppleCare+ subscribers, HomeView coverage is available for $2.49 monthly, or $24.99 annually.

It’s worth noting that Apple hasn’t confirmed whether these fees cover full-unit replacements or repairs to individual components.

We’ll keep an eye out for any updates to Apple’s service and repair pricing, including whether the company adds more specific repair categories or fees.

title: Cerebras CEO pushes back on AI doomsday warnings
snippet: Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman has a message for AI leaders spreading doomsday warnings: Maybe stop talking? At TechCrunch Disrupt, he argued that the industry's focus on AI's risks is drowning out its potential benefits.
fullText:
Cerebras Systems CEO and co-founder Andrew Feldman thinks the AI doomer narrative isn’t doing the industry any favors. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, the AI chipmaker exec quipped that “some of the leaders in the AI world maybe shouldn’t be allowed to talk in public.”

He’s referencing the negativity now spreading around the dangers of AI, from models breaking containment to AI insiders debating the percentage chance that AI may kill all of humanity by the end of the decade. The argument has become so mainstream that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was recently parodied in a skit on “Saturday Night Live,” where the fictional character summed up the discourse, saying, “We do not condone what we are doing.”

Feldman, however, thinks the promise and potential that go hand in hand with AI developments are getting overlooked. He thinks AI leaders should spend more time telling people that AI could lead to a world where your grandkids will “never meet anybody who dies of cancer,” for instance, even if they have concerns about AI risks.

Clearly, Feldman has a vested interest in AI being successful, as the company’s customers include big names working with the technology, like OpenAI, Block, Figma, pharmaceutical giant GSK, and Lovable.

However, he’s pragmatic about weighing the trade-offs between risk and reward.

“I don’t think there are powerful technologies that don’t come with the challenge of ‘what happens when powerful technologies are in the hands of bad people?’ I think you can’t make one and not have the other,” Feldman said during his interview at Disrupt.

“I think what we have to say is that this technology is powerful,” he added. “We have to be thoughtful about it. We have to regulate it reasonably,” he added.

The chipmaker CEO also suggested that some of the negativity around AI has to do with how the data center industry has approached the new buildouts created by AI demand.

“As an industry, we weren’t super good for the past few years at working with local communities, particularly in the U.S. We — the industry — didn’t do what others have done in the power industry in oil and gas. They didn’t work with the community. They didn’t engage the community as they should have, and that was a problem,” Feldman said.

He compared the NIMBY-ism — “not in my backyard!” — of what’s going on in the U.S. with other countries, naming Brazil, Canada, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Mexico, and Sweden as markets where they’re encouraging companies to build data centers.

Feldman also wasn’t concerned that efficiency improvements would create less demand for his chips, or those from other companies competing with Nvidia, as Cerebras is. 

“We can do our job as hardware vendors to make our compute more efficient, and then the model makers can do improved work in making their models more efficient to achieve the same goals. All of this has to come together to make meaningful strides forward,” he noted.

title: Samsung Smart Glasses Unveiled, and They’re Superlight
snippet: They might be called Galaxy Glasses, and they’re coming in November.
fullText:
Samsung won’t unveil its first smart glasses until November, but now we know what they will look like — and how light they will be. They’ll come in a variety of styles and colors and weigh only 41 grams, according to a report from tech news outlet SammyGuru.

Samsung is expected to launch the smart glasses, possibly called Galaxy Glasses, next month. They will compete in the marketplace against Meta’s Ray-Bans and AI glasses from Apple, which reportedly won’t arrive until next year. XREAL reportedly will launch its Aura glasses sometime this fall.

In November, US customers can buy the Samsung smart glasses at the Warby Parker website and Gentle Monster website, and also at Samsung Experience Stores in the US. No prices have been announced, according to the report.

			

More from CNET

Samsung’s glasses will include six styles from South Korean eyewear brand Gentle Monster, which partnered with Huawei several years ago for audio smart glasses, and three styles from US brand Warby Parker, SammyGuru said.

The new Samsung smart glasses will have six styles from Gentle Monster.SammyGuru

There will be six frame shapes from Gentle Monster — squared, rounder, bolder square, cat-eye, slim oval and regular oval. The various lens colors include clear, light blue, gray, brown, black, light gray, pale lilac, burgundy and cream, according to SammyGuru.

Two of the Warby Parker styles, Alden and Wren, will include colors pine, dark green and reddish-brown Saddle. Reid is offered in Jet Black, the report said.

Only 41 grams in weight

The new Samsung smart glasses will weigh 41 grams with standard lenses, lighter than the 43 grams for the lightest Meta Ray-Ban model, according to the leak. They’ll include a Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 chip, 2 GB of RAM, 64 GB of storage, a 12 MP camera, 3K video at 30 frames per second, two open-ear speakers and four microphones. The battery can last up to 9 hours or up to 72 hours if also using the charging case.

The glasses are similar to Meta Ray-Bans in that there is no visual display for text messages. You’ll compose them by speaking into the microphones and hear them via the speakers.

Read more: Samsung Promises Stronger, Better Smart Glasses. But What About Privacy?

Users will need Galaxy S, Z Fold or Z Flip phones running One UI 9 or later to use Galaxy-specific features with the glasses. To use the watch features, users will need a Galaxy Watch running on Wear OS 7 or newer.

What can the glasses do?

Samsung’s smart glasses will use Google Gemini AI and run on the Android XR operating system. People wearing them will be able to perform various tasks with the AI, including taking pictures and videos, making calls and sending texts, translating, getting turn-by-turn navigation and listening to songs and podcasts.

Fast-growing market

The demand for smart glasses is rapidly growing worldwide. Sales in the US doubled over the past year, with global shipments topping 4.2 million, according to research firm Omdia. Another analysis estimates that the global market for smart glasses will grow by more than 24% yearly until 2033.

Smart glasses manufacturers are focusing on “hands-free photo and video capture, open-ear audio and AI assistance within everyday frames,” Omdia analyst Qiran Ju said in a recent report.

title: Apple’s $299 HomeView Is Ready to Take Over Your Countertops and Walls
snippet: Apple’s new smart display and speaker marks the company’s Siri AI-ification of your home. Preorders are open now.
fullText:
Apple has welcomed an entirely new product type to its ever-growing family of devices. The company unveiled the HomeView smart speaker at its Welcome Home event in New York on Tuesday — a long-rumored addition that looks like a hybrid between a HomePod and a giant Apple Watch.

The HomeView’s square screen is a 7-inch Liquid Retina display, making it quite unobstrusive. In spite of its diminutive size, this bold design choice will set Apple’s smart speaker apart from most rivals on the market, such as the Amazon Echo Show, which tend to have rectangular landscape screens.

On the front of the HomeView, a 12-megapixel camera uses Apple’s Center Stage technology — a zoom feature designed for video chatting, which you might be familiar with from its iPad lineup. Inside the display, two full-range drivers will help deliver room-filling Spatial Audio. The device is powered by Apple’s homegrown A18 chip — the same silicon inside the iPhone 16 Series and the MacBook Neo.

			

More from CNET

Apple’s home hub functions as a central portal for entertainment, connection and controlling your smart home devices, but also for interacting with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. This builds on the Siri AI revamp that Apple announced back at WWDC in June, which saw the company introduce a more capable, conversational voice assistant that matches up-to-date AI smarts with the company’s privacy and security standards.

“It is little surprise that the HomeView coincides with Apple’s renewed push on Siri AI and Apple Intelligence,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at FDM CCS, speaking from the company’s New York event. “The company has undoubtedly been waiting for the upgraded Siri experience, given how important the voice interactions are with this product.”

The HomeView will tap into information from your personal apps.Apple

Unlike most Apple devices, which are either designed completely for personal use (the iPhone or the Apple Watch) or designed to be shared by everyone in the home (the Apple TV or HomePods), the HomeView straddles both worlds. “Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user,” said Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing in a press release. If you don’t already use them, it sounds like it might be time to tap into shared photo albums and shared Apple Music playlists in order to make the most of the HomeView.

Apple’s HomeView will recognize your family members using built-in facial recognition, and will allow you all to check your personal content in Messages, FaceTime, Calendar, Reminders and Find My. Furthermore, when paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled device, HomeView will draw on your personal context to provide personalized answers to any questions you might ask.

Your HomeView device can either sit on your tabletop or be mounted to a wall, depending on your preference. One thing to note is that you have to decide this when you buy — either you pick the wall-mounted option or one with a domed speaker base attached. If you opt for the wall-mounted version, it can be attached using three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home, with the option to install it yourself or have a professional do it for you.

Apple

A collection of playful and informative faces is available — some with your personal photos, others with an animated Snoopy. These faces respond dynamically to your physical and presence and movement, which sounds like a fun feature for a kitchen dance party. The idea is true personalization — whether you want interactive art, a functional interface or something in between.

Customers in the US, Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand and the UK can preorder the HomeView right now for $299, with devices available from Nov. 13. It comes in silver, starlight, rose pink and space gray, so there’s bound to be at least one option that will fit your home decor scheme.

title: Facebook is giving users more control over their algorithm
snippet: Meta announced the launch of its new AI-powered feature, “Your Algorithm,” a feature it first launched on Instagram.
fullText:
Image Credits:Facebook	

	

						

11:05 AM PDT · October 13, 2026

											

			

Facebook is the latest social media platform to give users greater control over the algorithm that determines what appears in their feeds. 

Meta announced the launch of its new AI-powered feature, “Your Algorithm,” on Tuesday, a feature it first launched on Instagram. The new tool allows Facebook users to influence the content they see in Feed and Reels by describing their preferences in their own words using natural language. Rather than relying entirely on automated recommendations, users can now communicate directly with the platform about the topics and content they want to see more or less frequently.

According to Meta, the feature is designed to make content recommendations more relevant. Users can adjust their preferences and interact with the algorithms responsible for ranking and recommending posts, with changes reflected in their recommendations in real time.

The company has also updated Facebook’s three-dot menu, making it easier for users to manage their content preferences directly from individual posts. By opening the menu, users can access “Your Algorithm” or select the “Interested” and “Not interested” options to indicate whether particular content aligns with their preferences. 

Meta says the platform may ask follow-up questions to better understand what users liked or disliked, allowing them to provide more detailed feedback. Users can explain what they want to see more or less of, helping Facebook refine its recommendations based on their responses.

Image Credits:Facebook

The introduction of “Your Algorithm” reflects Meta’s broader effort to give people more influence over their social media experiences as AI increasingly shapes content discovery. The move signals a shift away from the traditional recommendation systems that have shaped social media experiences for years, bringing the platform closer to streaming services that allow users to personalize recommendations based on their interests and preferences.

The launch also builds on Meta’s existing personalization efforts across its other platforms. Instagram introduced Your Algorithm in June, extending customization options across Feed and Explore after first launching the feature for Reels in December 2025. 

Threads also introduced its own related feature, called “Dear Algo,” which allows users to influence the content recommended to them.

title: Apple TV 4K Gains Onboard Mics and Better Processor, but Whoa, That Price
snippet: The fourth-gen Apple TV 4K is now three times the price of Roku’s top streamer.
fullText:
Apple has unveiled its latest streaming box, the Apple TV 4K (fourth generation), which has a faster processor and onboard microphones for better integration with Siri AI. It’s coming in November for $299.

The new Apple TV has an updated A19 chip, which Apple says is 50% faster than the existing A15 processor and has twice the graphics performance. The TV 4K boasts 128GB of storage space which is the same as the previous flagship.  

The new set-top box has three onboard far-field microphones for conversing with Siri, as well as a familiar-looking remote with a traditional microphone button. The remote also includes Find My with Precision Finding if it gets lost behind the cushions.

			

More from CNET

The Apple TV 4K (fourth generation) and remote will be available in November for $299.

Connectivity includes:

Bluetooth 6

Wi‑Fi 7

HDMI 2.1

Gigabit Ethernet

All of the relevant formats are included, such as Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision and HDR10 Plus. You can now also create a four-speaker surround system by pairing the Apple TV 4K (fourth generation) and the new HomePod Mini 2. 

At $299, though, the Apple TV is more expensive than every other premium streaming box on the market. For instance, it’s $200 more than the Roku Ultra and the (seemingly discontinued) Google TV. The outgoing Apple TV 4K (2022) recently had a price hike of its own, with the entry-level model leaping from $129 to $199, and the company blamed the increase on an electronics shortage also known as RAMageddon.

While it’s the most expensive streamer, the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K is also likely to be capable, especially if you’re a gamer. The outgoing TV 4K was great for streaming games via Steam Link or Xbox Remote Play, and the new box should be even better. For everyone else, who simply want to watch TV, a $50 streamer from Amazon or Roku should do just fine.

The new Apple TV 4K is available now for preorder at Apple’s website. It’s due in stores on Nov. 13.

title: Samsung is now rolling out Android 17 to these older Galaxy devices in the US
snippet: Samsung’s One UI 9 update is now available for the Galaxy S24 and Z Fold/Flip 6, a month after the official rollout was initiated. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s One UI 9 update is now available for the Galaxy S24 and Z Fold/Flip 6, a month after the official rollout was initiated.

Samsung announced that One UI 9 is officially rolling out to devices that didn’t launch with it preloaded – i.e., the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra.

That means the Galaxy S24 series, Galaxy Z Fold 6, and Galaxy Z Flip 6 are the next to get Android 17 (via SamMobile). Of course, the rollout includes all three Galaxy S24 models. The update should appear in the settings app on those devices as a standard download.

For the time being, the update appears to be available in South Korea and the US, though it’s expected that more regions will follow within the next few days.

	

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Flip 8 were the first to get One UI 9 because Samsung switched up its update schedule a year ago. A month ago, the Galaxy S26 was given access to the new One UI 9, based on Android 17.

The update has been trickling down Samsung’s Galaxy S lineups ever since. Since the Galaxy S24 and Galaxy Z Fold 6 are just getting One UI 9, it’s expected that the Galaxy S25 and Galaxy Z Fold 5 aren’t far behind. Samsung has not updated those devices just yet.

One UI 9 includes a few notable changes, including:

My FanCam: Automatic video tracking & reframing of a subject

title: The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is almost the Android tablet we needed
snippet: The screen looks good no matter what’s on it. Star Wars helps, though. | Photo: David Pierce / The Verge We have to talk about this screen. It's the first thing you notice, and maybe the only thing that matters, about the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. It's a 12-inch, 2800 x 1840 panel with a new technology Amazon calls "Nanomatte" that is meant to decrease glare and increase the feeling that you can reach out and touch the things you see onscreen. When Amazon set out to build the best tablet the company has ever shipped, it started with this screen. The $549.99 device I've been testing is one of four new models in the Alexa Tablet lineup, which ranges from a $229.99 8-inch model up to a $679.99 12 Pro with this Nanomatte coating and some extra RAM you … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
We have to talk about this screen. It’s the first thing you notice, and maybe the only thing that matters, about the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. It’s a 12-inch, 2800 x 1840 panel with a new technology Amazon calls “Nanomatte” that is meant to decrease glare and increase the feeling that you can reach out and touch the things you see onscreen. When Amazon set out to build the best tablet the company has ever shipped, it started with this screen.

The $549.99 device I’ve been testing is one of four new models in the Alexa Tablet lineup, which ranges from a $229.99 8-inch model up to a $679.99 12 Pro with this Nanomatte coating and some extra RAM you don’t really need. The pitch for all those devices is the same: They’re well-made, midrange tablets that can access the full universe of Android apps through the Play Store and come with a whole bunch of Amazon bloatware whether you want it or not. I haven’t tested those other devices, but I’m glad they exist — cheap, good Android tablets are too hard to come by.

6

Verge Score

$550

The Good

Screen is gorgeous

Android apps!

Nice design and build quality

The Bad

Amazon bloatware everywhere

Alexa Plus isn’t great

Some middling specs

But the Nanomatte. The Nanomatte! The etching on the display, which Amazon says it partnered with Corning to do at a sub-pixel level to reduce glare without causing the slight rainbow-shimmering effect you can get on other matte screens, absolutely does its job. When I use my iPad outdoors, I can often see what’s behind me like I’m staring into a mirror; the 12 Pro reflects only a small sheen of light, and does it without losing any sharpness. The viewing angles are incredible, too. I’d like the display to be a little brighter, but since the main reason to crank the brightness is to fight glare, it hasn’t really been a problem.

The screen is not perfect. The anti-glare texture gives the Alexa Tablet a bit of shimmer, especially when you’re looking at light text on a black background. And the iPad’s blacks are still blacker; watching a movie, the letterboxes above and below are still slightly lit on the Alexa Tablet’s LCD, and they’re just flat-out off on the iPad’s OLED panel. Some of this you can fix: The 12 Pro has specific modes that automatically tweak tone and color to make reading more pleasant, and you can even control the overall picture through a few presets like the ones you’d find on your TV. My review unit came with “Boosted” mode turned on, which made every color just a smidge too colorful. I turned it to “Natural” and immediately liked the picture better.

I’m not sure this screen counts as some revolution in display technology, but then again, I did reflexively say “whoa” the first second I turned it on, and all that was showing was the Amazon logo. I like this display for everything. The 120Hz refresh rate looks great when running Star Wars: Galactic Racer, and the 3:2 aspect ratio feels right for web browsing and side-by-side work. The more muted display modes even make reading more pleasant than your average giant screen, though it’s lame that they only work in the Kindle app. After a few days of using the tablet indoors and out, I prefer the 12 Pro’s screen to any iPad I’ve tried. (Unfortunately, I don’t have an iPad Pro with the nano-texture glass to compare it to, but that’s a $2,200 tablet. I doubt anyone’s debating between the two.)

All that display tech in a $549.99 device requires tradeoffs basically everywhere else, and Amazon makes lots of them. The MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor benchmarks somewhere between a flagship high-end Android phone from last year and a flagship phone from two years ago, and gets absolutely lapped by practically every current iPad. In one graphics-heavy benchmark, the current 13-inch iPad Pro scored about nine times higher.

I’d like more horsepower here, but in my day-to-day use there’s plenty of power in this tablet. In several days of playing games, doing work, and watching a lot of NFL RedZone, the only slowness I’ve detected has been little niggling things in the Android experience. The app switcher sometimes stutters when it loads. I suppose I worry a little about how this tablet will age, given that it doesn’t share the iPad’s preposterous oversupply of processing power, but for now it’s fine.

Come to think of it, “it’s fine” explains most of the 12 Pro’s hardware. The four speakers are a little thin and muddy, but loud and clear enough. The cameras wash out some colors, but they work for video calls. The $149.99 keyboard case is nice to type on, but a little awkward to detach and manipulate. The $89.99 pen is smooth and responsive, but not many Android apps support a stylus. The battery lasts me about eight hours of screen time, which is a little less than I’d like and less than Amazon advertises. Nothing here is a deal-breaker, it’s just a lot of fine.

The software, on the other hand, is all extremes. The great news: The Alexa Tablets run full Android, not the weird off-brand operating system Amazon’s Fire tablets have used for the last 15 years. That means you get all the apps in the Play Store, a vastly improved interface, and access to things like Google’s Gemini assistant. All by itself, that change makes these the most functional Amazon tablets ever.

Unfortunately, Amazon did to Android exactly what you’d fear — and maybe expect. It Amazon-ed the crap out of things. I’m fine with the slide-over panel to the left of the homescreen filled with content recommendations; the overlap of Alexa Tablet owners and Prime subscribers / Kindle readers is probably pretty high, and at least that screen isn’t staring you in the face every time you unlock your tablet. I can even live with Amazon preloading its own browser, photos, and music apps, none of which are better than their competition. But it is frankly outrageous that Amazon thinks it can get away with adding two separate, non-removable homescreen widgets that serve no purpose other than advertising Amazon’s products.

If you’re going to say you “obsess over customers,” you don’t get to borrow the top left corner of my homescreen and then use that space to show me an ad vaguely offering to “Cook with premium ingredients” that launches an also unhideable Alexa chat window in the bottom right corner of my homescreen.

Luckily, this is Android, and installing a new launcher takes 30 seconds. If you buy an Alexa Tablet, I recommend doing so immediately.

I would be less annoyed by Alexa’s overbearing presence on this tablet if Alexa Plus were actually useful, which it mostly is not. If you’re looking to buy whatever’s on your screen, Alexa’s your bot: You can invoke the assistant in any app, and it’ll almost always assume your goal is to shop for whatever you’re currently looking at. If you want, well, anything else, you’re probably out of luck. Almost a year after its launch, Alexa Plus is not a very good assistant. It’s slow, it gets lost in back-and-forth conversations, and it still doesn’t have enough access to my apps and data to be useful. You can switch to Gemini in the device’s settings, and you should.

Once you de-Amazon the tablet, you’re left with a pretty useful Android device. And this is where the Alexa Tablet gets tricky to evaluate. I wouldn’t recommend using it as a primary computer, given the still sorry state of large-screen Android apps. (Between this and the ongoing Googlebook fiasco, I really hope Google is learning a lesson about incentivizing developers to care about big screens and keyboards.) But between the Kindle-specific display mode, all the streaming and reading apps in the Play Store, and this terrific screen, this is immediately one of the best tablets-for-tablet-things you can buy.

Realistically, you’re probably debating whether to buy the Alexa Tablet or an iPad. (Apologies to the Samsung Galaxy Tab shoppers out there, but this one’s a way better buy for almost everybody.) For the same $550 you’ll drop on the 12 Pro, you can get a base-model iPad with 256GB of storage. I’d probably tell you to buy the iPad; it has much better tablet software and much better big-screen apps, and Apple has a much better track record in tablets.

And yet for the last few days, I’ve had an iPad and an Alexa Tablet sitting on my desk, and every time I want to watch or read something I’ve found myself gravitating to Amazon’s device. It is really nice to look at.

title: Report: HomePod mini 2 to release on October 30 with these upgrades
snippet: In just a couple days, Apple should be unveiling its long-awaited new lineup of new Home products. That includes an updated HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K, the brand-new smart home hub called ‘HomeView’, as well as a new lineup of smart home accessories, in collaboration with LG. Here’s what to expect with the HomePod mini 2. more…
fullText:
In just a couple days, Apple should be unveiling its long-awaited new lineup of new Home products. That includes an updated HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K, the brand-new smart home hub called ‘HomeView’, as well as a new lineup of smart home accessories, in collaboration with LG. Here’s what to expect with the HomePod mini 2.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the new HomePod mini should equip the S10 chip, up from the current S5 chip. This isn’t quite the latest silicon, but it’s still a massive step-change from the outgoing model.

With the S10 chip, the HomePod mini will be able to offer Siri AI features – a first for any of Apple’s Home products. It’ll also “extend” your HomeView throughout your house, with voice control and music playback all being able to sync up to your HomeView. Of course, the updated Apple TV and HomeView will also support Siri AI.

The new HomePod mini will come in a fresh array of colors, including pink, green, and blue – on top of the traditional midnight and white.

Outside of the S10 chip, the HomePod mini 2 is expected to offer Apple’s N1 networking chip to serve as a Thread and Matter radio, as well as offering Wi-Fi 7 support. Currently, the HomePod mini only offers Wi-Fi 4.

Pricing and release date

	

While pricing isn’t necessarily clear, it’s worth noting that HomePod mini increased in price from $99 to $129 back in June with Apple’s wave of memory-related price hikes. I personally expect pricing to stay the same, as Apple likely anticipated the upcoming hardware when it set them. Only time will tell, though.

As for release date, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that the second-generation HomePod mini should arrive in stores on October 30th, alongside the new Apple TV 4K. The HomeView, on the other hand, is expected to slip into mid-November. You can read more about the HomeView here.

title: Formlabs Just Announced the First Resin Printer Aimed at Safe Home Use
snippet: Formlabs is bringing its walled garden to home users, which may be a very big deal.
fullText:
Resin printers are very cool, but difficult to recommend for home crafters. When most people think about 3D printers, they think about filament and a printhead that moves around in front of you to create something. Some of this is due to availability and cost, but the biggest reason that kind of printer has become the most popular is safety. Resin printers, which use light to create a 3D shape inside a container of liquid resin, are historically best used in workshops and creative studios over a shelf in your home. Not only is the resin not safe to get on your hands, but most also produce fumes that are not safe to inhale for extended periods of time. As a result, the software driving these machines is generally less user-friendly as it’s not aimed at casual home use.

Today, the team at Formlabs is announcing the Form Studio 1, a $699 resin printer promising a home-friendly user experience and a collection of resins that don’t put off those unhealthy fumes.

	

			

	

			

									

						Form Studio 1					

							

		

Formlabs’ most affordable printer to date is a clear attempt to expand beyond the more industrial settings you would previously find these printers, without sacrificing the things that make other printers from this company stand out. Form Studio uses a backlight system with 28 LEDs with their own lenses to more accurately place light where it’s needed, which is a significant departure from the traditional LCD system seen in most affordable resin printers. The resin itself is loaded into the tank through the unique Formlabs cartridge system, allowing the printer to accurately tell you how much resin is left in the tank as well as allow for cartridge swapping to keep a print going when resin runs low. In terms of print speed, Formlabs promises the Form Studio is capable of printing at 130mm per hour when using its proprietary resin.

			

More from CNET

The real star of the show here, in my opinion, is the resin that is safer to use in your house, as well as the printer accessory that helps it even further. Formlabs’ Alpha Resins carry the UL Greenguard Gold certification for the low-emission quality, and the resin itself gives off very little odor. While a full review from CNET is still underway, I can say from early testing that odors from this printer are practically nonexistent when using the provided resin. When you combine that with the $180 VOC extractor accessory, it paints a clear picture of where this printer is designed to be safely used.

Our first print on the Form Studio 1, with its dedicated resin cartridge

Speaking of accessories, Form Studio has a ton, and they vary quite a bit in price. The flexible build plate and resin tanks are easy to swap in and out, so you can have multiple at the ready to rapidly switch resins in the printer and not have to pour anything back into a bottle. You can also upgrade to a flexible platform that makes getting the print off the plate way easier, as well as a pro-level resin tank for resins with higher curing temperatures. But my personal favorite launch accessory is the combination wash and cure station for resin prints. This combination unit takes up just about the same amount of space as the printer itself, and allows you to quickly clean and cure a resin print without making a mess or complicated drainage needs. It’s also only $200, which is incredible for what you get.

Starting today, Formlabs has opened up orders for what it’s calling the Founders Edition of the Form Studio with a few options. For a limited time, the printer will be available in four colors, with the option to upgrade to the flexible build plate for $750. If you choose to go with the standard edition, you can still grab that $700 price, but the flexible plate really is worth the extra money. Accessories for Form Studio are also available now, including resins for this printer starting at $29 for a one-liter cartridge. And don’t forget to check back, we will be conducting a thorough review of just how home-friendly this printer is soon.

title: Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17
snippet: Samsung is now rolling out its Android 17-based update, One UI 9, to its collection of supported Galaxy smartphones and tablets. Here’s the full list of devices that have been updated so far, and what you should know about the update. more…
fullText:
Samsung is now rolling out its Android 17-based update, One UI 9, to its collection of supported Galaxy smartphones and tablets. Here’s the full list of devices that have been updated so far, and what you should know about the update.

What’s new in Android 17 on Samsung Galaxy?

One UI 9, Samsung’s Android 17 update, continues the trend of evolution more than overhaul. The update introduces some slight design tweaks, more AI-powered features, and other changes built on the redesign that debuted in One UI 7 and was iterated in last year’s Android 16-based One UI 8. 

Some key changes in One UI 9 include:

Warranty & Samsung Care status in the Settings menu

Broader support for Now Nudge

My FanCam automatic video cropping based on a select subject

More Quick Panel (quick settings) customization

AI privacy alerts

Upgrades to Samsung DeX

New lock screen clocks that can adapt to your wallpaper

Samsung Galaxy devices with Android 17 – The full list

While Samsung hasn’t confirmed an exact schedule for its One UI 9 and Android 17 rollout for Galaxy devices, there are updates now rolling out in parts of the globe. Below you’ll find a regularly-updated list of every Samsung Galaxy device that has received a stable Android 17 update so far.

	

Galaxy S devices with Android 17

Galaxy S26

Galaxy S26+

Galaxy S26 Ultra

Galaxy S25 (rolling out more widely)

Galaxy S25+ (rolling out more widely)

Galaxy S25 Ultra (rolling out more widely)

Galaxy S25 FE (limited availability)

Galaxy S25 Edge (limited availability)

Galaxy S24 (limited availability)

Galaxy S24+ (limited availability)

Galaxy S24 Ultra (limited availability)

Galaxy Z devices with Android 17

Galaxy Z Fold 7 (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Flip 7 (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE (limited availability)

Galaxy Z TriFold (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Fold 6 (limited availability)

Galaxy Z Flip 6 (limited availability)

Galaxy A devices with Android 17

Galaxy A57 (limited availability)

Updating…

One UI 9 changelog

Here’s the full changelog from Samsung for One UI 9, as listed for the Galaxy S26 series. Some features may vary by device.

Galaxy AI

Enhanced Now nudge

Now nudge provides helpful suggestions in more places throughout your Galaxy experience. In addition to the keyboard, suggestions will now appear in conversation notifications and in a floating button in the bottom right corner of the screen. There are also several new types of suggestions, like entering reservation details or addresses and saving places in Google Maps.

Focus on someone important

My FanCam lets you select a person in a video and follow them automatically while cropping out the rest of the video.

Interpreter keeps your conversation in front of you

In conversation mode, you can scroll through the whole conversation while you’re still talking.

See useful information during calls

See relevant events and other information related to your current call on the call screen.

Productivity and multitasking

More customizable quick panel

You can now rearrange and customize the controls in your quick panel even more than before. You can change the size of the brightness and volume sliders as well as the media player. You can also separate the sound mode button from the volume slider.

Privacy, security, and device protection

Warranty and care

The new Warranty and care menu in settings lets you check your warranty information and access diagnostic checks and useful information for keeping your Galaxy in top condition.

Lock down your phone quickly

It’s now easier to securely lock your phone in a hurry. Just press and hold the Volume down and Side buttons at the same time or tap the Power button in the quick panel. This prevents biometrics from being used the next time you unlock your phone.

Location access transparency

Stay on top of your location privacy. A blue indicator will appear at the top of the screen when an app accesses your location. Tap the indicator in the quick panel to see which app it is.

Stronger security and privacy protection

Alerts will appear in your Now brief to let you know about risks from malware, apps from unknown sources, unnecessary permissions, and other issues that may put your security and privacy at risk. Apps that have been identified as malicious or vulnerable will be blocked from opening until you make a decision about whether to remove them.

AI privacy alerts

Get help protecting your personal data. AI will monitor how apps use permissions and notify you about unnecessary access to your personal data.

Samsung Health

New look for Samsung Health

Samsung Health has been redesigned to make your health data easier to understand. Enjoy clearer visuals, improved charts, and a more engaging experience to help you reach your health goals.

Customize your Health home screen

Resize cards and organize them by category, like Activity, Sleep, Mindfulness, and Nutrition, so your top priorities are easy to access.

Log health data quickly

It’s now easier to add your health information right from the Samsung Health home screen. You can log your mood, meals, and more. You can even use the camera for faster input.

Advanced trend analysis

Track your progress with improved trend charts in Samsung Health. View data in hourly, daily, or weekly intervals, pinch to zoom in for a closer look, and overlay multiple charts to compare your performance across different periods.

Monitor changes in your sleep vitals

Samsung Health helps you notice meaningful changes in your sleep health data. Use Galaxy Watch or Ring measurements to better understand your daily health patterns.

Manage your heart health

Track key health metrics and lifestyle factors that affect your heart. A daily score based on your sleep, exercise, BMI, and blood pressure helps you better understand your current heart health trends.

Track your cardio load

See how your workouts and activity impact your heart so you’ll know when to push harder and when to rest. Your target cardio load range adjusts daily based on your recent activity and training focus.

Check your fitness index

Your Fitness Index is an overall score calculated using five key fitness metrics: body composition, cardio, strength, flexibility, and endurance. Set a goal and unlock personalized insights tailored to your results.

Keep your ears safe

The new Hearing tracker monitors sound levels detected by your Galaxy Watch and headphone audio levels to help you manage your exposure to loud sounds.

View your cycle and body rhythm

Get a more personalized view of your cycle and body rhythm with new cycle tracking options. You can view your cycle information in your calendar and better understand your health patterns.

Bixby

Activate Bixby with a gesture

Talk to Bixby just by raising your phone close to your mouth and speaking. No wake-up word needed.

Manage your conversations

Keep your chats organized. Search them, rename them, or pin your favorites. You can also delete all of your past conversations at once.

Bixby on the Home screen

Add a Bixby widget to type or talk to Bixby or jump directly to your conversation history.

Accessibility

Discover new Accessibility features

Check the What’s new menu in Accessibility settings to learn about and try the latest Accessibility features for your Galaxy.

Text spotlight for easier reading

Need a closer look? Tap any text on the screen to show it enlarged and highlighted in its own window. You can also customize the font size, colors, and other settings to match your preferences.

Physical keyboard shortcuts

Use shortcuts on your physical keyboard to access the Accessibility settings you need without touching the screen.

Mouse keys enhancements

New options are available when using your keyboard for mouse interactions including speed and acceleration control. You can also use the keyboard’s number pad to point and click.

Replace swipe with single tap

The Replace swipe with single tap option is now located in the Dexterity and interaction menu instead of the Assistant menu for easier access.

Select to speak

Get quick audio readouts without turning on full TalkBack. With the new Select to speak feature, you can select an item on your screen, like text or an image, and hear it read or described out loud.

Improved TalkBack updates

TalkBack updates can now be applied with a simple app update from the Play Store, helping you get the latest accessibility features and enhancements.

Even more improvements

New Lock screen clock

The default clock on your Lock screen has been redesigned with a cleaner and more modern look that adapts to match your wallpaper.

Samsung DeX enhancements

It’s easier to move an app window from one desktop to another using the menu at the top of the window. Desktop previews are now available at the top of the Recents screen, making it easier to switch with a single tap.
