title: Apple gets a $360 price target from JP Morgan despite iPhone demand concerns
snippet: Just days after Apple’s stock took a hit over reports of iPhone 18 Pro production cuts, JP Morgan has raised its AAPL price target by $20. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Just days after Apple’s stock took a hit over reports of iPhone 18 Pro production cuts, JP Morgan has raised its AAPL price target by $20. Here are the details.

iPhone Duo to help offset staggered release window

Last Friday, Nikkei Asia reported that, according to “multiple people familiar with the matter,” Apple had told select suppliers to cut component production for the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max due to “soft demand.”

The report sent Apple shares down roughly 2.5% in early trading, although the stock has recovered much of that loss and closed at $340.97 today.

That said, JP Morgan released a new investor note today (via AppleInsider), arguing that the reported cuts are consistent with Apple’s usual production patterns and don’t necessarily point to an unexpected drop in demand.

The report also comments on Apple’s staggered iPhone launch schedule, with JP Morgan expecting the iPhone Duo to offset the sales shortfall caused by the absence of the regular iPhone 18, which is expected to hit shelves early next year.

Interestingly, earlier today, a separate report from China’s Securities Times claimed that Apple had increased its iPhone Duo orders by 30%, potentially bringing its production for the remainder of 2026 close to 10 million units.

Looking ahead to the December quarter, JP Morgan expects Apple to sell 8.5 million iPhone Duo units. JP Morgan also projects a roughly 2% decline in iPhone revenue year-over-year, but a 2% increase in Apple’s overall revenue.

The firm also continues to flag supply constraints and broader economic pressures that could affect consumer demand.

All in all, JP Morgan raised its AAPL price target from $340 to $360, while maintaining its Overweight rating on the stock.

title: Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case
snippet: A federal judge ruled that Apple can access OpenAI's interview materials involving former Apple employees, as well as private messages and testimony from key figures in the case.
fullText:
A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July.

Specifically, the court will allow Apple to view documents associated with OpenAI’s interviews with former Apple employees who applied for roles within its consumer hardware and robotics groups ahead of the rumored launch of OpenAI’s first hardware device.

These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components.

The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited.

The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers’ lives and how they engage with software and services. 

In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data.

Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations.

U.S. District Judge Edward Davila didn’t greenlight all of Apple’s requests for expedited access to OpenAI documents and messages relevant to the case. But he did rule that Apple could access the interview materials, alongside private LINE messages (from a messaging app) between individuals named in the case, including OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng.

The judge also approved depositions for Liu and Peng, along with a third individual, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer, Tang Yew Tan. All three are former Apple employees.

However, the judge denied Apple’s request to expedite its access to OpenAI’s research and development in specific areas, like metal finishes and power management. He also denied several of Apple’s broader discovery requests, like access to OpenAI’s hardware research or information about what its former employees created while working at OpenAI. 

That denial isn’t final, though; the judge left the door open for Apple to narrow its requests and try again.

snippet: We broke the news this week that a next-gen Google TV Streamer is incoming, but it also arrives as Google’s smart home hardware strategy faces a tough spot and new competition. 9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. fullText:
We broke the news this week that a next-gen Google TV Streamer is incoming, but it also arrives as Google’s smart home hardware strategy faces a tough spot and new competition.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

Google’s smart home efforts have been a bit sporadic over the years. 2021 seemed like a turning point as the company rebooted its Nest camera lineup, but it was followed by a good bout of silence. That was broken up by the occasional new camera, streaming device, and the Google Home Speaker earlier this year, but it’s all felt rather unfocused and unpredictable.

And that leads into this week’s news: Google has a new TV Streamer coming.

	

This next-gen release is pretty similar on paper, though with the additions of far-field microphones, presence sensing, and a new remote. 

Next-gen Google TV Streamer in the works with microphones, presence sensing, & new remote

Sounds good! 

But, at the same time, it feels like Google should have much bigger priorities in its smart home ecosystem. Those aforementioned 2021 Nest cameras are still in need of refreshes. The 2K updates for the wired cameras have been welcome upgrades, but I do wish my battery-powered models had the same quality. The Nest Hub Max is way overdue for an update at this point, and I’d argue that should have been the priority over a new audio speaker. Google Home has done a great job over the past couple of years at building out a third-party ecosystem of smart home devices, but the first-party hardware has been lacking, and there’s not enough tight integration with most third-party hardware to bridge the gap.

So while I’m all for a new Google TV Streamer, I’m also struggling to feel like this is the release we should be seeing right now. 

Especially in the context of this week’s other news. Apple is making a big smart home play. On top of the “HomePad” smart display, the company is teaming up with LG for some second-party hardware with deep integration. Putting aside that Google has really dropped the ball on its massive lead in the smart display space, integrations like these are exactly what I wish Google Home saw more of. Walmart cameras, the Yale smart lock, and the First Alert smoke alarms are a good start, but there’s so much room for more.

As a fan and a genuine user of Google’s smart home ecosystem, I really feel like Google is leaving so much out there right now. Just me? Let’s discuss!

This Week’s Top Stories

Amazon did the thing!

Well I never thought this day would come. After well over a decade of Fire Tablets that were inherently limited, Amazon this week announced new “Alexa” tablets that have the Google Play Store installed. Wild times folks, wild times.

Amazon’s new Alexa Tablets are an iPad-inspired reboot, complete with the Play Store

Google Wallet updates

An assortment of Google Wallet updates are out, including more ID support and a new design. Plus, it sounds like car key support for certain GM vehicles is not too far off.

Google Wallet for Android adds 12th digital state ID

Google Wallet rolling out stacked card list redesign on Android

Pixelated has video – no, this is not a drill!

Our podcast, Pixelated, has long been audio-only, but this week’s episode features a video component and a tier list of every Pixel released to date!

More Top Stories

Google Cloud announces ‘Gemini agent’ as ‘universal agent for work’

Google Labs announces ‘Playground’ for prompt-based game creation

Gemini app limiting what models free & AI Plus users can access, AI Pro adding Deep Think

Motorola is rolling out its Android 17 update to more devices

Claude launches Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides integration with sidebar and more

YouTube says Shorts recommendations won’t surface unoriginal content

Google rolling out ‘massive’ Pixel Buds Pro 2 and 2a update [U]

Google is ending support for Pixel Watch’s emergency LTE ‘Safety Signal’

Android Auto rolling out fix that stops auto-playing music when you start your car

Google starts rolling out its upgraded Pixel screen savers to the Pixel 9

Pixel 11 Pro vs. iPhone 18 Pro: Copy-copy-paste or just copy-paste [Video]

title: Google Antigravity is now built into Gemini app for macOS
snippet: As part of today’s Gemini 4 Argon rollout, Google is making a big update to the Gemini app for macOS by integrating Antigravity. more…
fullText:
As part of today’s Gemini 4 Argon rollout, Google is making a big update to the Gemini app for macOS by integrating Antigravity.

Antigravity is Google’s agent-first development platform, with version 2.0 introduced at I/O 2026. It was previously a standalone app for Mac, Windows, Linux, and most recently Googlebook (Android). Since May, Google has been updating Antigravity at a rapid pace, with major updates coming on a weekly basis, or even every few days.

Google is now bringing Antigravity directly into the Gemini app on macOS. You’ll see a new Liquid Glass pill for Antigravity in the top-right corner, with the same button letting you exit. This launches the full experience found in the dedicated application.

Gemini 4 Argon’s upgraded coding capabilities are cited as the reason for this integration. This lets users code apps, web experiences, and more from one app. As of today, the new model requires AI Pro and above in the Gemini app, but Antigravity access requires AI Ultra.

	

Meanwhile, the Gemini app for macOS has been updated with the new “Chat” and “Task” switcher, with the latter being the new name for Gemini Spark. It appears below the prompt box, while the navigation drawer also sees a big update. Search is now in the top-right corner of the panel. There’s a new Scheduled view that shows both Spark tasks and Scheduled actions.

Additionally, @ (mention) is now how you access Skills, replacing the / (slash) command. In the side panel, “Customize” lets you access Skills and Connectors, which is the new name for Connected Apps.

Make sure you’re running the latest version of the Gemini app for macOS.

title: Apple Tried Hard to Sell Me on the HomeView as a Seamless Smart Home Experience and Succeeded
snippet: I’m not easily impressed when it comes to smart home hubs, here’s why the HomeView is different.
fullText:
I test smart home devices for a living, but even I find it challenging to use and manage the ones in my home. I have Hue bulbs, Govee lamps, Dreo smart ceiling fans, TP-Link plugs, Eufy cameras, Whisker smart litter boxes and robot vacuums, among many other devices, all “bolted” together, with an Amazon Echo Show 8 and Alexa integration layer to interact with them. The result is….functional, which is the highest praise I can offer it.

Apple promises that its HomeView will be different. I spent over an hour at Apple’s Welcome Home event in New York City, where I got to view and interact with the HomeView across a variety of scenarios and environments. I’m not someone who’s easily convinced that a new smart screen is the solution to my problems, but after seeing the Apple HomeView in action, I’m on board.

No third-party apps required is huge — everything goes through Apple Home

Yes, the HomeView has a clock view.Ajay Kumar/CNET

The HomeView’s biggest and most compelling appeal is that you don’t need to download, install and set up an account with a third-party app for each and every smart home device you own.

			

More from CNET

With most smart home products, you’re lucky if they integrate with the voice assistant you normally use. Once set up, in the best circumstances, you need only to interact with their app when its connection or functionality breaks (and it will), and then you’ll need to dig into settings to find out why and fix it. Sounds awful, right?

If you’re the average person trying to connect and navigate different smart home devices for the first time, the setup prospect is daunting, as the 10-plus third-party smart home apps on my phone can attest. It’s hard to overstate how big a barrier to entry Apple has just removed by exiling third-party apps from this process.

In the case of the HomeView, I watched an Apple representative instantly find, pair and register a new smart home device on both her phone and the HomeView as she carried on a casual conversation with me, not missing a beat. Everything was managed through the Apple Home app. It seemed to work like pairing new AirPods or a HomePod. I didn’t have time to dig into the process before being shepherded to the next demo, but what I saw was one of the most compelling things I’ve seen in the smart home world: an easy, intuitive setup.

It should work with all the new Apple Home collection devices from LG and Schneider Electric, as well as Matter and Apple Home accessories. This isn’t an exhaustive list, and I expect most devices, including those from Amazon and Google, should work as well.

Face ID recognition and personalized profiles make a big difference

From the side, the HomeView gives off strong iMac G4 vibes.Ajay Kumar/CNET

Personalized profiles for a smart home hub are an underrated feature, and their current implementation is pretty poor. Echo devices let you set up multiple profiles for family members and even guests, but God forbid you have to navigate the Alexa app to set what a guest has access to or trust that the voice print actually works. Despite having plenty of voice records for my wife and me, our Echo never seems to be able to differentiate between us.

With the HomeView, you have Face ID integrated, and in the brief time I had, it worked quickly without any bugs. An Apple representative showed me how they envision the HomeView being used in a nightstand setup in a bedroom, an environment where you want privacy and don’t want a stranger having access to your entire smart home.

The HomeView registered the owner and the correct profile immediately and pulled up relevant information, such as a calendar, scheduled events, and preferred home screen and customization options. The same carried over to the other HomeView devices Apple had set up in its simulated home environment, with the exterior HomeView offering a security camera view while limiting access for guests, while granting them certain features like temperature control or Safari access.

It can register up to six people by face and set up personalized profiles for each. While Apple didn’t go into detail or confirm this, I imagine that these include child and family accounts where you can set up parental controls. 

The 7-inch square Liquid Retina display works well for a kitchen setup

The HomeView can keep your coffee and grinder company on the counter.

I keep an Echo Show and an Apolosign smart calendar in my kitchen. One helps with recipes and timers, while the other lets my wife and me coordinate meetings, appointments and important events. Both take up too much space on our kitchen counters because we don’t like how they look wall-mounted (more on that below).

The HomeView comes with a 7-inch square Liquid Retina display. I heard several people in the demo areas complain that it was too small. On the contrary, I think the size and shape are actually perfect for a smart home screen, especially one in my narrow galley kitchen with limited countertop space. 

The square screen makes it easier to view and scroll through recipes, and it’s also hands-free while you’re cooking, adjustable and tiltable to suit your needs. The base also keeps the screen directly off your dirty countertops. Apple placed it next to a fancy-looking espresso setup in a demo kitchen, and it looked great without being overwhelming. By contrast, my Apolosign calendar looks like a giant eyesore and immediately draws the eye of everyone who walks in and shows them our full schedule.

Smaller footprint and better functionality in my kitchen? Sold. 

Wall mounting looks remarkably good and not like you nailed a tablet to your wall 

When you buy a HomeView, you can choose between one ready to mount on a wall or one with a speaker base.Ajay Kumar/CNET

I like the idea of a smart home hub on my wall, but I hate how it looks in practice. I briefly considered mounting our Android-powered smart calendar to our kitchen wall as a central hub for our devices. Not only was it unsightly, but it also looked like we’d just taken a tablet and nailed it to our wall, with an ugly, dangling power cable off the bottom.

Apple showed me several examples of mounted HomeViews in different settings, and they all looked great. In Apple’s case, they’re professionally installed with a hidden, wired power connection in the wall, which the company recommends if you’re planning to use the HomeView as your main smart home dashboard for temperature control or as a security screen by your entryway, for instance. But if you don’t want to cut into your wall, you can also use an external adapter and cable to a nearby wall outlet. I like the look of a seamless wall-mounted HomeView enough to consider taking that extra step.

Don’t underestimate how useful a FaceTime panel is for seniors 

The HomeView can be used for FaceTime video calls.

I’m not a big video call person, but as my parents get older, they default to video calls. Those calls are often shaky and low-quality on the selfie cameras of whatever ancient device they’re using. Apple’s FaceTime demo for the HomeView makes its use case particularly clear. You can get your older relatives a HomeView, even set it up for them, and they can use Siri AI to video call you as needed without needing an iPhone or iPad.

It also has easy Find My integration. Apple representatives demonstrated the feature multiple times, showing how you can ask Siri AI to find a missing phone, remote or AirPods case. It worked without a hitch each time and notably, without requiring you to reach for a phone. 

I also watched as the Apple representative demonstrated how the HomeView autoframed and autofocused on the video caller, and it did a good job of avoiding focusing on me as I lurked over her shoulder. (Hey, it’s my job to test these things!) Again, this is the sort of small but important quality-of-life feature that makes the HomeView more usable than its older competitors.

The smart displays I’ve tested don’t work that well. Is the HomeView really different?

I’ve used a lot of smart home screens that have promised a seamless home hub experience, including the Amazon Echo Show 8, Google Nest Hub, and various Android-powered smart calendar options like Apolosign and Skylight Calendar. While all of them worked, none did so well enough that I thought setting them up and managing them was particularly easy. Demoing the HomeView was a much smoother experience than I was expecting. Naturally, there were some hiccups — Siri AI didn’t always cooperate or register voice commands, but that may have been due to the loud environment, and nothing ever goes perfectly in a demo.

But overall, I was impressed with what I saw, and I can easily see the HomeView working for my own smart home. If it can pull off the miracle of integrating my disparate third-party apps and hodgepodge of systems together in one seamless interface for just $299, well, that’s an easy sell for me.

title: Enable This Secret iOS 27 Feature to Help Protect Against Scams
snippet: Impersonation Risk Detection uses on-device analysis and simple risk warnings to help protect you from scams.
fullText:
When Apple released iOS 27 in September, everyone’s attention went to the new Siri AI, the splashiest feature of the new OS. However, Apple also introduced smaller features, such as Impersonation Risk Detection, which can help protect against certain scams that bypass traditional safeguards, including two-factor authentication.

The tool protects against active social engineering scams, which try to scoop up money or account information by posing as trusted entities, such as your bank or a government agency. Impersonation Risk Detection analyzes factors such as interaction patterns, timing and context to indicate one of three risk levels:

Unknown: There’s no evidence or detection of suspicious activity. This doesn’t mean the action is confirmed safe.

Medium: The action shows some signs of suspicious activity.

High: There are significant signs of suspicious activity.

		

			

The analysis happens on-device, which means your personal data is never sent to Apple or the app you’re using. The app — not Apple — receives only the determined threat level and can decide any necessary actions to take. Based on the risk level, the app might show a warning, add a delay or ask you to verify your identity.

Here’s how to enable Impersonation Risk Detection for an extra layer of scam protection. But note that it’s only available in supported apps, so it won’t work with everything.

How to enable Impersonation Risk Detection

1. Open Settings.

2. Tap Privacy & Security. 

3. Tap Impersonation Risk Detection.

4. Enable the Share with App Developers toggle.

CNET/Apple

After enabling or disabling this toggle, Apple notes it can take up to 24 hours for the feature to activate or deactivate. That delay serves as a barrier against scammers who might tell people to turn off the feature so they can keep their schemes moving. Once the feature is active, you can return to this menu and see which apps have requested a risk assessment and why.

This feature won’t catch everything, so you should stay vigilant. For example, if someone wants you to turn this feature off, they could be trying to scam you. 

CNET/Apple

If you find yourself bombarded with constant requests to verify your identity, or you want to turn off the feature for any other reason, just toggle off the Share with App Developers option. You can also disable access to individual apps by following the above steps, tapping the individual app and then tapping the toggle next to the app.

For more iOS news, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and what iOS 27.0.1 fixes on your device.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Zachary McAuliffe
						

						

							Senior writer						
					

											

								

											Zach began writing for CNET in November, 2021 after writing for a broadcast news station in his hometown, Cincinnati, for five years. You can usually find him hanging out with his wife, son and dog. You can reach him at zmcauliffe@cnet.com.

title: Google Play adding ‘personal library’ to access your vibe-coded Android apps
snippet: Google today announced a slew of Play Store updates across vibe-coding, game discovery, social features, and more. more…
fullText:
Google today announced a slew of Play Store updates across vibe-coding, game discovery, social features, and more.

The biggest update is Google Play’s embrace of vibe-coded Android apps. Since May, Google AI Studio has allowed you to generate Android apps and quickly deploy them to your phone using ADB.

Google is now going a step further by letting you “launch personal apps on your own device” via the Play Store. A “Your personal library” section allows you to access apps across multiple devices for an easy restore and install experience. This is rolling out starting today in the US and other select markets.

The Play Store will soon let you privately share your apps with select users. These generated Android apps are kept “secure, private, and separate from the public store catalog.” It’s intended for small-scale sharing, with these apps going through a security review.

	

In the future, Google Play will let you “graduate to a professional developer account with the same Trust & Safety reviews and high-quality standards.”

Game Finder is the next big update and starts with your “Gamer DNA.” This is an “analysis of how you play and preferences you’ve shared.” You can specify “games, genres, mechanics, and more to finetune.” Gamer DNA will let you “easily find games that match your taste.” It’s rolling out initially in the US with more markets coming soon.

Plus, see how players with similar Gamer DNA are engaging with a title, find out how many people you follow are playing it, read user review summaries and learn which games are trending and why. 

This will be joined by Game Playlists that let you curate and soon share a collection of titles.

The Play Store is boosting social competitions with Sprints, or “high-energy, 48-hour micro-challenges” that involve matching with groups of two to five players for “fast-paced contests.” The Sidekick in-game overlay is also adding “30-second Playback” clips for sharing.

Elsewhere, Google Play is expanding Sports Topic Pages that show live scores and compatible streaming apps to the Premier League, Champions League, La Liga, Liga MX, and Major League Soccer. Ask Play can now generate app comparisons that highlight “key differences and user sentiment.”

title: New Apple TV 4K vs previous model: Here’s everything new
snippet: Apple just launched a brand new Apple TV 4K (pre-order here), the fourth generation of the product. Here’s how the new Apple TV 4K compares to the previous, third-gen model from 2022. more…
fullText:
Apple just launched a brand new Apple TV 4K (pre-order here), the fourth generation of the product. Here’s how the new Apple TV 4K compares to the previous, third-gen model from 2022.

Performance: A19 chip vs A15 Bionic

The new Apple TV 4K has an A19 chip, the same chip that debuted in the iPhone 17 last year.

The third-gen Apple TV 4K from 2022 includes an A15 Bionic chip that first shipped in 2021. So any sort of chip upgrade would have been a big one, but A19 is an especially sizable leap with several years worth of improvements.

Apple says the new chip “delivers up to 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to 2x faster GPU performance,” which results in “greater responsiveness, faster navigation, and smoother animations.”

A19 also has a new, dedicated AV1 decoder which enables “more efficient, high-quality streaming while using less bandwidth.”

Siri AI, plus hands-free Siri interactions with far-field mics

Siri AI debuts in the new Apple TV 4K, but Apple says it’s also coming to the second and third generation models. Presumably Siri AI will be more responsive on the latest hardware with A19, but it’s great that users won’t have to upgrade just to get the new Siri.

Apple says Siri AI supports features like “personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions.” Some example queries include:

“What Apple TV shows won at the Emmy Awards this year?”

“Where was Pluribus filmed?”

“Is this appropriate for a 15-year-old?”

“Play the show Alinda recommended.”

One exclusive upgrade with the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K is that it includes a three-microphone array with voice isolation built right into the box itself for hands-free interactions.

This enables you to say “Siri” or “Hey Siri” to interact with the assistant. You’ll no longer have to press the button on the Siri Remote, though that’s still an option too.

Upgraded Siri Remote with Precision Finding

The Siri Remote has been upgraded to include Find My support with Precision Finding. 

If you’ve ever used Precision Finding to locate a lost AirTag or another device, you’ll know how valuable this experience should prove for the Siri Remote.

When you lose the Siri Remote, you’ll be able to get guided, step-by-step directions to its location. And thanks to a new built-in speaker, you can even play a sound on the remote to help you find it.

You can order the new Siri Remote here for $59, it’s compatible with older Apple TV 4K models so you won’t have to buy a whole new Apple TV to get it.

New four-speaker surround sound feature with HomePods

If you have several HomePods in your house, or plan to invest deeply in the Apple Home ecosystem, the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K has a new surround sound feature.

Using either HomePod mini 2 or HomePod 2, Apple TV 4K will support a four-speaker surround sound experience. Apple says, “The four speakers work together with Apple TV 4K to intelligently recognize their position in the room so audio timing and levels are automatically calibrated to the space.”

You can also mix and match HomePods, as long as they’re in matching pairs. For example, you can use a HomePod 2 front pair and a HomePod mini 2 rear pair—or opt for four of the same model.

Internal storage: 128GB standard vs 64GB

Apple used to sell Apple TV 4K in two models: one with 64GB storage and a more expensive 128GB model.

With the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, 128GB is the standard storage configuration. There are no options to pay more for higher storage. It’s still unclear how necessary the extra storage is, but perhaps we’ll see tvOS 27’s Smart Downloads feature resurface soon.

Connectivity upgrades

There are several connectivity improvements with the new Apple TV 4K. On the wireless front, you get the following:

Wi‑Fi 7, up from Wi-Fi 6

Bluetooth 6, up from Bluetooth 5.0

Thread (previously limited to 128GB model)

	

It’s expected that these upgrades are due to the inclusion of Apple’s N1 wireless chip, though that hasn’t officially been confirmed.

Additionally, Gigabit Ethernet is now included standard on all models. Previously, it was excluded from the base 64GB model that most people bought.

New Apple TV 4K is now available for pre-order for $299.

title: HomeKit Weekly: Onvis releases a Matter over Thread outdoor smart plug with energy monitoring
snippet: Onvis has released a new outdoor smart plug that checks all the boxes you’d want in an outdoor smart plug: Matter over Thread, real-time energy monitoring, and IP65 weather resistance. If you’ve been looking for an outdoor plug that works natively with Apple Home without a hub of its own, this is a great option as you think outdoor lighting for Christmas, etc. more…
fullText:
Onvis has released a new outdoor smart plug that checks all the boxes you’d want in an outdoor smart plug: Matter over Thread, real-time energy monitoring, and IP65 weather resistance. If you’ve been looking for an outdoor plug that works natively with Apple Home without a hub of its own, this is a great option as you think outdoor lighting for Christmas, etc.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Most of your outdoor smart plugs that work with Apple HomeKit over Wi-Fi depend on your router’s signal reaching outside, which depending on what your house is made out of (mine is brick for example, so Wi-Fi outdoors can be rough). Thread is a mesh protocol in which devices route traffic through one another, making it more reliable for outdoor locations that might be on the edge of your Wi-Fi coverage. Onvis built this plug on top Matter over Thread, so it works with Apple Home, Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and SmartThings without being locked into any single smart home platform. You do need a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K to take full advantage of it, though.

Energy monitoring

A really nice feature for this plug is that it tracks real-time power usage and energy consumption through your Matter-compatible smart home system, so you can see exactly how much electricity your landscape lighting, pool pump, or outdoor heater is using. That data appears directly in Apple Home’s energy view without requiring a separate app as well.

Onvis’s outdoor smart plug is rated IP65, which means that it’s protected against dust and low-pressure water jets (from sprinklers or rain). It handles up to 1800 watts, which is enough for landscape lighting, holiday decorations, outdoor fans, etc. Schedules and automations work natively inside of Apple Home, so you can set landscape lights to turn on at sunset and off at a specific time without building anything complicated.

Wrap up

Onvis is filling a nice product gap at a good price point with its new outdoor plug that has Matter over Thread, energy monitoring, etc. If you’ve been waiting to buy an outdoor plug that has all the modern smart home tech built in, this is a great pickup. They’ve been a solid vendor for Apple Home for years as well. 

The Onvis Outdoor Smart Plug is available now on Amazon.

title: IDC: Apple gains ground as China’s smartphone shipments plunge 15.4% in Q3 2026
snippet: According to a new report from IDC, Apple’s share of smartphone shipments in China grew during Q3 2026, despite a 4.3% year-over-year decline in iPhone shipments. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
According to a new report from IDC, Apple’s share of smartphone shipments in China grew during Q3 2026, despite a 4.3% year-over-year decline in iPhone shipments. Here are the details.

Apple gains ground as China’s smartphone shipments plunge 15.4%

In a new report released today, IDC says that rising component costs and retail prices continue to weigh on the broader Chinese smartphone market.

According to IDC, Apple accounted for 17.8% of smartphone shipments in China during Q3 2026, up from 15.8% in the year-ago period. The gain came despite a 15.4% year-over-year decline in overall smartphone shipments in China, with Apple itself seeing a 4.3% year-over-year decline and a 15.1% drop from the previous quarter.

This means that while Apple lost ground, it didn’t lose as much as most of its competitors, thus increasing its overall shipment share.

And speaking of Apple’s competitors, Huawei was the uncontested winner for the quarter, with a massive 17.3% year-over-year increase in shipments, bringing its market share to 21.1%, up from 15.2% in Q3 2025. However, its shipments still declined 17.6% from the previous quarter.

Other than Huawei, Lenovo was the only other brand in China’s top 10 to record year-over-year shipment growth, at 1.1%. On a quarter-over-quarter basis, however, Lenovo, Honor, and Samsung all recorded increases, with Samsung posting a whopping 106.5% jump.

On the other end of the spectrum, Wiko saw the biggest year-over-year decline among the top 10, with shipments plunging 74% in Q3 2026, bringing its shipment share down to 0.8%, from 2.6% in the year-ago period.

Here’s IDC on these numbers, which it notes are preliminary (translation ours):

Despite the overall market downturn, Huawei maintained its strong performance throughout the year, supported by its diverse product lineup and relatively restrained price increases. Its shipments recorded double-digit year-over-year growth.

Apple’s newly released iPhones received a better-than-expected market reception. However, shipments declined slightly year-over-year due to fewer models available this year.

Other major Chinese smartphone brands faced significant challenges but continued to demonstrate varying degrees of resilience under pressure.

Among them, Honor was the only major manufacturer to record quarter-over-quarter shipment growth, suggesting a potential rebound.

IDC says it expects component costs “ to remain elevated over the next several quarters,” which will in turn keep increasing device prices and stretch replacement cycles further as consumers “accept and adapt to higher prices.”

The company doesn’t expect cost pressures to subside “through much of 2027, with the market likely to continue experiencing significant declines.”

title: Apple HomePod Mini 2: Hands-On Impressions, Siri AI and More
snippet: We saw and heard Apple’s new HomePod mini today. Here’s what you should know.
fullText:
Following Amazon’s new Echo Studio and Google’s Home Speaker release in the past year, it felt like Apple was left out of the upgrade cycle. Today’s “Welcome Home” event changed all that, revealing not only the luminous HomeView smart display, but also the next generation of the HomePod, called the HomePod Mini 2.

The small smart speaker, measuring about 4 inches across, will come equipped with the S10 chip, which Apple says analyzes music in real time to optimize it. Apple promises a future update will add an array of Siri AI features too, which is when this speaker should really get interesting.

The HomePod Mini 2 is available to preorder starting at $149 and comes in five new colors, including green and blue. It will arrive in stores on Oct. 30. As expected, Apple is sticking with the Mini line to help keep prices under control, although this model costs nearly $50 more than the previous HomePod Mini.

			

More from CNET

The HomePods sound great when working as a team.Ajay Kumar/CNET

At Apple’s Home event, my colleague Ajay Kumar was there to test out the HomePod Mini 2 and hear the audio personally. Apple’s setup focused on the multispeaker experience, which allows you to link HomePods together so they act in concert.

“The four HomePods set up for the Mini 2 produced surprisingly room-filling sound,” Ajay said. “While I won’t say that it’ll fully replace a 7.1 surround sound home theater on the cheap, it was richer audio than I expected from such small devices in a large space and when the two HomePods behind me were toggled off as part of the demo, I could actually tell how much less robust the sound was.”

When we get the HomePod Mini 2 for testing, it will be interesting to compare its tandem capabilities with speakers like the Amazon Echo Studio, which is a similar size and also focuses on the ability to connect multiple models together for your TV.

A Siri AI experience made for iPhones

The HomePod Mini 2 is available in five colors.Apple

Basic Siri voice commands are all available on the HomePod Mini 2, including the ability to ask questions, set reminders and control Apple Home devices, including the many new home security and smart home products also announced at Tuesday’s event. So, what will the “AI” part add?

Apple is promising Siri AI will let HomePod Mini 2 owners tailor their interactions with the speaker to their own preferences and habits. By analyzing iPhone usage, Siri AI can use contextual data to answer commands more effectively. Apple gave the example of playing a song based on a past text message from a friend, even if you don’t really remember what the song is called. Another demo showed finding a recipe sent in an email and adding its ingredients to a shopping list. The latest Siri AI conversational features will also be available.

It’s worth noting Ajay also found out some Siri AI abilities are backwards compatible with older devices, but it’s difficult to know what, and how much of this compatibility will apply to older HomePod speakers users may already have. 

This sounds much like what Gemini for Home can do on the Google Home Speaker, but naturally more intertwined with Apple’s own apps. Also, full Gemini for Home features can cost up to $20 a month, but Apple didn’t provide much pricing information for these smart speaker AI features, so they could be significantly less or even free.

A few final tricks include the ability to hold a conversation out of the HomePod Mini 2 using the Home app on iPhone, as well as a feature that listens for fire alarms and alerts you when you’re not home. But how does the audio perform?

How does the new HomePod audio really sound?

The HomePod Mini 2 is facing serious competition this year.Ajay Kumar/CNET

The HomePod Mini 2 is equipped with a full-range driver and dual passive radiators, made for 360-degree sound. That sounds just like the design of the first-gen HomePod Mini, so it’s not immediately clear what Apple has done to enhance the audio beyond software adjustments.

You can also link up to four models together for surround sound. It also works with the new Apple TV 4K model, also announced at the event. However, music streamers take note: While the speaker supports Apple Music, TuneIn, iHeartRadio and Audacy, there’s no mention of support for popular apps such as Tidal and Spotify.

We look forward to testing the HomePod Mini 2 alongside other new smart speakers to see how the audio improvements really compare. The older HomePod Mini was showing its age compared to the Google Home Speaker the last time I tested them, especially in the lower register, so it will be interesting to see any changes.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home						
					

											

								

											Tyler has worked on, lived with and tested all types of smart home and security technology for over a dozen years, explaining the latest features, privacy tricks and top recommendations.
With degrees in business management, literature and technical writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon, gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. But when not at work, he can be found hiking the trails, trying out a new food recipe for his loved ones, keeping up on his favorite reading or gaming with good friends.

title: Galaxy phones reportedly ‘yield no profit at all’ when sold as Samsung cuts production
snippet: A new report alleges that Samsung is cutting way back on Galaxy smartphone production plans through the end of 2026, by as much as 30%. more…
fullText:
A new report alleges that Samsung is cutting way back on Galaxy smartphone production plans through the end of 2026, by as much as 30%.

Korean media, MoneyToday, reports that Samsung is cutting Galaxy smartphone production by up to 30% through Q4 2026. Where original forecasts expected Samsung to produce around 270 million smartphones in 2026, the company may just barely surpass 200 million at this point.

The reason for the reduction is, of course, the surging price of memory. 

	

Despite Samsung’s major role within the memory market, Samsung Mobile still has to deal with the same downsides as other manufacturers. The report points out that 12GB of RAM has jumped in price by 175% since last year and, in Q3 and Q4, it’s expected to rise by around 20% compared to the previous quarter alone. Samsung’s Q4 is generally a bit quiet as the lead-up to 2027 flagships looms and as other launches start to age out.

	

The big kicker here is that Samsung is apparently making “no profit at all” when it sells a Galaxy smartphone. This is presumably a layered statement, as one would imagine that more expensive devices like the Galaxy S26 Ultra and Galaxy Z Fold 8 still manage some level of profit, but even if it’s just a general statement about the whole lineup, it certainly explains Samsung’s recent price hikes. Samsung’s mobile division is expected to mount a 19 trillion won loss in Q3 2026, the report brings out, which is around $14 billion USD.

AI is just great, isn’t it.

fullText:
Update, 5:56 p.m. ET: The public beta is now available as well.

Apple is rolling out the fourth developer beta for macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, ahead of the official release in the coming weeks. Here’s what to expect.

Apple rolls out macOS 27.2 developer beta 4

Apple appears to be back to its weekly cycle of the 27.2 beta, after a two-week gap between developer betas 2 and 3.

The company is now rolling out macOS 27.2 beta 4 to developers, which is on the lighter side of user-facing features. The biggest addition to the system so far is Siri AI’s support for five additional languages, following its English-only initial rollout last month with macOS 27 Golden Gate.

Siri AI in macOS 27.2 Golden Gate will add support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, as Apple promised during the Surprise and Shine event.

One particularly interesting addition to macOS 27.2 beta 3, released last week, was the discovery of new gesture recognition tools in several built-in apps, which could be laying the groundwork for Apple’s upcoming touchscreen MacBook Pro.

Apple is expected to unveil its first-ever touchscreen MacBook Pro later this month, with an announcement currently rumored for October 27. The company is also expected to introduce a new iPad mini with an OLED display, alongside updated iMac and entry-level MacBook Pro models powered by the M6 chip.

Back to today’s beta, its release build is 26B5112a, which indicates this might be the last release before the first RC. We are digging through the system and will report back if we find any noteworthy tidbits.

Installing macOS 27.2 beta 4

Here’s how to install the first macOS 27.2 beta 4:

Back up your Mac

Open System Settings

Go to General ⇾ Software Update

Click the ‘i’ icon next to Beta Updates

From the dropdown menu in the top-right, select the macOS Developer Golden Gate Beta

Hit ‘Done’

title: There’s a clear divide between Galaxy S27 tiers, as the latest leak lists price
snippet: Samsung’s Galaxy S27 launch is getting closer, which means pricing and final details are being finalized and, further, leaked. The latest report lists Galaxy S27 series pricing and one spec that divides the lineup into two distinct tiers. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s Galaxy S27 launch is getting closer, which means pricing and final details are being finalized and, further, leaked. The latest report lists Galaxy S27 series pricing and one spec that divides the lineup into two distinct tiers.

It’s been known that Samsung wants to add another device model to the Galaxy S27 series. It tried last year, but the Galaxy S26 Edge never came to be and was replaced by a rushed S26+. Recent reports specify four different Galaxy S27 models, and none of them seem to be thin. The Galaxy S27 will consist of a base model, S27+, S27 Pro, and S27 Ultra.

A Twitter/X post by @phonefuturist adds a little more context around pricing in the US and Korea for the Galaxy S27 series (via Android Headlines). The common sentiment has everyone expecting a price increase again. The post pushes back on that, stating that the Galaxy S27 will start at $899 in the US. Here’s the list, according to the leak:

Galaxy S27 – $899

Galaxy S27+ – $1,099

Galaxy S27 Pro – $1,299

Galaxy S27 Ultra – $1,399

Technically, the Galaxy S27 is listed here as cheaper than the current Galaxy S26, because Samsung recently jacked the prices up on an existing phone. But due to an added device in the middle, the structure gets a little wonky and can’t be compared to the previous series 1:1.

	

But going by launch pricing, the Galaxy S27 Pro could cost the same as the Galaxy S26 Ultra, and the new version of the Ultra will bring the series to a peak of $1,399. For reference, a good foldable device like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is only $500 higher.

The leak also points out a divide in the group based on display specs. The Galaxy S27 and S27+ could get Samsung’s M14+ OLED panel, while the Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra get the M16 OLED panel. The latter could mean a privacy display for both devices, while the two more affordable options are left without. The M16 panel is new this year and is also used on the outer iPhone Duo display.

🚨 EXCLUSIVE: Galaxy S27 series pricing

🇺🇸 US/ 🇰🇷SK | 🌍 Int'l*

S27: $899 | $999 — M14+

S27+: $1,099 | $1,199 — M14+

S27 Pro: $1,299 | $1,399 — M16

S27 Ultra: $1,399/$1,499 | $1,499–$1,549 — M16

Regional pricing varies. Current targets, subject to change. https://t.co/SdwG7g5ac2

— Schrödinger (@phonefuturist) October 7, 2026

Pricing is something that can quickly change, so take this information with a grain of salt. Still, the line between the top-tier premium devices and second-best options is clearer. And now, users get another choice, even though the “Ultra” could cost $100 more.

title: Bloomberg: New iPad mini with OLED display will be significantly more expensive than current model
snippet: The current iPad mini sells for $599 in its starting 128 GB configuration. Apple is set to introduce the next-generation iPad mini later this month and — while the starting storage may increase — interested buyers should start probably bracing for a price rise. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says he is hearing that the new iPad mini will be “considerably more expensive”, floating a new price closer to the $799 mark. more…
fullText:
The current iPad mini sells for $599 in its starting 128 GB configuration. Apple is set to introduce the next-generation iPad mini later this month and — while the starting storage may increase — interested buyers should start probably bracing for a price rise.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says he is hearing that the new iPad mini will be “considerably more expensive”, floating a new price closer to the $799 mark.

If that turned out to be the case, it would represent a $200 jump compared to the current iPad mini baseline, and slot it above the 11-inch iPad Air starting price in the current lineup. 

Of course, Apple will argue that you are getting more product for that money. The new iPad mini is expected to feature an OLED display for the first time, with a new chassis design including thinner bezels. 

The new iPad mini is also getting upgraded speaker system and a much more powerful chip upgrade. We believe it will be powered by the A20 Pro chip, the same chip as found in Apple’s high-end iPhone 18 Pro models.

However, it remains unclear whether the OLED display in the new iPad mini will be technically comparable to the iPad Pro’s industry-leading tandem OLED panel. There have also been conflicting reports about whether it will support 120Hz ProMotion.

The new iPad mini should be announced at a media event later this month, alongside new OLED MacBook Pros. But first, on Tuesday, Apple will host a ‘Welcome home’ event where it will unveil a new smart home strategy, including its first smart home display product.

title: Niobia takes the guesswork out of some of tech’s most expensive mistakes
snippet: The San Francisco startup aims to help battery and chip manufacturers identify defects on production lines, reducing downtime and costly mistakes.
fullText:
San Francisco-based startup Niobia is betting big on a critical but often overlooked part of battery and chip making: helping engineers understand how and why things go wrong. Its AI software flags production defects and lets engineers ask a chatbot what caused them, aiming to deliver answers in minutes rather than days.

How it works (broadly): The company’s customers place AI agents on their production lines to look for defects, then loop in human engineers to work out what might cause a product to fail. The agents run on self-contained GPUs mounted directly on manufacturing equipment, much like a sensor. They can spot pinhole-sized flaws such as scratches. Niobia’s AI also gathers all the data in one place so engineers can ask a chatbot what went wrong and dig deeper into the cause.

Speed is so critical because chips and batteries are some of the world’s most important products, while also increasingly in short supply. As manufacturers continue to develop and improve their technologies, things inevitably go awry during research and development. Engineers then spend days or longer figuring out a fix before they can restart production. Each flaw or mistake can prove costly — sometimes running into the millions of dollars — and set back manufacturing timelines. 

Niobia co-founders Gaurav Jha and Harveen Kaur both have PhDs in chemistry and have worked at chipmakers and battery manufacturers, giving them firsthand experience with the challenges within the industry. In a call ahead of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, where the company is a Battlefield finalist, Jha explained that while what Niobia does is specialized, it serves a multibillion-dollar market that includes some of the biggest battery and semiconductor makers today.

“It’s extremely niche; maybe people will never know about it,” said Jha, speaking of the battery and chip manufacturing market that his company aims to serve. “But it’s like behind the scenes, this is powering everything… we just don’t see it in the regular world.” 

“Every product around you, like glasses or shoes, slippers, wallets, and headphones — these processes touch every single part of it,” added Jha.

Niobia’s agents run on open source models that the company trains further with battery and chip research and other data. That training is what lets them identify pinhole-sized defects. Jha said that Niobia chose open source models largely because its customers don’t want their highly sensitive company information going into a public AI cloud where it might be used to train the model.

“None of our customers want their proprietary data to go to the cloud, even if we tell them it’s safe,” said Jha. The startup also outlines how it approaches cybersecurity, given the high-stakes race among adversarial nations to innovate in the battery and chip space. Niobia, for instance, lets its customers hold their own encryption keys so that the startup cannot decrypt the customers’ data.

Jha said that the company’s priority for now is to focus on three specialties, such as film coating, electroplating (which is coating a surface with metal using an electric current), and fluidized bed reaction (a chemical process where solid particles are suspended in a gas or liquid). 

He said that the company also wants its technology to become more autonomous, with the eventual aim of building out a fully self-driving factory for its customers.

If you’re curious to learn more, Niobia will present onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt this afternoon in San Francisco. Join us to catch the company and the 19 startups against which it’s competing as part of our storied Startup Battlefield competition, happening today, Tuesday, through Thursday, October 15.

title: Google’s new ‘Shop devices’ tab sells Pixel and Samsung Galaxy devices side by side
snippet: Google has launched a new “Shop devices” portal that lets interested buyers pick up a Samsung Galaxy smartphone from the Google Store, right alongside a Pixel phone or Watch. more…
fullText:
Google has launched a new “Shop devices” portal that lets interested buyers pick up a Samsung Galaxy smartphone from the Google Store, right alongside a Pixel phone or Watch.

The Google Store is the main place you’d go to buy a Pixel smartphone or any other Google product, and that’s all the store directly carries. But, over the past several months, Google has been not-so-quietly selling Samsung devices. Through the Play Store’s Play Points program, buyers have been able to place an order for Samsung Galaxy devices through the Google Store. 

Until now, that’s been the only way to do it. Just through selective offers or redemptions.

Now, Google is elevating this with a dedicated “Shop devices” tab in the Play Store. This addition, which appears to be rolled out fairly widely, pulls up a page with a variety of Google Pixel and Samsung Galaxy devices including:

	

Galaxy S26 and Galaxy S26 Ultra

Pixel 10a

Pixel Watch 4

Pixel 11 Pro Fold

Galaxy Z Flip 8

Google TV Streamer

Pixel 11

Galaxy Watch 9

Pixel 11 Pro

The order is a bit scattershot, but the functionality is simple enough. Pick your device, check out via the Google Store. You’ll get the same 10% Google One cashback benefit as well as the ability to use Google Store credit on Samsung devices and Pixel devices alike. 

Notably, Google hasn’t raised the price of Samsung’s Galaxy S26 series through this portal yet.

This certainly won’t be for everyone, but it’s a nice bit of flexibility on Google’s part.

title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
snippet: University of Michigan spinout Laplace Intelligence uses AI agents and interactive simulation to stress-test robots and self-driving vehicles before deployment. The profitable startup is competing in Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt, October 13-15 in San Francisco.
fullText:
If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable. 

“Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence, told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.”

Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it.

“Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said.

Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon, October 13.

Howie Sun, CEO, Laplace Intelligence.Image Credits:Laplace Intelligence

Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas. 

“I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said. 

Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision.

“We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said. 

At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world. 

The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale. 

Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom. 

Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision. 

“It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.”

While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop. 

“They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said.

Henry Liu, chief scientist, Laplace Intelligence.Image Credits:Laplace Intelligence

Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world. 

“There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.”

Despite Sun and Liu coming from academia, with no shiny Silicon Valley tech company pedigrees, the two have managed to start generating revenue and even turn a modest profit. Most of the money is coming from autonomous driving use cases, with customers including Japanese trucking manufacturer Isuzu and Texas-based autonomous trucking firm Bot Auto. 

Nvidia is also a customer, says Sun. The two companies, alongside T-Mobile, are working together on a free smart city pilot for San Jose, California, to provide high-level traffic operations. Laplace is also in the early stages of working with partners building humanoid robotics for warehouses.  

Most of Laplace’s customer contracts are project-based today, and the company is working toward turning that into recurring revenue. The startup’s near-term goal — which it hopes will be aided by competing at Disrupt — is to raise funds and scale so it can compete with its rivals. 

Chief among its rivals is Applied Intuition, a buzzy late-stage startup that’s raised $1.2 billion to date at a $15 billion post-money valuation. Isuzu is also one of Applied’s customers. 

Sun isn’t too worried. He believes Laplace’s core methodology of using AI to test AI is a “new paradigm that changes the testing of physical AI entirely,” turning it into a “dynamic interactive testing process.”

“That will be the biggest moat,” he said.

title: Google Play now lets anyone build private, vibe-coded apps that run on Android
snippet: Google is making it easier to build and use personal Android apps created with AI, without having to make them available to everyone on the Play Store.
fullText:
Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private.

These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator. 

The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android.

Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use.

Image Credits:Google

These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android.

Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up. 

“That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.”

In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store.

And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews. 

Related to AI’s impact on app development, Google said it’s also building better ways to curate the Google Play experience — for instance, by leveraging Google’s AI to create a personalized game recommendation engine, called Game Finder. The feature, first available in the U.S. in English, will be based on what the user likes to play combined with Google’s knowledge derived from its game community’s 1.2 billion players. 

Image Credits:Google

Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates. 

Image Credits:Google

Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations. 

The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience.

title: MIT startup says it can turn diesel trucks into cheaper hydrogen haulers — see it at Disrupt
snippet: Diesel is expensive and polluting, and LNK Energies says it has come up with a way to replace it with hydrogen, all while undercutting diesel on cost.
fullText:
Diesel fuel powers everything from shipping to agriculture, and with prices hitting record highs in recent weeks, governments around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout. 

For now, that’s meant releasing fuel from stockpiles, but in the coming years, the answer might be a new technology from an MIT startup called LNK Energies.

LNK has created a way to convert existing heavy-duty trucks from diesel to hydrogen, slashing pollution and costs while shielding operators from the price spikes that result from geopolitical instability like the war in Iran. “If you look at total cost of ownership of a Class 8 truck, it’s 13% cheaper than diesel,” Alexis Huynh, chief technology officer at LNK Energies, told TechCrunch. (Class 8 is the heaviest category of trucks, including big rigs.)

Automotive companies have been exploring the use of hydrogen in long-haul trucking in part because refilling a hydrogen tank is faster than recharging the massive batteries those trucks require. But hydrogen is challenging to move to refilling stations, and the pressure tanks required to store it on the truck are large and costly. 

LNK’s approach is to carry hydrogen chemically attached to another compound. Liquid organic hydrogen carriers, or LOHCs, are liquids that can absorb and later release hydrogen, and they have been widely studied, but mostly for moving large quantities of hydrogen from refineries to fueling stations. The equipment needed to separate hydrogen from the LOHC, known as a reactor, has been too big to fit onto a truck.

“A lot of the reactors that LOHC companies have today are really large. They’re about the size of a shipping container,” Huynh said. “We have shrunk that basically to the size of a mini fridge.”

Moving the reactor onto the truck saves a surprising amount of energy. When hydrogen is stored on a truck, it must be pressurized to more than 11,000 psi (800 bar), roughly 800 times normal air pressure, and squeezing it that hard takes a lot of power. Because LNK’s fuel carries the hydrogen in liquid form and releases it on board as needed, that step goes away. “We’re eliminating the expensive compression step,” Sayandeep Biswas, co-founder and CEO of LNK Energies, told TechCrunch. 

In LNK’s system, once the hydrogen is released on the truck, it can be burned in a conventional internal combustion engine, the kind in today’s diesel trucks, with just a few modifications. The company uses waste heat from the engine to help power the on-board reactor. Or, if the trucking company wants to fully eliminate combustion emissions, it can use fuel cells instead, which convert hydrogen into electricity to power electric motors.

The LOHC can be stored in a traditional fuel tank and dispensed using pumps, just like diesel. “The entire hydrogen infrastructure doesn’t need to exist,” Biswas said. “It’s just a standard diesel station.”

Biswas and Huynh have a demonstration reactor working in the lab that can power an engine from a lawnmower. In 18 months, they plan to install a larger version in a commercial truck. 

The trucks will cost more up front, but promise to be cheaper to operate. The duo are confident that they can undercut diesel at a price of $6.50 per gallon after they’ve made just 50 to 100 trucks. None of their projections include government subsidies. “The idea isn’t to have a technology that is cheaper at scale, but one that is cheaper even during that adoption period,” Biswas said.

LNK will present live onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco, as part of our Startup Battlefield pitch competition. Come join us in San Francisco and take part in the action.

title: Hey Google, where is the next Nest Hub?
snippet: Apple’s long-rumored smart home display is finally here and it begs the question – why hasn’t Google released a new Nest Hub in half a decade? more…
fullText:
Apple’s long-rumored smart home display is finally here and it begs the question – why hasn’t Google released a new Nest Hub in half a decade?

Following the explosive popularity of smart speakers, 2018’s Google Home Hub helped usher in a new step forward with smart displays, combining the always-listening hotwords with additional functionality in visual responses, video streaming, live camera feeds, and more. It was a pretty immediate hit that was eventually rebranded as the “Nest Hub” and later spawned two sequels: the larger Nest Hub Max and the second-gen Nest Hub.

And that’s where we’ve been for five years now.

Half a decade later, Google’s smart display efforts have been completely silent. Outside of bringing Gemini for Home to smart displays in the exact same capacity as smart speakers, virtually nothing has changed on a Nest Hub in the past few years. Just look at our coverage over the past couple of years – no new features, no groundbreaking changes of really any kind. Google impressively replaced the underlying operating system without anyone really noticing, but functionally, it’s just status quo.

	

That’s not to say status quo isn’t still good. The Nest Hub experience still checks a lot of boxes. Visual responses to voice commands is at the center, with easy controls for your smart home and doorbell previews also being core to it all. Top that off with casting of video apps (great for the kitchen), setting timers, and the Nest Hub Max’s ability to double as a Nest Cam, and it all gets the job done. There’s a reason that myself and millions of other Nest Hub buyers still use these devices. 

But did Google really hit a wall so hard that not only nothing has changed on the software side, but hardware has just been completely stagnant? Maybe, but it’s hard to believe if so, especially as Amazon has been plugging away with new form factors and ideas for its Echo Show series for years now – the bigger Echo Show 15 with Fire TV is a great example; I’d love a tiny Google TV for parts of my home that can’t justify a “real” TV.

Fast forward to today, and now we’ve got Apple’s entry to the market. “Homeview” is a little 7-inch display on an iMac-like pedestal that also mounts itself to the wall. At its core, there’s not a ton here beyond what you get on a Nest Hub. Visual responses to voice commands are the central functionality, with Apple also picking up Nest Hub Max’s ability to recognize individual users and adjust the software accordingly. Where Apple builds on it is with faster software – Nest Hub, even at launch, has always been a laggy mess – and a reboot of its smart home efforts with other new hardware in tow. It’s really just a ton of Apple’s usual polish to integrations and apps, just in the form factor of a Nest Hub.

But again, it begs the question; where is Google in all of this? 

Google hasn’t ignored the smart home space over the past few years, with its own smart home reboot coming in 2021’s Nest Cam revival and further releases since, as well as a complete reinvention of the Home app to better serve as a hub for not just Google’s ecosystem, but a deep catalog of compatible smart home devices. And there’s been a lot of good on that front, with the more recent effort to use Gemini helping to clean up what was a crumbling experience in Assistant. It’s still not perfect, but Google’s ecosystem has all of the right parts to back up a smart display. 

The last time Google acknowledged smart displays was around when the Google Home Speaker was announced. Roughly a year ago this week, in fact. At the time, Google Home chief Anish Kattukaran called the smart display the “ultimate form factor” for the smart home. And yet, it’s now Apple that’s delivering on that promise before Google.

Google seems to have something in the works, with “Google Home Display” showing up in code earlier this year, but nothing has come of it yet. 9to5Google readers pitched their ideas for the product, including keeping the Pixel Tablet’s detachable display and generally improving the performance and the display quality, the latter being things that Apple’s Homeview display absolutely do.

	

Google’s lack of action is going to hurt it pretty directly here. Apple’s launch isn’t cheap at $300, but for iPhone users, it’s a pretty easy sell. Just like how the Nest Hub was an easy sell as a smart home controller that displayed your pictures, that’s all Apple has to say to sell its own. Amazon’s Echo Show has a bigger uphill battle because, frankly, who wants to invest in Amazon’s ecosystem, but Google at least served as a nice middle ground for everyone. Out-of-the-box integration if you use an Android phone, and just a step or two if you already have a Gmail account, which is true of basically everyone anyway. But, right now, Google simply doesn’t have an option. Not only does it not have a competing option, but it just doesn’t sell anything. 

What do you think?

title: Smartphone shipments dropped by 20%, lowest point in 14 years amid memory crisis
snippet: RAMageddon continues to have wide effects throughout the tech industry, with a new report revealing that the smartphone market has just hit its lowest point in well over a decade. more…
fullText:
RAMageddon continues to have wide effects throughout the tech industry, with a new report revealing that the smartphone market has just hit its lowest point in well over a decade.

Counterpoint Research reports that global smartphone shipments dropped by 20% in Q3 2026, reaching the lowest numbers in the past 14 years. The last time smartphone shipments were this low, Samsung’s latest release was the Galaxy S3. 

Yikes.

The drop has not only impacted overall shipment figures, but also the share of the market that major smartphone brands take up. Chinese brands including Xiaomi, Vivo, and Oppo all make up a smaller share of the overall market in Q3 2026 compared to the same time the prior year, with Samsung continuing to hold the top spot at 23% of the overall market and Apple at 22%, up from 19% and 18%, respectively.

	

Counterpoint says that Samsung’s overall shipments only dropped by 3%, with the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s success playing a major role in the company’s quarter. Meanwhile, a recent report claims that Samsung makes no profit when it sells Galaxy phones at this point.

Apple, meanwhile, saw a 22% year-over-year decline with the absence of its base iPhone 18. Oppo and Vivo both saw drops of around 20% while Xiaomi dropped shipments by 30%.
