title: Will HomeView support third-party apps? Here’s what Apple says
snippet: Apple today announced HomeView, a $299 smart home display with a 7-inch screen that lets users control connected accessories, make FaceTime calls, and enjoy music and video content. But what about third-party apps? Here’s what Apple says. more…
fullText:
Apple today announced HomeView, a $299 smart home display with a 7-inch screen that lets users control connected accessories, make FaceTime calls, and enjoy music and video content. But what about third-party apps? Here’s what Apple says.

Apple HomeView’s support for third-party apps will be limited

Apple says the new HomeView smart home display is “designed for life at home,” with a wide range of features for managing connected accessories, staying organized, and enjoying entertainment.

That includes everything from controlling smart home devices and checking calendars to watching videos, listening to music, and making FaceTime calls.

However, one question Apple’s announcement didn’t fully answer is the extent to which HomeView will support third-party apps.

According to Apple, in addition to a selection of Apple apps, including Music, Podcasts, and Safari, HomeView will also support “compatible third-party audio and video apps from your iPhone for a familiar experience across devices.”

Interestingly, the fine print for this feature differs between Apple’s HomeView marketing page and the product’s press release.

While the produt page says:

Subscription may be required to access some content and services. Some applications are not available in all areas.

The press release, however, includes an additional detail (emphasis ours):

Subscription may be required to access some content and services. Some applications are not available in all areas. Select apps require a paired and compatible iPhone nearby.

Some of Apple’s own first-party apps will also be available from the iPhone, the company notes. That includes Audiobooks, Apple Music Classical, News, and TV.

Apple has yet to detail how the iPhone proximity requirement will work, and whether developers of apps in supported categories will need to take any additional steps to support HomeView.

	

According ot Wired, “a handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps.” Wired adds that “if your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup.”

So it looks like HomeView’s third-party app support will rely on the existing CarPlay framework, rather than requiring developers to build apps specifically for the device. It remains unclear, though, whether this will extend to other CarPlay app categories, such as communication and AI assistants, or also be limited to media apps.

We have reached out to Apple for clarification on how third-party app support will work, and will update this post if we hear back.

title: Apple marks first Apple TV 4K ‘vintage’ with new model imminent
snippet: The original Apple TV 4K from 2017 has just been added to Apple’s “vintage” products list. Here’s what that means. more…
fullText:
The original Apple TV 4K from 2017 has just been added to Apple’s “vintage” products list. Here’s what that means.

Original Apple TV 4K is ‘vintage’ and may have reduced repair availability 

If you’re still running the first Apple TV 4K model, which debuted nearly a decade ago, repairs for the product might get more complicated soon.

That’s because as spotted by MacRumors, the original Apple TV 4K has been marked “vintage” by Apple.

The company keeps a list of vintage and obsolete products here on its website.

’Vintage’ means over five years have passed since a product stopped being available for sale

’Obsolete’ means over seven years have passed since sales discontinued

If your product is marked “obsolete,” then Apple will no longer offer service or hardware repairs. 

If it’s “vintage,” then Apple can still service it in most cases. However, that’s dependent on parts availability.

So if you have an original Apple TV 4K and might need to get it serviced, you’ll want to do that as soon as possible. Or alternatively, you can check out the new Apple TV 4K that’s being unveiled next Tuesday at the ‘Welcome home’ event.

fullText:
Oppo has officially revealed ColorOS 17, its Android 17 update, to global markets this week and, along with that, confirmed a list of devices poised to get the update.

ColorOS 17 is Oppo’s Android 17 update, and it has two main focuses – smooth performance, and AI. It’s also packed with Liquid Glass design elements, as if that should surprise anyone at this point. 

Oppo calls its Liquid Glass copy “Flow,” with the “Luminous Rendering Engine” powering animations that react to your touch. Oppo says:

ColorOS 17 reimagines how you interact with the system. It senses the pressure and direction of your touch, responding with fluid, elastic motion and nuanced lighting effects that make every interaction feel truly alive. With the all-new Unified Rendering Architecture, transitions between elements are more seamless and refined than ever.

Oppo says that ColorOS 17 is also faster and more reliable, touting 55% “more stable app launches” and 25% better app retention in memory. 

	

As with anything else in 2026, AI is a big part of the update, with Oppo continuing to build out features like AI Mind Space (similar to Pixel Screenshots and Nothing’s Essential Space), adding “AI Mind Pilot” as an agentic AI service, “AI Mind Suggest” as a proactive flight companion, an “AI Photo Agent” is a prompt-based photo editor.

title: Apple’s new ‘Switch to Safari’ campaign details why you should ditch Chrome
snippet: Apple is kicking off a new campaign today to promote Safari’s benefits over Chrome. With a new “Switch to Safari” page on its website and a pair of new YouTube videos, Apple wants everyone to know Safari is “a more powerful and private browser than Chrome.” more…
fullText:
Apple is kicking off a new campaign today to promote Safari’s benefits over Chrome. With a new “Switch to Safari” page on its website and a pair of new YouTube videos, Apple wants everyone to know Safari is “a more powerful and private browser than Chrome.”

On the new website, Apple touts several advantages of Safari over Chrome, including better battery life, stronger privacy protections, and faster performance.

Safari offers up to 5 hours more video streaming on your Mac compared with Chrome.

Chrome doesn’t remember which distractions you want to keep hidden.

Chrome lets more third-party trackers follow you across the web and collect and sell your data to advertisers.

Safari is up to 35% faster than Chrome when loading frequently visited sites on Mac.

The site also includes a side-by-side Safari vs Chrome comparison chart, alongside details on features including Reader Mode, Notify Me, Profiles, Apple Pay, and more.

	

In addition to the new “Switch to Safari” website, Apple has also published two YouTube videos showcasing Safari’s Distraction Control and Intelligent Tracking Prevention.

You can check out the new page on Apple’s website and watch the new videos below. This is only the latest example of Apple’s head-to-head promotion of Safari vs Chrome. Earlier this year, the company launched a new “Privacy on iPhone” campaign promoting Safari as the more private alternative to Chrome.

snippet: iCloud+ is best known for adding iCloud storage, but Apple keeps improving and expanding its suite of benefits for subscribers. Here’s everything new for iCloud+ added in the last few weeks. more…
fullText:
iCloud+ is best known for adding iCloud storage, but Apple keeps improving and expanding its suite of benefits for subscribers. Here’s everything new for iCloud+ added in the last few weeks.

iCloud+ additions include HomeKit Secure Video upgrades, free Apple TV and Arcade for many, higher AI usage limits, more

If you subscribe to iCloud+ or Apple One, you’re probably getting more benefits than you realize.

	

Beyond extra storage, iCloud+ includes features like Hide My Email, iCloud Private Relay, full Apple Invites access, and more.

Here’s everything new for iCloud+ subscribers added in the last few weeks:

HomeKit Secure Video upgrades: Ahead of new Home products launching this week, Apple has upgraded HomeKit Secure Video in several ways. iOS 27’s powerful new features include 4K support, generated video descriptions, clip searching, and noteworthy clips.

Custom Email Domain: If you run a small business or want to use custom emails for your family or for any other reason, iCloud+ lets you set up personalized addresses for domains you own. You were previously limited to three personalized email addresses, but now you can create up to 10 per domain.

Apple TV and Arcade added in 100+ countries: It doesn’t apply to the US, but iCloud+ subscribers in more than 100 countries now get Apple TV and Arcade thrown in at no additional cost. It’s a huge upgrade for many users that makes the service more of a no-brainer in supported territories.

Higher AI usage limits in iOS 27: Specifics are still unclear, but when Apple unveiled iOS 27, it said select iCloud+ plans would include higher usage limits for AI features. We haven’t yet seen evidence of Apple restricting access to AI features, but affected features include Siri AI, new Photos editing tools, Image Playground, and more.

All of these improvements have been added with no price change for subscribers.

title: New Apple TV 4K launching this week with five big upgrades
snippet: A new Apple TV 4K will be unveiled tomorrow as part of Apple’s ‘Welcome home’ event. Here are five upgrades it’s rumored to bring. more…
fullText:
A new Apple TV 4K will be unveiled tomorrow as part of Apple’s ‘Welcome home’ event. Here are five upgrades it’s rumored to bring.

This Tuesday, October 13 Apple is holding its ‘Welcome home’ event where it will unveil several long-awaited Home products.

One of those is a new Apple TV 4K, the first update to the device since 2022.

Here are five new features reportedly coming:

A19 chip, up from the current A15 Bionic

Siri AI

Microphone built into Apple TV box for Siri

Updated Siri Remote with built-in speaker

N1 wireless chip

The A19 chip should make the Apple TV 4K run smoother than current hardware, and offer a significant upgrade over the A15 in the 2022 model. It will importantly also add support for Siri AI.

As is clear from the list of features above, Siri AI is a central focus of the new Apple TV.

Siri won’t merely get a software improvement. It will also be easier to interact with thanks to the built-in microphone in the Apple TV 4K box.

	

Similar to a HomePod, this will enable interacting with Siri entirely by voice, with no need to hit the button on the Siri Remote. I suspect you’ll even be able to ask Siri to find the remote, and it will play a noise on the new Siri Remote so you can find where you left it.

The N1 wireless chip is expected to enable improved reliability with features like AirDrop, and could tie into other Apple Home-related feature improvements.

title: LineageOS support finally comes to Pixel 10 and 10a lineup
snippet: After a protracted wait, LineageOS is now officially available for the entire Pixel 10 lineup and the more affordable Pixel 10a. more…
fullText:
After a protracted wait, LineageOS is now officially available for the entire Pixel 10 lineup and the more affordable Pixel 10a.

Over a year since its release, it’s great news that Pixel 10 owners now have the option to flash LineageOS on their devices, but the long wait is likely due to circumstances beyond the Lineage team’s control.

Google has made it harder for ROM projects in recent years, making it harder for projects like Lineage and Graphene, as the company is no longer sharing device trees and driver binaries. This coincided with the launch of Android 16, and so it has likely stalled some of the development for the last generation of hardware.

On top of that, delays to public kernel downloads for Pixel devices haven’t been ideal.

	

Some of this likely accounts for the delay in LineageOS builds for Pixel 10. At least the good news is that builds are now available for download on the same day LineageOS 24 was announced. This latest version is the Android 17 build for the custom ROM and comes with a number of changes to take better advantage of the enhancements added in early June 2026.

This release includes a whole host of Material 3 Expressive changes to the default app suite with a brand new “Canvas” image editor. Security patches are accounted for up to October 2026, meaning you are fully secure if you do prefer an AI-free experience with Lineage on your Pixel 10.

It’s worth noting that Pixel 10 Pro XL, 10 Pro Fold, and Pixel 10a builds are not yet live, but nightly Pixel 10 and 10 Pro builds are live right now.

title: Apple TV 4K and HomeView: The best and worst of $299
snippet: Wow, $299. That’s a very surprising price. For HomeView, Apple’s all-new smart display, $299 feels surprisingly affordable. For Apple TV 4K, $299 feels surprisingly painful. more…
fullText:
Wow, $299. That’s a very surprising price. For HomeView, Apple’s all-new smart display, $299 feels surprisingly affordable. For Apple TV 4K, $299 feels surprisingly painful.

HomeView for $299 feels like an invitation to try a new product category

HomeView looks like a hit. Without actually seeing or hearing it, the verdict is still out. What we can judge now is the pitch. 

In classic Apple fashion, the company is hardly the first to deliver a smart display. Yet HomeView appears to have the polish and consideration that an iPhone user would expect.

At $299, it seems Apple is pricing HomeView more as an invitation to try a new category of product. I’m intrigued.

Apple TV 4K for $299 feels like Apple already knows the customer

Then there’s the Apple TV 4K. At $299, it feels priced more like specialized hardware. Unlike HomeView, Apple TV 4K has a price history.

In 2021, Apple sold two Apple TV boxes: Apple TV HD for $149, and Apple TV 4K (2nd generation) for $179.

Both boxes ran tvOS with an App Store, but customers didn’t love that 4K support costed nearly $200.

By the end of the following year, Apple TV 4K (3rd generation) arrived in two flavors: 64GB with no Thread or Ethernet for $129, or 128GB with Thread and Ethernet for $149.

This was viewed as a great cost correction compared to the previous generation. Better hardware and a better price? That sounds too good to be true.

But it was true for a while. Then Apple raised prices on a number of existing products in June. You may recall Apple TV 4K being one of the more painful price jumps, both due to the percent increase and the age of the hardware.

The $129 model jumped to $199, and the $149 model jumped to $249.

Today’s Apple TV 4K replaces the $249 model with an even higher $299 price.

We’re now back to the original Apple TV starting price from 2007. Boy, what a relief when Apple switched from local storage to streaming with the vastly different Apple TV (2nd generation) puck for $99.

Apple TV 4K the best experience, but it’s for fewer people now

Anyway, things are different in 2026. You can literally buy a 65-inch 4K LED TV with the Apple TV app (and all the other streaming apps) built-in for $299.

Where does that leave the Apple TV 4K? It’s increasingly positioned not as a way to add streaming apps to your TV, but as a very particular way to bring the full Apple experience to your TV.

But did Apple get the feature set for the price right?

Adding mics to the box itself is a nice touch, especially since other set-top boxes already do this. There’s also the chip upgrade.

Another big new feature is support for creating a home theater experience beyond stereo speaker output with a pair of big HomePod speakers and a pair of new HomePod mini 2 speakers. That’s a $1300 experience between the set-top box and four speakers.

Personally, I’ve stayed on the Apple TV 4K (2nd-gen) from 2021 without any complaints. I don’t know how much I’ll use Siri AI from my TV, but having it come to the box I already own is a nice surprise.

A specialized home theater experience isn’t a priority in the budget right now, so I’m plenty happy with my 55-inch 4K LED that costed me $168 on sale from Hisense. It’s not the absolute best TV I’ve ever owned, but it’s plenty enough for me. Attaching a $299 Apple TV 4K to it would almost feel wrong.

	

But if a premium home theater experience is at the top of your priorities and cost isn’t a concern, Apple TV 4K at $299 is a sure upgrade over built-in TV experiences for Apple users.

For now, I’m just grateful that I’m getting most of that experience from a purchase made years ago.

Hopefully there’s an Apple TV option in the future that feels less overpowered and overpriced needs and budgets like mine in the future. At this point, even a version without the $59 Siri Remote in the box would feel more palatable.

Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Nothing’s CMF launches new wireless speakers that look like milk cartons
snippet: Nothing’s CMF brand has launched new wireless speakers, the first in the lineup, and they look like milk cartons. more…
fullText:
Nothing’s CMF brand has launched new wireless speakers, the first in the lineup, and they look like milk cartons.

The CMF Speaker S is a single-driver speaker with 10W output and 18-hour battery life, Google Fast Pair, and the ability to pair two speakers together for stereo or party modes. 

Meanwhile, CMF Speaker M has the same feature set but with a 25W woofer and 10W tweeter for a broader soundstage, as well as tossing in IP68 dust/water resistance for better outdoor use.

Both feature NFC pairing and controls through the same Nothing X app used for Nothing’s earbuds and headphones. 

	

As far as the design goes, both speakers look a lot like milk cartons. Each comes in black/gray, orange, white, and turquoise color options, each with a different design for the multi-function knob. That knob controls volume, play/pause, and other functions which are customizable. There are dedicated buttons on the back for pairing and Auracast.

CMF Speaker S starts at $59 while Speaker M starts at $109. Both are available now.

title: Apple unveils new HomeView smart display: pre-order today for $299
snippet: Apple today officially unveiled its new HomeView smart display. HomeView features a 7-inch square display and comes in two versions: one with a speaker base and another for wall mounting. You can pre-order HomeView today for $299. It will start arriving to customers on November 13. Here’s everything you need to know about HomeView. more…
fullText:
Apple today officially unveiled its new HomeView smart display. HomeView features a 7-inch square display and comes in two versions: one with a speaker base and another for wall mounting.

You can pre-order HomeView today for $299. It will start arriving to customers on November 13.

Here’s everything you need to know about HomeView.

Apple HomeView: Features, specs, price, and more

HomeView features a 7-inch Liquid Retina display that’s connected to a domed speaker base with a stainless steel hinge with tilt support. The display features Apple’s True Tone technology and 500 nits of brightness. It can also dim to 0.3 nits, making it great for a nightstand. 

There’s also a separate wall-mounted version of HomeView. This model can be “attached to a wall using three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home, with options for self-installation or professional installation.” 

Here are the details on those wall-mounting options from Apple: 

HomeView (Wall Mounted) will be available with a choice of three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home. Power Mount USB‑C Wall Connector, available starting at $59.95 (U.S.), and Power Mount AC Wired, available starting at $79.95 (U.S.), can be ordered starting today from apple.com/store and in the Apple Store app. Power Mount PoE Wired will be available starting in early 2027 for $129.95 (U.S.).

Apple says the HomeView interface will intelligently adjust based on how far away you are. It will show “simpler information that’s viewable from across the room” as well as “richer detail” as you step closer. 

HomeView can also recognize up to six different people and deliver a “personalized experience” for each one. This includes a personalized Home Screen with apps and widgets. “Personal content stays private from others, while shared photo albums and music can be easily enjoyed by everyone in a household, including guests,” Apple says. 

There is a collection of “playful and informative” faces for HomeView: 

Users can personalize HomeView with a collection of playful and informative faces that display information at a glance, taking full advantage of the vibrant Liquid Retina display. The Photos face brings cherished memories to life with stunning Portrait-style depth effects that keep the subject sharp while creating a beautifully blurred foreground and background. 

By selecting a shared album, users can turn HomeView into a living photo frame that loved ones near and far can help fill. The Flow face dynamically responds to physical presence and movement, transforming HomeView into a piece of interactive art. And even Snoopy comes to life on HomeView, with animations that reflect the time of day, the weather, sporting events, and holiday moments.

HomeView supports Siri AI. Apple says that users with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad can tap into personal context. Users without an Apple Intelligence-capable device can still use Siri AI on HomeView for world knowledge and music discovery. 

For audio quality, Apple says HomeView has a “custom-engineered acoustic system” with two full-range drivers in the display, plus a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators.

Here are some more HomeView tidbits: 

It has a Center Stage camera for FaceTime calls. 

There’s a “Home Modular” face that gives easy access to smart home accessories. The “Home Camera” face can livestream up to nine video feeds at once.

HomeView isn’t available in the European Union because Siri AI isn’t available there either. Apple says it is “working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward.” 

The table-top version of HomeView is available in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray. The wall-mounted version is available in space gray and silver. You can pre-order both today for $299, with availability beginning November 13.

snippet: After releasing a carrier settings update last week to address cellular issues affecting some iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T, Apple is now rolling out a different carrier bundle update for devices running the iOS 27.2 beta. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
After releasing a carrier settings update last week to address cellular issues affecting some iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T, Apple is now rolling out a different carrier bundle update for devices running the iOS 27.2 beta. Here are the details.

Apple updates AT&T carrier bundle for iOS 27.2 beta

Last Friday, Apple confirmed to 9to5Mac that a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T were experiencing an issue that could cause their devices to lose cellular service and become unable to make calls.

Apple said iOS 27.0.1, alongside a new carrier settings update, was meant to prevent the issue from affecting additional devices. However, iPhones that had already lost service would still require a hardware replacement.

Tonight, as spotted by Aaron Perris on X, Apple began rolling out another carrier bundle update for iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T, this time specifically for devices running the iOS 27.2 beta.

Apple has just released an emergency carrier bundle update for AT&T users using an iPhone 18 Pro Max on 27.2 beta.

Version 72.0.3 up from 72.0.2

This comes after Apple released 72.1 for iOS 27.0 users last week

— Aaron (@aaronp613) October 9, 2026

Reports of the problem first surfaced in late September, when some iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T found that their devices had suddenly lost access to calls, texts, and cellular data, instead displaying “SOS” in the status bar.

Notably, the issue has only affected the iPhone 18 Pro Max, which uses a Qualcomm modem in the United States. The iPhone 18 Pro, which uses Apple’s C2 modem, has not been affected.

Apple’s carrier settings update released last week brought AT&T users on iOS 27.0 to version 72.1. However, users running the iOS 27.2 beta remained on the older 72.0.2 carrier bundle.

Tonight’s release reportedly bumps those devices to carrier bundle version 72.0.3, likely extending Apple’s AT&T carrier changes to iPhone 18 Pro Max users who are testing the iOS 27.2 beta.

title: Apple says beloved MacBook is now ‘obsolete,’ more products too
snippet: Apple has just updated its list of vintage and obsolete products, adding the final model of the beloved 12-inch MacBook to the “obsolete” list alongside two other products. more…
fullText:
Apple has just updated its list of vintage and obsolete products, adding the final model of the beloved 12-inch MacBook to the “obsolete” list alongside two other products.

All 12-inch MacBook models are now obsolete, as iPad 6 and BeatsX join list too

Today Apple marked three additional products as “obsolete” on its website.

The company keeps a public list of vintage and obsolete products here. It’s regularly updated with new additions based on how long ago a product stopped being available for purchase.

Essentially, if a product stopped being on sale from Apple 5 or more years ago, it’s considered “vintage.” This means Apple will still service the product, but parts availability may be limited.

If a product stopped being sold 7 or more years ago, it’s marked “obsolete.” Obsolete products are no longer eligible for repairs or any other servicing from Apple.

The latest obsolete products include:

MacBook (Retina, 12-inch, 2017)

iPad (6th generation) in Wi-Fi and Wi-Fi + Cellular models

BeatsX in a variety of colors, including Burned Red, Defiant Black-Red, Deep Black, Pure White, and Sky Blue

If you own any of these products, Apple will no longer be able to service them.

The most notable addition is the MacBook, as the 2017 model is the last one Apple produced before the line was discontinued. The 2015 and 2016 models were already on the obsolete list.

While the 12-inch MacBook was pitched by Apple as a type of MacBook Air successor, it never took off with consumers despite having a loyal base of fans who loved it.

title: Apple wins early access to OpenAI documents and employee testimony in trade secrets lawsuit
snippet: Judge Edward Davila today granted some of Apple’s requests for expedited discovery in its trade secrets lawsuit against former employees, OpenAI, and io Products. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Judge Edward Davila today granted some of Apple’s requests for expedited discovery in its trade secrets lawsuit against former employees, OpenAI, and io Products. Here are the details.

A bit of background

A few months ago, Apple filed a trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products.

In a nutshell, Apple says Liu and Tan improperly accessed or used confidential information about its products and technologies to help advance OpenAI’s consumer hardware development efforts. Apple also accuses the defendants of improperly obtaining information from other Apple employees during recruitment interviews.

You can read more about Apple’s original filing here.

As part of the lawsuit, Apple asked Judge Edward Davila to issue a preliminary injunction to prevent the defendants from further embedding the alleged trade secrets in their hardware development while the case plays out.

Apple also requested expedited discovery, seeking early access to internal documents, forensic evidence, and testimony from OpenAI employees to better understand the extent of the alleged misappropriation and support its injunction request.

OpenAI opposed the motion, arguing that Apple’s demands were overly broad and that expedited discovery was unnecessary given that the regular process was about to begin.

Which brings us to today.

Judge partially grants Apple’s requests

In a decision issued today, Judge Davila granted most of Apple’s requests, while rejecting others and postponing a decision on those he considered overly broad.

That includes ordering the defendants to turn over several categories of documents and evidence, including:

All forensic images that Defendants have already collected in connection with the subject matter of Apple’s claims, including those [examined by OpenAI’s forensic expert];

All documents used to guide or conduct the interviews of candidates from Apple for OpenAI’s Consumer Hardware Products Group, […] including checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts; and all documents, including Technical Deep Dive presentations or other technical presentations, summarizing or otherwise memorializing the content of those interviews with Apple employees or any reference to any Apple technology or parts.

All LINE conversations between Mr. Liu and Ms. Peng since January 1, 2026, including the conversations that include the messages cited in [a previous filing made by the defendants]

Additionally, Judge Davila authorized Apple to depose Liu, Tan, and Yu-Ting “Alyssa” Peng, as well as corporate representatives from OpenAI and io Products.

On the flip side, Judge Davila rejected Apple’s request for expedited access to OpenAI’s research and development documents regarding metal finishes, power management, and battery functionality for consumer hardware products. Instead, he decided that these will be addressed through the regular discovery process.

Finally, he postponed a series of decisions involving what Apple described as “Apple Originated Information,” finding Apple’s definition “amorphous as currently defined.” On that point, Apple has five days to consult with the defendants and submit a narrower definition to the court if it wishes to take another crack at those requests.

title: LineageOS 24 launches based on Android 17 with app redesigns and simple flash tool
snippet: LineageOS 24 is now official, with the latest builds rolling out based on Android 17, bringing a surprise early release alongside a fresh coat of Material Design 3 Expressive paint, new WebUSB flashing tools, and more. more…
fullText:
LineageOS 24 is now official, with the latest builds rolling out based on Android 17, bringing a surprise early release alongside a fresh coat of Material Design 3 Expressive paint, new WebUSB flashing tools, and more.

Announced in a dedicated and detailed blog post, LineageOS 24 arrives just ahead of a major milestone for the custom ROM project, which celebrates its 10th anniversary on December 24, 2026.

Compared to previous release cycles, the team is well ahead of schedule this time around. Releasing earlier than anticipated following Android 17’s initial June launch, LineageOS 24 gives those running existing builds the opportunity to upgrade to Google’s latest OS version. The release lands as LineageOS 24.0 and incorporates security patches from August 2025 up through October 2026 across supported branches.

While moving to Android 17 is notable alone, there are some other changes that are key to LineageOS 24.

	

One of the biggest headline changes in this release is a heavy focus on app design refreshes. Almost all of the core Lineage apps have been updated to Material Design 3 Expressive, highlighted by a brand-new built-in image editor called Canvas, which handles all the image editing regular stuff like basic cropping, white balance, and filters to pair nicely with Glimpse and Aperture. 

There’s also a major visual overhaul to the Updater, which now supports streamed updates by default to drastically cut down installation times on A/B devices. 

LineageOS 24’s music player, Twelve, has even faster load times for large media libraries, improved Jellyfin support, and a dedicated tab for your most-played tracks. This player was introduced back with LineageOS 22.

Not to be left out, the default browser Jelly now supports PWA-like apps using a new shortcut. This could be huge for those not wanting to install apps from third-party stores.

Installing LineageOS 24 is also getting a bit simpler for those usually not confident in flashing custom ROMs. The team is launching new WebUSB-based flash tools directly via the browser for common installation processes like ADB Fastboot, Amlogic Burn, and Samsung Odin protocols. While standard device wiki guides remain the default and fully supported path, these optional web tools help streamline the process for users looking to avoid extra desktop software.

On the maintenance side, LineageOS is formally restricting future builds for older devices running Linux Kernel versions 4.4 and 4.9. While these legacy kernels can no longer be submitted for LineageOS 23.2 or 24.0 builds, they will remain supported on LineageOS 22.2 with ongoing monthly security patches. Meanwhile, the team has expanded SoC-specific common kernels and commonized legacy device shims to simplify maintenance across popular chips from Qualcomm and Amlogic.

Rollouts will begin hitting a growing selection of supported devices in the coming weeks as maintainers bring them up to compliance. To check if your device is ready or to follow the upgrade path, you can head over to the official LineageOS Wiki.

title: Tim Cook on his first month after Apple CEO transition: ‘I’m not meddling’
snippet: Tim Cook visited Apple’s Battersea campus in London this week, mingling with King Charles as part of the company’s new partnership with The King’s Trust. At Apple’s Battersea headquarters, Cook also sat down with The Independent for an in-depth interview on the partnership and his first month as Apple’s executive chairman. more…
fullText:
Tim Cook visited Apple’s Battersea campus in London this week, mingling with King Charles as part of the company’s new partnership with The King’s Trust.

At Apple’s Battersea headquarters, Cook also sat down with The Independent for an in-depth interview on the partnership and his first month as Apple’s executive chairman.

Cook stepped down as Apple CEO last month, passing the torch to John Ternus. In this week’s interview, Cook outlined that the transition “actually started years ago.”

“It’s been an interesting transition. We really set out to have the best transition ever, a textbook example that people could look back to and learn from. It actually started years ago. Obviously, these things are not quick things and I feel so great about how things are going I think everything has gone sort of exactly the way I had envisioned it. And it feels fantastic. Because Apple deserved the best.”

Ternus’s tenure as CEO began with the launch of the iPhone Duo, which Cook said was fully planned. “I wanted John to have some wind at his back,” Cook explained. “And the wind at Apple is very much based on the product cycle.”

Cook also emphasized that he’s focused on “worldwide policy” as Apple’s executive chairman, noting the “incredible level of trust” between him and Ternus. While Cook is helping Ternus in “any way he sees fit,” he makes it clear he’s “not meddling.”

“First of all, John and I have an incredible level of trust in each other. The relationship must be based on trust, and the communication must be frequent and significant. But other than that, what I’m focused on right now is worldwide policy. And the interface with governments around the world matters because there are lots of things where we’re trying to advance or advocate for change. There’s a significant amount of work in that, and I’m doing that and helping John in any way he sees fit. I’m not meddling. I’m not a meddler.”

What kind of advice has Cook given Ternus? “Don’t mimic me.” You can read the full interview over at The Independent. It includes a great discussion on Apple’s new partnership with The King’s Trust.

title: Cambridge Heavy Industries has been quietly building a desktop fusion device
snippet: Fusion power startup Cambridge Heavy Industries is building a small, laser-powered fusion device to fuel the coming wave of fusion power plants.
fullText:
Fusion power usually conjures images of massive industrial facilities laced with large lasers or magnets, but a startup in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has been quietly building a device that can fit on a tabletop.

The optics of the device were on display behind Yun Kai, co-founder and CEO of Cambridge Heavy Industries, while he chatted with me on a video call. The company has been operating in stealth out of a small lab near MIT, and Kai gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at the technology it has been developing.

“We purposely built a small modular reactor. It’s tiny, it’s benchtop,” he told me. “Because it’s small, it makes everything easier.”

The small size has allowed Cambridge Heavy to experiment and iterate quickly. “The small module nature can enable 50 to 80 experiments, 50 to 80 shots per day,” he said. Data from those experiments will feed simulations that use AI to optimize the design.

That nimble approach has attracted investor attention. The startup recently raised a $6.2 million seed round led by Azolla Ventures with participation from Overlay, Neta Foundation, P3A, MassCEC, and the Rothrock family.

Cambridge Heavy’s fusion reactor uses lasers to compress a fuel target, similar to the groundbreaking experiment that proved controlled fusion reactions could produce more power than they consume. But unlike other inertial confinement designs, Cambridge Heavy’s minimizes the number of lasers required to spark fusion.

The system uses two main lasers to drive ignition. One laser is split into multiple beam lines that deliver light in concentric rings. Those rings of laser light are timed to hit the flat, round fuel target successively, starting from the outside and working in. The first ring starts a compression wave within the target that starts traveling inward. The subsequent laser rings are timed to boost the wave at just the right moment to further compress the fuel. 

As the shock wave reaches the center of the target, a laser fires on the target, generating heat and producing a magnetic field. With the right amount of pressure and heat, fusion occurs. 

Cambridge Heavy’s design generates high pressures with relatively low laser power, Kai said. The concept emerged from the lab of Keith Nelson, a chemist at MIT. There, researchers used the laser pulses to study materials under extreme conditions. As they ramped up pressures, they realized they were approaching fusion-ready conditions.

In about a decade, Cambridge Heavy plans to develop a power plant from the concept, though that’ll require scaling up the design. It will be larger than the current benchtop prototype, though not quite as large as other fusion power plants. Kai said it should be about the size of two basketball courts, and it will test whether the approach can generate enough energy to support a power plant.

Before that happens, though, Cambridge Heavy plans to use its smaller-scale devices to make tritium, a rare isotope of hydrogen that will be used by nearly all fusion power plants in the works today. Tritium sells for around $30,000 per gram today.

Each power plant won’t need a lot of tritium — on the order of grams per year — but the substance is so rare that only about 40 kilograms exist today. One recent study predicts that without new sources, the fusion power industry will be short by about 28 kilograms in 2054. At current prices, that’s about $840 million worth of tritium.

Fusion startups are in the process of designing fuel systems that will help the reactors be largely self-sufficient when it comes to tritium supplies, though they may need occasional top-ups. But that process could take up to 10 years, Kai said, giving Cambridge Heavy years of potential revenue as it pursues its power plant.

title: Licube wants to be the fuel provider to the fusion power industry — see how at TechCrunch Disrupt
snippet: Fusion power plants will need a lot of lithium, and Licube is preparing to be a key supplier.
fullText:
If fusion power pans out, and there are signs that it will, the world will need a lot more lithium.

That’s the bet behind Licube, a startup that has licensed technology from Hirosaki University in Japan, to purify lithium-6, the form of lithium that fusion plants need to make their own fuel, out of naturally occurring lithium.

The reason comes down to the fuel supply. A lot of things have to go right for fusion power to hit the grid, and one of them is the fuel. Most planned plants would run on a mix of two fuels, deuterium and tritium. Deuterium is easy to come by, but tritium is extremely rare in nature, and it’s an open secret in the fusion world that there isn’t enough of it to power every planned plant.

The proposed workaround is to make tritium on site, inside the power plant itself. A fusion reaction gives off a stream of fast-moving particles called neutrons. Startups plan to surround the reactor with a blanket of lithium, so that when a neutron strikes a lithium atom, the atom splits into helium and tritium. The tritium can then be collected, purified, and fed back into the reactor as fuel.

Not all lithium does this job equally well. It comes in two slightly different forms, lithium-6 and lithium-7, named for their weights. Lithium-6 is far better at capturing neutrons and producing tritium, but it makes up only about 7.5% of natural lithium, and the rest is the heavier lithium-7. Separating the two is difficult, and there is little capacity to do it today, so the world doesn’t have enough lithium-6 either.

Licube sees a big market in solving that problem. “If fusion comes online, it should be a $50 billion market by 2040,” Yohei Kiguchi, co-founder and CEO of Licube, told TechCrunch.

Licube is one of 20 startups that are presenting onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco as part of the Startup Battlefield pitch competition.

While fusion has the potential to capture a significant chunk of the multitrillion-dollar energy market, fusion startups are still years away from building their first power plants. 

“Fusion is the biggest market in the future, but we also understand the future might be late by a few years,” Kiguchi said.

Until fusion becomes a major market, Licube plans to use the same technology to purify lithium for use in semiconductor, pharmaceutical, fission reactors, and spacecraft industries.

The core technology is based on the electrolyzer, a device that uses electrical current to drive chemical reactions. In Licube’s case, lithium is dissolved in a liquid on one side of a ceramic membrane. As electrical current flows from one side of the membrane to the other, lithium-6 moves faster. Licube can then draw off that liquid and separate the lithium-6.

The goal is to enrich the lithium to at least 99.995% lithium-6. Fusion companies can feed that highly enriched lithium into their fuel breeding systems. 

Kiguchi was inspired to start Licube after visiting ITER, the experimental fusion reactor being built in the south of France. He said he was living a couple of hours’ drive away in Monaco after retiring from his previous company, Enechange, an energy-switching platform network in Japan.

“I found out that I was too young to retire,” he said. “I’m an energy guy. I want to do something bigger.”

title: Forget rockets — Longshot wants to fire cargo into space from a gun. See it at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
snippet: Longshot is trying to build a gun big enough to make space data centers a reality.
fullText:
Rockets are, infamously, a real pain in the butt. Our old friend physics forces rockets to be built with almost no room for error, and even then only a small fraction of their weight makes it to orbit.

There are, at least in theory, other ways to do the job — space elevators, centrifuges, or a big chain hanging from a satellite in space and scooping up cargo from Earth. (Blue Origin spent some time thinking about that one before the idea wound up in a Neal Stephenson novel.)

And then there’s an idea dating all the way back to Jules Verne: Use a big gun to shoot a projectile into space. 

Longshot Space Technology, a startup based in Alameda, California, is working on exactly that. The co-founders, CEO Mike Grace and CTO Nato Saichek, see an opportunity to take a technology that has already proven its worth and apply it to the pressing need for space launch. The startup has raised about $20 million from venture investors in service of its mission.

When it comes to frontier technology, Grace says, “you can build something that has a lot of novelty, or you can do something really hard. You don’t get to do both.” He points to SpaceX as an example of a company that has “taken classically de-risked technology and scaled it aggressively.” What SpaceX did with NASA rocket research, he says, Longshot will do with multi-injection guns — designs that give a projectile extra boosts as it moves down the barrel — built for World War II and during 1960s research programs.

The idea is to take all the work done by the first stage of a launch vehicle and collapse that into a reusable accelerator on the ground. Picture a steel pipe mounted horizontally over the ground, with tanks of high-pressure gas attached at ports spread across its length. When a projectile is fired and moves down the barrel, the tanks fire off at precise times to accelerate it — to speeds as high as Mach 4, thus far.

The company is currently firing a 70-foot gun with a six-inch diameter at its test site near Barstow, California, and says it can accelerate projectiles up to near-hypersonic speeds. Soon, it expects to start firing a 140-foot-long gun with a 30-inch diameter at its Alameda test site. After that, the company is preparing to build out a 30-inch diameter gun that is 328-feet long, with plans to extend it to about 3,000 feet — making it the largest gun on the planet. It will be capable of launching 220-pound payloads up to speeds of Mach 8, the team says.

A multi-injection gun built by Longshot Space Technology is fired at a test site in CaliforniaImage Credits:Longshot Space Technology under a Longshot Space Technology license.

These guns will let Longshot keep proving its technology works while also generating revenue from performing hypersonic testing for the U.S. military, which has awarded the company several contracts. Grace envisions building one of his guns on a U.S. military installation like Fort Bliss, where it could be part of the infrastructure for testing the next generation of U.S. interceptors. (And no, the guns don’t need to point up at an angle. Longshot’s projectile is a lifting body, meaning its shape generates lift, so it will aerodynamically gain altitude once it exits the barrel.)

“If you want to practice shooting down a Chinese or Russian hypersonic missile, wouldn’t it be nice not to pay $30 million for that?” Grace asks. “This is a way for half a million, a quarter of a million bucks, of doing hypersonic clay pigeons, throw them and shoot them down, and do it really fast and really cheap.”

The ultimate goal, however, is putting large payloads into space. The team is confident it can scale up its current design to accelerate payloads to as much as five kilometers per second (more than 11,000 mph). That’s fast enough to get into space if the payload, which effectively serves as the second stage of a rocket, has its own propulsion system. But doing that would require a gun 10 kilometers (about six miles) long and nearly 10 feet in diameter. As you might imagine, one problem the company faces is simply finding suitable worksites.

“The hard part is not building the thing, it’s finding a place where they will let you build the thing,” Saichek jokes.

But if Longshot can realize its vision, the math is very attractive: The system is cheap to construct and to fuel, and is highly reusable. Grace expects that if everything works out, they can send payloads to space for a hard-to-believe $50 per kilogram (about $22 per pound). Considering that the much-hyped orbital data center industry needs prices to fall to around $300 per kilogram to get off the ground, that leaves Longshot plenty of room to offer a competitive price.

It will require some modification to launch spacecraft in this form factor and conditions, but at that price point, satellite operators will be willing to try.

title: Justice Department says North Koreans have infiltrated dozens of US companies
snippet: U.S. authorities warn that sanctioned hackers are increasingly targeting Americans to act as facilitators between breached U.S. companies and Pyongyang.
fullText:
The U.S. Department of Justice is warning that hackers working for the North Korean regime are increasingly relying on Americans to facilitate the hacking of U.S. companies.

In an announcement on Tuesday, prosecutors said they have indicted and arrested at least two people, and conducted searches across dozens of suspected “laptop farms” in Texas. The computers were allegedly used by North Koreans to remotely hack into American companies and steal sensitive data.

According to the DOJ, federal authorities seized over 180 computers that they believe American companies had shipped out to their newly hired employees, not realizing that they were sanctioned North Korean spies who had used stolen identities of U.S. citizens to gain employment. The DOJ said that it raided over 40 laptop farms across Texas, the largest disclosed number of homes and residences used for facilitating North Korean hacks, which were owned by at least two American facilitators.

CrowdStrike, which helped the FBI investigate and disrupt the latest North Korean operations, said that laptop farms are “vital” to North Korea in helping its hackers overcome physical, financial, and legal challenges of not physically being in the United States.

The prosecutors said at least 70 U.S.-based companies had been infiltrated by the hackers, who are believed to have generated around $3 million in stolen funds. The DOJ did not name the affected companies, but described them as healthcare, cyber support, retail, communications, and manufacturing sectors across Ohio and 16 other states, including the District of Columbia.

“Increasingly, North Korean IT workers are turning to recruiting American facilitators to counter improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions. These workers are hiring facilitators to complete a wider variety of tasks, and in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals,” the Justice Department said. 

Oftentimes, North Korean hackers use real-looking email addresses, spoofed LinkedIn profiles, and extensive online and social media accounts as cover for their activities.

In a separate public service announcement, the FBI said that there are “thousands” of North Korean state-controlled IT workers working at Western companies, which “pose a significant national security and intellectual property theft insider threat.”

This is the latest wave of arrests, indictments, and enforcement action targeting North Korean activities in the United States in recent years. The breakaway regime has used this “remote IT workers” scheme to allow North Koreans to gain employment with U.S. and European companies, earn a wage, and then steal sensitive information and intellectual property while as employees. The victim companies are then extorted into paying the hackers further. 

The remote IT workers’ scheme is one of several strands of illicit revenue that the North Korean regime aims to generate, including hacking crypto exchanges and open source developer projects, with the aim of funding its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program. The regime is thought to have stolen at least $2 billion in crypto during 2025 alone.

Experts on North Korea have put the number of hacked companies and the amount of stolen crypto as likely much higher than reported.

Earlier this year, CrowdStrike said in a separate report that North Korean hackers were behind around half of all documented “hands-on-keyboard” intrusions over the past year, referring to hacks that are carried out by humans and not automated tools or AI.

title: Science Corporation implants its vision-restoring chip in its first Stargardt disease patient
snippet: Max Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, detailed onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt how his company's work with PRIMA is part of its path toward a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).
fullText:
Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak announced that the company has implanted its vision-restoring chip, PRIMA, into its first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited eye disease that gradually destroys central vision. Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, the brain implant company, explained onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt how the company’s work with PRIMA fits into its broader pursuit of a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).

“The retina is part of the central nervous system,” Hodak said. “We consider cochlear implants, retinal prostheses, motor prostheses, these are all different types of BCIs.”

Hodak outlined a vision in which BCIs expand into a wide range of medical technology applications, rather than simply being a way to control computers.

While PRIMA is commercially available in Europe for patients who’ve lost their sight to geographic atrophy, an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration, the company believes its approach can be applied to multiple diseases, including Stargardt disease, which is currently considered incurable.

Stargardt disease affects the outer retina, causing the gradual death of the eye’s light-sensing cells while potentially sparing the inner retina, the part that passes visual signals onto the brain. It causes a central blind spot that gradually enlarges over time. Approximately 150,000 people worldwide have lost vision due to the disease.

“One of the nice things about this device approach, when I was saying the brain’s a computer, vision is electrical potential, like electrical activity down the optic nerve,” Hodak said. “That’s all vision is to the brain, and so if you can get the optic nerve to signal the rest of the brain correctly, then you can provide vision to it.”

Image Credits:Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch

The company says its first patient with Stargardt disease received the PRIMA implant in May as part of its ongoing trial at the Sydney Eye Hospital in Australia. During the patient’s first rehabilitation session, he saw a letter, and during the second, he was able to read a word.

To use the device, patients undergo an hourlong procedure that plants a small chip in the back of their eye, where the photoreceptors have degenerated. Then they wear camera-equipped glasses that transmit a view of the world to the chip. The implant essentially works like artificial photoreceptors.

“The device that this patient has is a two millimeter by two millimeter implant placed in the back of the eye, and so it’s like looking through a straw,” Hodak said. “It is not a big field of view color vision. It’s a patch in their central vision where … it’s black and white, but it is sharp. It’s high-contrast sharp, and so they can see a couple letters at a time. The next step is to make the field of view bigger. So to make a bigger implant, you have to deal with the curvature of the eye, and we need to make the electrodes smaller so that we get closer to native levels of detail.”

He continued, “I think we have a clear path. There’s a ‘next generation’ that’s being worked on that’ll be in humans in the next year, and over the next five years, I think we’ll be able to get pretty close to native acuity.”

When Hodak founded Science Corporation in 2021 after leaving Neuralink, the company outlined plans to develop advanced neural engineering and brain-computer interface technology. But first, the company wants to prove its methods work and develop a sustainable business, which is why it’s working to restore vision with the visually impaired.

Image Credits:Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch

As for Science Corporation’s brain-computer interface technology, it has previously said that its sensor will be implanted inside the skull and rest on top of the brain, unlike a Neuralink device, which is inserted directly into brain tissue.

The company has said it believes the device could help address neurological conditions, such as possibly monitoring neurological activity in patients with brain tumors. 

“In the near term, we’re going to be applying our first clinical indication, which hasn’t been announced publicly, is a neurodegenerative disease that everybody’s heard of,” Hodak said. “We’re also looking at stroke. For example, if you’ve lost part of your brain because it’s been dead due to stroke, if you can get connections into the deep brain in two different areas, you can imagine adding new cortical areas, just like adding new brain areas entirely — something simply not possible with conventional electrodes. But, I’d say longer term, the long-term mission of the company is to understand how the brain creates the mind and to learn to build engineered brains.”

Hodak went on to note that Science Corporation’s belief is that many people will eventually use some kind of BCI. While the company isn’t designing for “healthy 40-year-olds,” he said,  it believes people will eventually need some kind of BCI by the age of 60 or 70.

“We want to figure out how do we extend not just lifespan but health span,” Hodak said.

title: No Man’s Sky Headlines Apple’s New Wave of iPhone and iPad Games
snippet: Sifu, Vampire Crawler and Dome Keeper also hit the App Store.
fullText:
When Apple revealed the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max last month, there was little about anything new for gaming on the devices. But not to worry, mobile gamers: a lineup of popular indie games is coming to the company’s phones and tablets.

No Man’s Sky, Sifu and Vampire Crawlers are in the first batch of seven new games as part of the App Store’s Indie Games Week, according to a post from Apple on Monday. The titles will be playable on both iPhones and iPads and are currently available for purchase in the store, with the exception of No Man’s Sky, which will be released on Oct. 28.

The new indie titles are: 

			

More from CNET

Sifu ($8)

Vampire Crawlers ($10)

No Man’s Sky ($20)

Little Kitty, Big City ($10)

9 Kings ($9)

Dome Keeper ($10)

Yes, Your Grace 2: Snowfall ($5)

No Man’s Sky, developed by Hello Games, is the standout of the bunch. First released in 2016, the space exploration game launched on PC and PS4 and was met with a negative reaction from players who expected big, beautiful worlds as shown in the original trailer. The backlash was so extensive that it led to an investigation by UK regulators over possible misleading advertising. Hello Games took that criticism and kept updating the game over 10 years, not only delivering on the promises made when the game was first announced, but also surpassing them while growing its player base.

With a vast galaxy to explore, including all previous content expansions, Hello Games says No Man’s Sky can run on the iPhone 11 and newer phones, as well as third-generation iPad Air tablets and newer models. iPhone players can use the touchscreen interface or a controller, while iPad users can use a keyboard and mouse if preferred. 

These games are currently not included with Apple Arcade. No Man’s Sky, 9 Kings, Yes, Your Grace 2: Snowfall and Little Kitty, Big City do have free trials available to those interested in trying out the titles. 

On Tuesday, Apple launched another set of hardware, including new smart home devices, at its Welcome Home event. The Apple HomeView is the company’s soon-to-be-released smart display for controlling new smart home cameras from LG, set to release in November, but preorders are now available.

title: Report: Apple cuts iPhone 18 Pro production due to ‘soft demand’
snippet: Apple has reportedly cut orders for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max due to “soft demand.” A new report from Nikkei Asia says Apple has told select suppliers to cut component production for the devices, as price increases allegedly “dampened consumer demand.” more…
fullText:
Apple has reportedly cut orders for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max due to “soft demand.” A new report from Nikkei Asia says Apple has told select suppliers to cut component production for the devices, as price increases allegedly “dampened consumer demand.”

Price hikes reportedly dampen iPhone 18 Pro demand

The report cites “multiple familiar with the matter,” and claims Apple has “turned more conservative on shipments since early September. Two of those sources claim that component orders for October have been cut by “at least 15%” compared to what Apple originally requested.

“In October alone, we are seeing orders from Apple reducing by 15% to 20% for both the premium models; we don’t know how things would develop from here,” said one of the executive-level sources. The order cuts will affect production volumes for some, but not all, suppliers in October due to differing production lead times, and it is not immediately clear whether Apple will make further adjustments from November onward.

Another anonymous supply chain manager told Nikkei Asia that demand is “not as strong as previous years when all the new models are introduced all together.” This, of course, refers to Apple not releasing the base iPhone 18 until next spring. Still, the suppliers say that this alone doesn’t account for the lower demand. 

	

One source added that they expect a “similar fate for the iPhone Duo” after it’s released, referring to potential production cuts.

Apple increased prices for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max by $100 compared to their predecessors. While hampering demand, this also means that the impact of that lower demand won’t “immediately translate to lower revenue for Apple,” the report explains.

Apple will report its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings on Monday, November 2. This will provide a look at the first several weeks of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max demand.

title: Industrial Next wants factory robots to switch tasks in minutes, not weeks
snippet: Industrial Next helps manufacturers automate complex, delicate tasks that have traditionally required human labor.
fullText:
In most factories, automation is fixed: robots and machines are programmed for one specific task and product. Changing a line means reprogramming and physical retooling, or swapping out equipment, which can take weeks or months. San Francisco-based Industrial Next says it’s changing that.

The startup, which presented today on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, builds AI-driven, self-contained robotic stations powered by proprietary foundation models that connect vision, task context, and motion. The company says this lets a production line be retooled in minutes rather than weeks without traditional programming. The goal is to let manufacturers automate complex and delicate tasks that traditionally require human labor.

The company announced onstage that it’s partnering with BMW Group Technology Office to evaluate Industrial Next’s AI-powered dexterous manipulation for manufacturing.

Industrial Next was founded in 2021 by Lukas Pankau and Allen Pan, both of whom previously worked at Tesla. Pankau served as a lead electrical architect at Tesla before moving on to Waymo. Pan led Tesla’s autonomous factory efforts and later became a chief architect at autonomous driving company Neolix.

The pair came up with the idea for Industrial Next while working together at Tesla. Pankau’s first encounter with Pan was literally tripping over him as Pan was asleep on a factory catwalk after pulling an all-nighter. Although the two didn’t get along at first, they soon realized they shared an obsession with getting things done and had complementary skills. 

After years of watching cutting-edge vehicle and self-driving technology get held back by decades-old factory equipment, the founders realized that manufacturing needed to be rebuilt.

Image Credits:Industrial Next

“We had all these fancy things that we could do on cars. I could run machine learning algorithms to design a car for me. But I couldn’t figure out how to program a robot, and this was pretty common for engineers at Tesla,” Pankau said. “You had this massive divide, right? You had people who are really good at what they’re doing — designing cars and designing self-driving systems — and then you had them effectively stumped at the factory looking at this equipment from the 1980s. And so we started rethinking what this should look like using the technology that we have today and using everything that we know today.”

The two kept thinking about their frustrations with industrial equipment even after moving on to their next jobs. They stayed in touch, often reminiscing about the machines that never functioned the way they wanted, and eventually decided they could do better.

“I was at Waymo at the time, kind of bored out of my mind because I was missing that pace of Tesla,” Pankau said. Pan, he added, was in a similar position at Momenta, a developer of self-driving systems in China. Pan recalled their conclusion: “We’re like, we’re not getting any younger, and we’re still obviously passionate about it. We still keep complaining about industrial technology. Like, this is three years later, we should start the company.”

Pankau notes that traditional industrial robots are typically programmed to perform highly specific, repeatable tasks. As a result, even a small change in the process or product can cause the robot to fail or trigger costly downtime, which forces manufacturers to simplify their products for repeatability.

Making robots truly flexible presents a different challenge. They need enormous amounts of training data and, unlike AI models trained on the internet, robotics lacks the vast datasets needed to teach machines how to perform complex physical tasks. 

Image Credits:Industrial Next

“We can make robots do all these cool things like dance around, because there’s data for that, but we can’t make them assemble high-precision things,” Pankau explained. “This is where we’ve made a lot of progress on using simulated environments to do these high-precision and high-dexterity tasks. The secret sauce for the robots that we have is that we have given them an understanding of the process in general, but we build that understanding using an extremely high-fidelity simulation engine that is close to the real dynamics to where we can let the robot do these kinds of high-precision tasks almost without seeing the parts at all.”

In other words, the robots practice in a highly detailed virtual world that closely mimics real-world physics. Industrial Next’s robotic stations can be reconfigured, combined, and redeployed across product lines. New tasks are taught through simulation and demonstration, rather than hard-coded scripts. 

Pankau explained that some of the startup’s workstations are already used in making one of the world’s most popular smartphones. They handle tasks that manufacturers had tried and failed to automate for years, such as threading a delicate flex cable and snapping a tiny connector cap into place. (He wasn’t at liberty to disclose the customer.) He also described a “film peeling” station, where their AI-powered robots strip protective film off camera modules and buttons at or above human speed with 100% accuracy, even when moved to a new phone model and production line they have never seen.

“We started this company because that is the kind of performance that we wish we had at Tesla, where we were bypassing robot stations because we couldn’t program them effectively enough using traditional technologies,” Pankau said. “Now we want to take this to more complicated tasks than just building a phone. We ultimately want to take this to building a full car end-to-end without any human touching ever.”

To check out more of the Startup Battlefield — along with a slate of established founders and VCs whose takes on the industry you won’t want to miss —  join us at Disrupt, happening this week in downtown San Francisco.

fullText:
For a car that’s supposed to be one of the fastest ever made, the new Tesla Roadster certainly took its sweet-ass time getting here.

It’s been nearly a decade since Elon Musk made the surprise announcement about plans to build a next-gen Roadster. Now, the Tesla Roadster is finally making its production-ready debut at an event in Waco, Texas, Thursday — and the timing couldn’t be worse.

The new Roadster is set to arrive in an EV market beset by high energy prices, political turmoil, and consumer uncertainty. The tax-credit-fueled exuberance of the post-covid years has since given way to slower sales and fewer options. Automakers are scaling back their EV plans as sales stall in the US. Even Tesla, the market leader that has weathered its own share of chaos, is still struggling with shrinking demand and lowered expectations.

But the Roadster isn’t your average EV. It’s the ultimate status symbol, defined by its outrageous promises and elusiveness. Musk has said the Roadster can accelerate from 0–60mph in less than two seconds, will have a top speed over 250mph, and will come with an optional “SpaceX package” that adds cold-gas thrusters, enabling it to “fly a little.”

The Roadster isn’t a compelling product because it might be able to briefly hover (although that would be pretty impressive). In the years since it was first announced, it’s become defined by its unattainability. It’s vaporware in the extreme. After years of missed deadlines, it seemed likely that the Roadster would go the way of the solar roof tiles, battery swapping, robot charging, and other Tesla projects that were once promised but never delivered. Several reservation holders, like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and YouTuber Marques Brownlee, canceled their orders under the assumption that the Roadster would fail to launch. For the average buyer, it was double-locked behind broken promises and an astronomical price tag.

Like a broken clock, Musk occasionally delivers on his outrageous promises — or at least a scaled-down version of the original promise. Tesla’s robotaxi service may not cover 50 percent of the US population, but dozens of its steering-wheel-less Cybercabs currently roam the streets of Austin, Texas. The Cybertruck may not be able to float in water, but it definitely exists. I’m told you can even buy one, though weak demand suggests few people want to.

It’s the ultimate status symbol, defined by its outrageous promises and elusiveness

Now that we know that some version of the next-generation Roadster is going into production, the question shifts to why it even exists. Musk, who has been pushing for Tesla to become less of a company that makes cars and more of a company that makes robots, has said that the Roadster will be the last Tesla vehicle built for human driving. Everything else will be autonomous. The company recently ended production of its original flagship models, the Model S and X, to make room for production of its humanoid Optimus robots. Musk is openly mulling the idea of merging Tesla with his other company, SpaceX, as a way to accelerate in the race for AI. The Roadster has been relegated to relic status before it even reaches a single customer.

The Roadster loses even more of its luster once you realize Tesla has already achieved some of its claimed performance goals. Tesla’s Model S Plaid was released in 2021 with a claimed 0–60mph time of 1.99 seconds (minus a 1-foot rollout), which was later confirmed by independent tests. When Tesla demonstrates its likely very quick Roadster on Thursday, some observers would be forgiven for feeling as if they’ve seen this movie before.

But Tesla watchers have been suffering from déjà vu all year. The company that used to reveal new products every year has since taken to rereleasing products it’s already shown off. This year saw the rereveal of the Cybercab (first announced in 2024), the Semi (2017), and now the Roadster (also 2017). In fact, the Cybertruck is the only new consumer vehicle Tesla has delivered in the last five years — and it’s been a noticeable flop.

Once it enters production, the Roadster will face fresh challenges. When the vehicle was first revealed, Tesla didn’t know that the electric hypercar market would be so chilly. Since then, there have been several automakers that have attempted to make two-door EVs at that price point and performance level, without any success. While hyper-EVs like the Rimac Nevera, Pininfarina Battista, and Lotus Evija achieved impressive engineering feats, they faced low sales volumes, severe production delays, and weak demand.

The Roadster has been relegated to relic status before it even reaches a single customer.

It turns out the super rich that can afford exotic cars that cost upwards of $1 million overwhelmingly prefer internal combustion engines. The appeal is rarely rooted in utility or straight-line 0–60mph numbers. Instead, it relies on brand loyalty, mechanical characteristics, engine noise, and manual or dual-clutch gear shifting. Bugatti CEO Mate Rimac has noted that despite setting dozens of world records with the 1,900-plus-hp Rimac Nevera, the company struggled to sell its planned run of 150 units. He compared high-end electric hypercars to high-tech smartwatches — capable of incredible feats, but lacking the emotional prestige of a handcrafted timepiece.

Ferrari opted for four doors when it designed its first EV and still faced near universal ridicule when the Luce was finally revealed. Porsche delayed pure-EV replacements for the 718 Cayman and Boxster multiple times. Even Lamborghini abandoned its planned pure EV in favor of an all-hybrid lineup.

Image: SpaceX

It’s not even clear that the Roadster’s performance capabilities — 0–60 under two seconds, or even less than one second in certain configurations, if Musk is to be believed — will help bring in customers. When the original Tesla Roadster arrived in 2008, sub-four-second 0–60 times were reserved for high-end exotics. Today, the physics of electric motors make extreme straight-line acceleration relatively easy to achieve across different form factors. There are other limiting factors, like weight and thermal mechanics, that could blunt the Roadster’s ambitions. Two-door sports cars are built to be light, agile, and engaging around corners. But battery packs are heavy and can weigh down a sports car on twisty roads or racetracks.

The Roadster doesn’t need to be a huge success in order to be a win for Tesla. The company has had two generationally successful products — the Model 3 and Model Y — that will define its legacy going forward. The Roadster is likely to be a limited-run, ultra-high-end supercar where success is measured not by sales volume, but by scarcity. It may be the case that selling only a handful of Roadsters plays directly into to Tesla’s strategy.

While Tesla builds human-driven sports cars as a legacy afterthought, Musk’s eyes are fixed on low Earth orbit, where SpaceX plans to launch solar-powered orbital data centers to fuel his AI ambitions. Tesla has already moved on to AI and autonomous tech, rendering its own human-driven halo car obsolete before it launched. The last time a Tesla Roadster captured the world’s collective imagination was when Musk launched one into space in 2018. That car is still drifting millions of miles away with a dummy “Starman” astronaut in the driver’s seat.

Eight years later, the next-gen Roadster likely arrives as a grounded, earthbound artifact of a future Tesla has already left behind.

title: Here’s how HomeView’s facial recognition works
snippet: Apple announced its HomeView smart display this morning. Apple says HomeView can recognize up to six different people to deliver a “personalized experience” for each user. John Gruber at Daring Fireball has more details on how HomeView’s facial recognition feature works. more…
fullText:
Apple announced its HomeView smart display this morning. Apple says HomeView can recognize up to six different people to deliver a “personalized experience” for each user.

John Gruber at Daring Fireball has more details on how HomeView’s facial recognition feature works.

HomeView’s face recognition support

According to Gruber, a user must have a “registered personal device” with Apple Intelligence support in order to be “recognized” by HomeView. That device must be on the home’s Wi-Fi network and have been “recently unlocked.”

Your first question might be how this facial recognition to identify users works, using a Center Stage camera alone, when other products (like, notably, the iPhone Duo) don’t let you unlock using the camera alone. HomeView does not have FaceID. I asked about this and Apple reps said that first, your home is (reasonably!) presumed to be a safe space. But in order for users to be recognized — by voice or face — they must have a “registered personal device” that supports Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, that device must be present on the home’s Wi-Fi network, and it must have been recently unlocked.

	

Gruber also points to a footnote from the HomeView press release, which reads:

Personal context requests require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad running the latest software version with Siri AI turned on and set to a supported language.

This means the Apple Watch does not count as a “registered personal device” for facial recognition on HomeView.

HomeView is available to pre-order today for $299 and will be released on November 13.

title: HomeView isn’t launching in the EU, here’s why
snippet: Apple unveiled its new HomeView product today, and it’s available for pre-order now. But unfortunately HomeView isn’t coming to the EU, at least for now. Here’s why. more…
fullText:
Apple unveiled its new HomeView product today, and it’s available for pre-order now. But unfortunately HomeView isn’t coming to the EU, at least for now. Here’s why.

Apple cites Siri AI’s absence from iOS as reason why it can’t launch HomeView in EU

Today Apple launched its Siri AI-centric ‘HomeView’ smart display product.

But if you’re in the EU, you can’t order one yet. And that’s not a mistake or oversight.

Per Apple’s press release:

Apple HomeView is not available for sale in the European Union, as Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS in the EU. Apple is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward.

	

It’s a surprising decision, since presumably Apple could launch HomeView with Siri AI in the EU—just not with support for features that tie in with iOS 27.

Siri AI is available with macOS Golden Gate and visionOS 27 in the EU, for example. That’s because macOS and visionOS aren’t deemed gatekeeper platforms the way iOS is by the Digital Markets Act.

If Apple did launch HomeView in the EU, it would likely need to disable certain personal context features related to Siri AI. And it seems the company believes a compromised experience like that wouldn’t be worth it. So it’s holding out until Siri AI is able to come to iPhone users in the EU.
