Typically, Apple’s fall updates for IT are around better way to manage devices, etc. This year, there was an underrated update that I think will be a real win in certain situations: remote AppleCare log collection.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

If you’ve ever opened an AppleCare support case for a hard-to-reproduce issue in your Apple fleet, you know how hard this process is. AppleCare needed a sysdiagnose and getting one meant either physically having the device or walking a user through a series of steps they’ve never done before. That process worked eventually, but it was slow, required the user to be available and willing to help, and, for remote employees or traveling executives, made it appear that IT didn’t have sufficient visibility into the logs of what was happening on the devices. The issue is that they somewhat didn’t.

The harder the issue was to reproduce, the more frustrating this was for IT. By the time you got the logs, the device had rebooted, the macOS state had changed, and you were starting over with your troubleshooting.

TriggerEnhancedLogCollection is your friend

Apple introduced two new device management commands in iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and tvOS 27: TriggerEnhancedLogCollection and a cancel command. The process is straightforward. You open an AppleCare case, AppleCare provides you a token, and you pass that token through your device management when you trigger the command. The device collects the logs and uploads them directly to Apple, where they are automatically attached to the ticket with Apple.

The device also reports its status through declarative management at all times, so you can see whether log collection has started, whether it’s finished, whether it’s waiting on user consent, and if the upload is in progress. 

Interactive vs non-interactive

There are two modes for this command, and the difference matters depending on what you’re managing. On iOS, non-interactive mode is available when the device has no passcode and no accounts, so it collects and uploads logs in the background without user involvement. I think this would be applicable in kiosk/POS type settings. On tvOS and Shared iPads, non-interactive is always available.

On macOS, interactive mode is required. The user sees a notification and is prompted to consent to both the log collection and the upload. They can decline, but this is still dramatically better than the old process, but it’s not completely hands-off. The user is in the loop., but at least it’s a simple UI box..

Wrap up

Remote and hybrid work make manual log collection harder and a remote user in a different city experiencing intermittent macOS issues is one of the more challenging support scenarios an IT team can face. With this feature, the moment that Apple’s team asks for logs, you can send the command from your device management console, the device does the work, and Apple has the info it needs to work the case.

title: TrendForce warns of higher notebook prices and weaker demand in 2027
snippet: TrendForce projects that global notebook shipments could decline by a high-single-digit percentage in 2027, depending on how manufacturers respond to rising component costs. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
TrendForce projects that global notebook shipments could decline by a high-single-digit percentage in 2027, depending on how manufacturers respond to rising component costs. Here are the details.

’Brands [to] face difficult trade-offs’

In a report released this week, TrendForce projects that global notebook shipments will decline in 2027, with the drop ranging from low- to high-single digits, depending on how manufacturers respond to rising costs.

TrendForce says the impact will depend on how much of the rising component costs manufacturers pass on to consumers through higher retail prices, rather than absorbing them at the expense of their profit margins.

From the report:

TrendForce’s latest notebook industry research reveals that the primary risk facing the market in 2027 is expected to shift from supply constraints to the impact of rising costs on demand. Global notebook shipments are currently projected to decline by a low-single-digit percentage in 2027.

However, if DRAM and CPU prices remain elevated, brands may be forced to pass more of these costs on to consumers. These higher retail prices could further extend replacement cycles, potentially pushing the full-year shipment decline into the high-single-digit range.

TrendForce says that notebook shipments in 2026 were supported by factors such as improved CPU availability, early purchasing by manufacturers, and replacement demand brought forward from later periods.

With some purchases originally expected in the second half of 2026 and beyond already brought forward, replacement momentum in subsequent periods is likely to weaken. Furthermore, as lower-cost inventories are gradually depleted, brands will face more direct pressure from rising CPU, DRAM, and SSD prices.

The report notes that 68% of the bill of materials for an unnamed “mainstream notebook with a manufacturer’s suggested retail price of US$900” was made up of CPU, DRAM, and SSD costs in the third quarter of 2026.

	

It adds that next year, if component costs keep rising, brands will likely have to choose between raising retail prices and risking weaker demand, absorbing the increases at the expense of gross margins, or reducing specifications, potentially making their products less competitive.

TrendForce says that DRAM supply is “likely to stay tight” next year thanks to AI-related demand, “while PC DRAM faces the risk of limited supply growth.” On the flip side, it expects NAND Flash supply constraints to “ease in the second half of 2027 with new capacity coming online. “

In 2027, brands are therefore unlikely to be able to maintain pricing, specifications, and profitability simultaneously. The extent to which they pass higher costs on to consumers will be a key factor shaping demand.

Finally, the report notes that if tariff pressures don’t increase further, manufacturers could move some notebook production back to China to reduce costs. TrendForce estimates that China’s share of global notebook production will rise from 76% in 2025 to 79% in 2026, potentially exceeding 80% in 2027.

title: iPhone Duo buyers to get a special surprise at U.S. Apple Stores, report says
snippet: According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, iPhone Duo buyers who purchase their device at an Apple Store in the US will be treated to a nice little surprise when they turn it on for the first time. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, iPhone Duo buyers who purchase their device at an Apple Store in the US will be treated to a nice little surprise when they turn it on for the first time. Here are the details.

Cool surprise in store for in-store buyers

When Apple launches the iPhone Duo on October 23, some customers who purchase the device at an Apple Store in the US will be able to have its initial setup screen personalized with their name.

According to Gurman, “Apple retail stores will have a system to customize the boot of the device,” allowing the iPhone Duo to display a greeting containing their name when it turns on for the first time. Gurman says the feature will be exclusive to the iPhone Duo, and support both English and Spanish.

Fun little touch for the iPhone Duo launch: Apple retail stores will have a system to customize the boot of the device with the buyer's name so it says "Hello, Mark" (for example) when it turns on for the first time. (US only, Duo only, English and Spanish).

— Mark Gurman (@markgurman) October 9, 2026

It is not clear how Apple will implement the feature, or whether it will rely on Presto, the system Apple Stores already use to wirelessly update iPhones without removing them from their boxes.

	

First reported by Gurman in 2023, Presto allows Apple retail employees to turn on an iPhone, install software updates, and turn it off again, all while the device remains sealed in its packaging.

Back to the iPhone Duo, it will be available to pre-order starting Friday, October 16, with deliveries and in-store availability beginning October 23.

Apple recently announced that customers will be able to get ready for iPhone Duo pre-orders beginning October 12, and you can read more about that here.

title: Next-gen Google TV Streamer in the works with microphones, presence sensing, & new remote
snippet: 9to5Google can report that development on a next-generation Google TV Streamer is underway. more…
fullText:
9to5Google can report that development on a next-generation Google TV Streamer is underway. 

According to a source familiar with the matter, the new Google TV device retains the same general design. The width is narrower for a slightly more compact footprint. 

The big upgrade is the presence of microphones on the Google TV Streamer itself. There are cutouts on the slanted, pill-shaped surface that will listen for “Hey Google” commands. 

	

Another new hardware feature is presence sensing. Last year, TCL launched the first Google TV with that capability to turn on the Google Photos screensaver when someone enters the room. If you get close, the display shows ambient information like the time and weather.

	

Meanwhile, the new Google TV Streamer will be powered by a faster processor and offer more storage than the current model’s 32GB.

Google is also updating the included remote. The design is largely the same but with two more shortcuts joining the existing buttons for YouTube and Netflix. Additionally, the Find My Remote button remains on the back of the streaming device. 

We don’t have any information on when this next Google TV Streamer is launching. There was a four-year gap between the Chromecast with Google TV 4K and the Google TV Streamer, with the lower-end HD dongle coming in between the two. This refresh comes as Google raised the price of the existing unit by $50 in August.

title: Googlebook’s app situation is a mess, and not just because things are missing
snippet: Having been using a Googlebook for the better part of a week, there are any number of headaches I could talk about, but easily the biggest problem I’m running into thus far is the app situation. Frankly, it’s a mess. more…
fullText:
Having been using a Googlebook for the better part of a week, there are any number of headaches I could talk about, but easily the biggest problem I’m running into thus far is the app situation. Frankly, it’s a mess.

Googlebook, like Chromebook, was never going to be in a “good” place for apps. The Android-based platform sets up a more capable foundation for the future but, without a major push from Google and partners, it was always going to result in a rough start. 

And, yeah, it’s a rough start.

The “main” issue is around desktop-class apps and programs. Staples like the Adobe suite are simply not here, and there’s no easy way to replace them. Not to mention the depth of niche apps that have been built out in the Windows and macOS over the decades. At launch, Googlebook was never going to compete with that, though I’d argue that stripping away the Linux support ChromeOS did have isn’t exactly helping matters.

	

The problem I’m finding much more frustrating is around the apps Googlebook can access, and the messy situation around that.

The Google Play Store is your main way to obtain apps on Googlebook. Android apps are the preferred method and, in time, I’m sure that’ll work better than it does today. But, at the moment, Google’s stopgap to varying levels of quality for Android apps on desktop was to give five quality labels to any given app. 

Built for mobile: Hasn’t been tested for desktop

Better on the website: The web app/browser version has full features and/or better performance

Compatible with Desktop: Works with mouse/keyboard controls

Optimized for Desktop: “Adapted for a comfortable desktop experience”

Made for Desktop: “Built for desktop with specialized features and controls”

These are all applied by Google — developers have no direct control.

In my book, that’s wildly confusing for the end user, especially as the Play Store doesn’t link out to where you can use the web app for the Android apps it tries to steer you away from.

And it sadly should steer you away from some apps. 

Telegram is a great example of my frustration. The Android app is “better on the website,” and that’s incredibly true. The Android app is broken on Googlebook in a lot of ways, but the most frustrating is that the enter key doesn’t send a message. But, on the flip side, the web app isn’t that much better, as I’ve frequently run into cases where it misbehaves or even crashes. 

Slack continues to be a daily source of frustration, with the Android app being truly a terrible experience on anything other than a phone, and the web app unable to be installed. This is not some niche or trivial app, it’s something that millions rely on for daily work on their laptops. 

Spotify says that it is “Optimized for desktop” and, while it’s not bad, the phone UI doesn’t even scale as well here as it does on a foldable. It gets better when the “Now Playing” panel is expanded out, but it’s still not on par with other desktop platforms. “Optimized” just feels like the wrong word for this label. “Compatible” feels more apt for this particular example, but Google’s categories are way too specific to let that work.

“Optimized for desktop” according to who, exactly?

	

There’s no easy solution here.

Googlebook is in its early days and, while the foundation presents a better future, the “now” is a huge headache, and one I struggle to get on board with because, well why would you subject yourself to this? Good Windows laptops are easy to find. The MacBook Air is easy to find for $1,099 (cheaper than most Googlebooks!). Good, established platforms that simply don’t have these shortcomings. Why would I give that up for some Android integrations that don’t even work with my phone yet?

Sound off in the comments, I’d love to hear what you think about this problem and how it impacts your view of Googlebook.

title: OLED MacBook Pro to help boost premium display shipments, per report
snippet: A new Counterpoint Research report says Apple’s next-generation MacBook Pro will help drive a 50% increase in OLED notebook display shipments in 2026 alone. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A new Counterpoint Research report says Apple’s next-generation MacBook Pro will help drive a 50% increase in OLED notebook display shipments in 2026 alone. Here are the details.

New MacBook Pro and premium AI PCs expected to fuel demand

In a report released today, Counterpoint Research projects that advanced notebook display shipments will grow 11% in 2026 compared to 2025, with OLED notebook display shipments expected to rise 50% for the period.

The report notes that the 11% growth in advanced notebook display shipments will comfortably outperform the broader notebook display market, which Counterpoint says it expects to decline 3% year over year.

Counterpoint says it also expects OLED to widen its lead over MiniLED in the advanced notebook display market, rising from 56% of shipments in 2025 to 75% in 2026, while MiniLED is expected to drop from 44% to 25%.

The research company says part of the growth in OLED notebook panel shipments is expected to come from Apple’s adoption of the technology in its next-generation MacBook Pro, currently rumored to be announced on October 27 with a touchscreen display and a redesigned, significantly lighter chassis.

Here’s Counterpoint:

OLED notebook display shipments are forecast to rise 50% in 2026 and another 24% in 2027. Apple’s anticipated adoption of OLED in next-generation MacBook Pro models, alongside continued demand for premium AI PCs, is expected to drive this growth.

Another factor contributing to OLED’s growth, Counterpoint says, is technology and manufacturing advances such as tandem OLED architectures, which improve brightness, power efficiency, and panel longevity.

Apple already uses tandem OLED in the iPad Pro, where two OLED layers work together to deliver higher full-screen brightness. The company is widely expected to use a similar two-stack tandem OLED architecture for the upcoming 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects OLED notebook panel shipments to grow at a compounded annual rate of 26% between 2024 and 2030, while panel revenue is forecast to grow at 35% per year over the same period.

title: Chrome 155 for Googlebook brings expanded web app installs, integration
snippet: With Chrome 155, Googlebooks now better support web apps by allowing for expanded installation and system integration. more…
fullText:
With Chrome 155, Googlebooks now better support web apps by allowing for expanded installation and system integration.

Previously, Chrome on Googlebooks (which is the Android version with desktop-level features) “only enabled the Install option for websites specifically configured as web apps.” As seen above, pages “without an installable web manifest” just opened as a browser tab.

Google reiterates today how that was a “conscious design choice,” but it heard the community feedback.

Chrome 155 this week lets you “manually install any webpage as an app directly from the Chrome browser so that it works as an app in its own window.” To do so:

	

On your Googlebook, open Chrome.

Go to a website you want to install.

At the top right, open the Chrome menu > Save and share > Install and create shortcut…

On some websites, at the top right of the address bar, select Install.

Select Install.

To complete the web app installation, follow the on-screen instructions.

Additionally, Google says: “If you previously created a browser-tab shortcut for a website prior to this update, remove the old shortcut first and re-install the page using the steps above.”

Meanwhile, installed web apps that appear in the app launcher can now be “pinned to your taskbar or homescreen and run in Chrome.” They will benefit from “shared Google Account login, cookies, site permissions, and installed browser extensions.”

With this release, Chrome Settings is no longer a fullscreen interface, which has been the case on mobile but not desktop platforms. As a separate tab, “you can more easily reference a web page while tweaking settings.”

Version 155.0.8059.79 of Chrome is rolling out via the Play Store on Googlebooks. We’re seeing it on all our devices.

title: PSA: Wall-mounted HomeView may not work if you buy the wrong power adapter
snippet: Earlier today, Apple confirmed that the wall-mounted HomeView does not come with a power adapter in the box. Now, the company has published a support document detailing the device’s power requirements, including what to look for when purchasing a compatible adapter. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Earlier today, Apple confirmed that the wall-mounted HomeView does not come with a power adapter in the box.

Now, the company has published a support document detailing the device’s power requirements, including what to look for when purchasing a compatible adapter. Here are the details.

Important information for HomeView (Wall Mounted) buyers

If you’re buying the wall-mounted version of the new Apple HomeView, Apple has published a new support article with some important information.

As the company announced earlier today, the HomeView (Wall Mounted) model does not include a mount, nor does it come with a power adapter in the box.

This means that users will need to buy those separately. As my colleague Ryan explained earlier today, “Apple is selling two different mount options that start at $59, and it says a third is coming in early 2027.”

As for the power adapter, Apple explains in a new support article that the wall-mounted HomeView requires a USB-C power adapter rated for at least 20W, with support for 9V at 2.22A or higher. If those requirements aren’t met, the device may display a “Not Enough Power” warning.

	

Alternatively, depending on the third-party mount, the wall-mounted HomeView can be connected directly to a home’s electrical wiring without a separate USB-C power adapter.

Here’s Apple:

HomeView ships with a power cable and adapter. HomeView (Wall Mounted) requires a compatible third-party mount and power solution for operation, sold separately. Depending on the mount, you can use a separate power cable and adapter or connect to line power (hardwired).

HomeView: Use a USB-C cable and a USB-C power adapter that’s at least 30W and supports 15V at 2A or higher.

HomeView (Wall Mounted): Use a USB-C cable and a USB-C power adapter (both sold separately) that’s at least 20W and supports 9V at 2.22A or higher.

Apple also links to a compatible power adapter for HomeView or HomeView (Wall Mounted), and details the troubleshooting process for a HomeView showing a “Not Enough Power” message.

title: Android Auto 18.0 update starts rolling out, continues to gear up for redesign
snippet: Announced earlier this year, Google continues to set the stage for its next Android Auto redesign behind the scenes, which might be codenamed “Cielo.” more…
fullText:
Announced earlier this year, Google continues to set the stage for its next Android Auto redesign behind the scenes, which might be codenamed “Cielo.”

About APK Insight: In this “APK Insight” post, we’ve decompiled the latest version of an application that Google uploaded to the Play Store. When we decompile these files (called APKs, in the case of Android apps), we’re able to see various lines of code within that hint at possible future features. Keep in mind that Google may or may not ever ship these features, and our interpretation of what they are may be imperfect. We’ll try to enable those that are closer to being finished, however, to show you how they’ll look in case that they do ship. With that in mind, read on.

Google is now starting its rollout – in beta – of Android Auto 18.0. While that sounds like some milestone, the update itself is just as underwhelming as most Android Auto app updates have been. No new user-facing features we’ve spotted, and likely just some assorted bug fixes throughout. 

In a teardown, “cielo_launcher” did appear as a new asset, which might be the best indication we’ve seen that this is the codename for Google’s next Android Auto redesign. This codename has been appearing for months in Android Auto’s flags – the folks over at Android Sage mention v15.9, but we’ve seen references as far back as v15.7 in November 2025 –  but “launcher” points pretty directly at this being the replacement for “Coolwalk,” which was the codename of Android Auto’s dashboard redesign back in 2023. “Coolwalk_launcher” showed up in Android Auto’s code years ago as the dashboard was being build out.

	
	

Prior Android Auto updates mentioning “cielo” also mentioned screen layouts, which might tie into how Android Auto’s new design is set to cover more of the display and support widgets. 

Android Auto is getting a redesign that takes up your whole display, adds widget support, more

“Coolwalk” didn’t have a direct meaning, but “Cielo” is a real word in Italian and Spanish meaning “sky.” It’s unclear if that has any meaning, though.

As far as Android Auto 18.0 goes, this update is purely just building on the redesign, as there’s nothing (at least that we’ve found) that actually implies it’s imminent. Notably, there’s also the use of “Coolwalk” in the flags here too around the light/dark theme that Google has been building out for what feels like an eternity at this point, but nothing particularly suggestive of when that feature might actually debut – it’s still not live in this update.

title: Apple TV unveils new heist thriller series coming soon
snippet: Apple TV released the trailer today for ‘12 12 12,’ a new heist thriller series premiering next month. Here are the details and the trailer. more…
fullText:
Apple TV released the trailer today for ‘12 12 12,’ a new heist thriller series premiering next month. Here are the details and the trailer.

title: I Put the Oppo Find X10 Pro’s Camera to the Test. These Are the Results
snippet: I’ve used Oppo’s Find X10 and these are my favorite example photos.
fullText:
Oppo’s latest flagship Android phone, the Find X10 Pro is set to be unveiled in the coming weeks, but Oppo kindly sent me a unit ahead of time to let me take its cameras for a spin. So I did. I’ve been on multiple walks around my home in sunny Edinburgh and have taken a variety of snaps with the phone’s multiple rear cameras.

The fun part here is that while I can show you the photos — and you can see the phone in my hand above — I’m not yet allowed to talk about any specs, including the resolution of the cameras or what technology is powering them. So instead, I’m presenting these photos just as they are, almost as a little teaser ahead of the phone’s full unveiling later in the month. I’ll have a full review ready then, along with all the information about the cameras and some comparisons against other top Android camera phones like the Leica Leitzphone.

But all of that’s to come. For now, enjoy some of my early test images taken with the X10 Pro, along with as much information as my non-disclosure agreement allows me to share. Keep in mind that all photos have been imported into Adobe Lightroom in order to be easily assessed and resized for publishing online. No other edits, including sharpening, have been applied unless otherwise stated.

			

More from CNET

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the main camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Taken with the main camera, this image is sharp, packed with detail and has natural colors. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the ultrawide camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

 I don’t think I’m breaking any rules in telling you that the phone has an ultrawide camera, so here’s a photo I took with it. It looks a little more drab than the one from the main camera, but it’s still got plenty of detail.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the main camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

There are various color filters, which I almost certainly can’t tell you about here, but you probably assumed it had them anyway, right? Right?! Anyway, I used one of them (I won’t say which) to take this shot, and I like the filmic vibes it’s produced.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the main camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I used a different, unnamed, color filter here and I like the punchy tones, especially from that flash of red at the bottom of the ship. 

Shot with the Oppo Find X10 Pro.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

While this color filter is much more subtle, it gives a bold blue that contrasts nicely with the building’s orange.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot in XPan mode.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The last two generations of Oppo phones (including the superb Find X9 Ultra) had Hasselblad’s XPan mode, so I can’t imagine it’s a secret that the new one does too. This mode allows you to shoot with a wide, narrow crop that’s reminiscent of Hasselblad’s legendary XPan panoramic film camera. Those cameras are rare and expensive, so this is the closest you’ll probably get to an authentic XPan experience. I love this wide, cinematic aspect ratio.

Shot with the Oppo Find X10 Pro.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

While I love the vibrancy of this image — and the sense of the warm evening glow — I do think the camera’s image processing has gone a bit hard with the “HDR” here, creating a less realistic-looking shot.

Shot with the Oppo Find X10 Pro.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

That over-processing is especially noticeable here. It’s as though the phone has desperately tried to eliminate any shadow in the image, creating a flat-looking shot that lacks the rich tones you’d expect from a good camera.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the main camera, in Master Mode.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The Find X10 Pro isn’t alone in this regard — I find most phones seem to go too hard on image processing, and that includes the Find X9 Ultra. The way around it is to shoot in Master mode, taking control of your white balance settings and shooting in DNG raw to avoid any built-in software and AI-based processing being applied. I made my own tweaks to this image in Adobe Lightroom.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the main camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

While this shot is a straight-out-of-camera image taken in the default mode. Again, I’d have to say that it looks over-processed, especially with the artificially brightened shadows.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the main camera, in Master Mode.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

I took this shot in Master Mode specifically so I could take control of the white balance and warm the scene up to emphasise that glorious morning sunshine. I took it in JPEG and have done no further editing.

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the telephoto zoom camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Yes, the phone has a telephoto zoom lens, but no I can’t tell you what that zoom factor is. What I can say is that I think this shot looks good. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the telephoto zoom camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And this telephoto zoom shot also looks good, with sharp details and vibrant colors. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the telephoto lens accessory.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Like the Find X9 Ultra, the X10 Pro will be available with an add-on telephoto zoom lens to take your zoom shots even further. Here’s a white pigeon I found. While the camera struggled to get focus on the bird (getting confused by the railing in front) it eventually achieved an impressively sharp image, with natural-looking bokeh from the out-of-focus railing. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot with the telephoto lens accessory.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And another with the add-on telephoto lens. This time it’s a seagull on a boat, even though it doesn’t need a boat because it can fly. This seagull just wants to have everything and it’s a real shame that late-stage capitalism has influenced the local birdlife in this way. 

Oppo Find X10 Pro, shot on the front-facing camera.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Speaking of capitalism, I’ll end on this photo of yours truly with a Leica M6 slung around my neck. Taken with the front-facing camera, this shot has nice-looking tones, both in terms of the shadows and the colors.

I like many of these early test shots I’ve taken, and I’m looking forward to spending more time with the phone over the coming weeks. It has some stiff competition – not just from the aforementioned Leica Leitzphone and the new iPhone 18 Pro, but also from its predecessor, the Find X9 Ultra, which impressed me with its photography skills when I reviewed it in June.

title: Researchers uncover new DarkSword spyware variant affecting unpatched iPhones
snippet: iVerify released a report today detailing P7 DarkSword, a new variant of the malware associated with the DarkSword iPhone exploit chain uncovered earlier this year. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
iVerify released a report today detailing P7 DarkSword, a new variant of the malware associated with the DarkSword iPhone exploit chain uncovered earlier this year. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Earlier this year, Google and iVerify revealed two sophisticated iPhone hacking tools known as Coruna and DarkSword, both of which chained multiple iOS vulnerabilities to compromise devices running outdated system versions.

In DarkSword’s case, once an iPhone was compromised, attackers could deploy additional malware with access to sensitive data.

Coruna targeted devices running iOS 13 through iOS 17.2.1, while DarkSword affected iPhones running iOS 18.4 through iOS 18.7.

This led Apple to release system updates for the affected older iOS versions, including iOS 15.8.7, iOS 16.7.15, and iOS 18.7.7. Apple went as far as to take the unusual step of making iOS 18.7.7 available to devices that could install iOS 26, so users who elected not to update to the latest system version would also remain protected against DarkSword.

At the time, Google said DarkSword was being used by multiple commercial surveillance vendors and suspected state-sponsored actors, with attacks observed against targets in Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Malaysia, and Ukraine.

New DarkSword variant found in the wild

Today, iVerify announced the discovery of P7 DarkSword, a previously unseen variant it found while investigating an infection on the iPhone of an employee at a financial institution just two months ago.

In additional details shared with 9to5Mac, iVerify noted that the P7 expands compatibility to iOS 18.7, up from iOS 18.6 in the earlier variant it had been tracking. Other DarkSword deployments observed by Google had already supported iOS 18.7.

The company also said the threat actor behind P7 is distributing it through malicious ads as part of watering-hole attacks, meaning victims do not necessarily appear to be individually targeted. Instead, users can be caught in broader campaigns simply by encountering malicious or compromised web content.

From the report:

In August 2026 we investigated a DarkSword infection that turned out to be a previously unseen variant, which we call P7 DarkSword. The name P7 comes from the threat actor’s use of the p7_ variable prefix in modifications to original DarkSword’s code. Compared with the variants we usually observe, P7 reduces its on-device footprint, adds on-device keychain and crypto-wallet theft, and adds two way C2 communication with the attacker’s infrastructure. This post describes the investigation, the variant’s capabilities, and the indicators that can be used to detect it._

The report says that P7 DarkSword improves on earlier variants in three main areas: stealth, stability, and functionality. The new variant reduces logging and the number of process injections it performs, uses browser storage to avoid repeatedly exploiting the same device, and expands its data-stealing capabilities.

iVerify also told 9to5Mac that the changes appear to reflect substantial work by the operators rather than simple AI-assisted modifications. The company says P7 is much better at hiding itself and cleaning up its behavior, so previous indicators of compromise (IOCs) are no longer valid.

Most notably, iVerify says P7 can extract Keychain data directly on the iPhone before sending it to the attackers, instead of copying the entire Keychain database for processing elsewhere.

P7 DarkSword can also target crypto-wallet data, and introduces more advanced two-way communication with the attackers’ command-and-control infrastructure.

That two-way communication also gives attackers considerably more control over an infected device. According to iVerify, P7 can receive commands to retrieve arbitrary files, upload photos, inventory installed apps, access Apple Notes databases, collect data from individual app containers, and scan the device’s filesystem.

By default, the spyware checks in with the attackers’ command-and-control server every 15 seconds for new instructions, although that interval can be changed remotely.

It’s worth noting that P7 is not a new iOS vulnerability, but rather a new version of the malware deployed after a successful DarkSword compromise. iVerify does not say which iOS version was running on the device where P7 was discovered in August.

To read iVerify’s full report, which includes technical details on how P7 operates, follow this link.

title: You can now use TextExpander for free across Mac, iPhone, iPad, and more
snippet: Incredibly useful keyboard shortcut utility TextExpander now offers a free plan, letting users access its core Snippets feature on the Mac, iPhone, iPad, Windows, and Chrome. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Incredibly useful keyboard shortcut utility TextExpander now offers a free plan, letting users access its core Snippets feature on the Mac, iPhone, iPad, Windows, and Chrome. Here are the details.

TextExpander now offers a free plan

I’ve written in the past about how TextExpander is one of the first apps I install as soon as I get a new Mac.

Over the years, I’ve built up a library of roughly 200 Snippets (TextExpander’s name for text abbreviations that automatically expand into pre-written text), most of which I expand regularly to quickly reply to emails, fill out forms, prepare podcast outlines, pull sponsorship reads, write up show notes, and more.

And while macOS has been steadily improving its native text replacement support, features such as variable support, conditional sections, nested snippets, and math macros make TextExpander an essential tool for me.

TextExpander recently launched a free plan that, as the company tells 9to5Mac, gives access to 5 active Snippets, unlimited library storage, unlimited text expansions, and up to 5 team members. The Free plan also works across Mac, iPhone, iPad, Windows, and Chrome, with the same Snippet library staying in sync across devices.

Granted, the 5-Snippet limit can feel a bit restrictive, particularly since the Free plan only allows one active Snippet to be swapped every two weeks.

Still, it can also be a good way to ease into TextExpander by keeping shorter, simpler text replacements in macOS, while reserving the app for longer or more complex snippets.

title: Google Home update fixes broken smart light color control
snippet: Color LED bulbs were refusing to do their job because of a Google Home bug. Google says the fix is rolling out now. more…
fullText:
Color LED bulbs were refusing to do their job because of a Google Home bug. Google says the fix is rolling out now.

According to a few users on Reddit, Google Home isn’t properly adjusting color on smart bulbs. Users say it hasn’t been limited to just one brand, but devices across multiple brands like Philips Hue, Tuya, and Lumiman. The issue was affecting both voice controls and app controls, which are usually more reliable and easier to adjust. But the color sliders did nothing for affected users.

Google responded to the Reddit thread to say a fix is currently rolling out. The post author has since updated the thread to say their voice commands and app are now reliably controlling bulb color.

The post was barely a day old when Google first let users know it was working on a fix. Just a few hours later, an update was rolling out. The quick turnaround is likely appreciated for this bug because it broke a critical component and selling point for not only Google Home but also smart bulb manufacturers.

	

Color control might have been broken while Google works on other additions to the app. Monthly updates are being released to address the functions and bugs appearing as Google Assistant fades into the background, which has officially happened as of last month.

Were/are you experiencing a bug that broke smart bulb color control? It should be fixed now, but if it isn’t, let us know.

title: Apple and Epic clash over document production in latest App Store court filing
snippet: Epic Games is accusing Apple of “manufacturing” a pause in the legal proceedings over its proposed new App Store commission rates. Apple disagrees. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Epic Games is accusing Apple of “manufacturing” a pause in the legal proceedings over its proposed new App Store commission rates. Apple disagrees. Here are the details.

In a joint status update, Epic Games and Apple present very different accounts of Apple’s efforts to turn over internal documents explaining how it arrived at its proposed App Store commission rates.

A bit of context

As a reminder, in August, Apple proposed a new commission structure for purchases made through external App Store links.

Under the proposed structure, developers would pay commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, down from the 27% fee Apple introduced in 2024 after a court ordered the company to allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods.

The court later found Apple in contempt of its order, a designation Apple is seeking to overturn before the Supreme Court, arguing that the order never forbade it from charging any commissions at all.

While the Supreme Court considers Apple’s challenge to the contempt ruling, a lower court is separately examining whether Apple can impose commissions on purchases made through external links, and if so, how much it can charge.

Apple recently tried to pause those proceedings until the Supreme Court reached a decision, but its requests were rejected by both the lower court and the Supreme Court.

As part of that process, Apple submitted its proposed 5% to 15% commission structure in August, along with evidence supporting those rates.

Under the agreement governing the proceedings, Apple was also required to hand over internal documents showing how it arrived at those rates.

The documents are meant to give Epic an opportunity to examine the basis for Apple’s proposed fees before formally responding to the court.

That’s where the latest dispute comes in, with Epic accusing Apple of deliberately delaying the proceedings and Apple rejecting those allegations.

Apple and Epic dispute evidence behind proposed App Store fees

In the joint status filing, Epic says that “[n]early two months after its production deadline, Apple has scarcely produced any documents,” adding that “Apple’s […] continued unwillingness to commit to a date certain by which it will complete its production demonstrates that Court intervention is essential.”

Apple disputes those accusations, arguing that it had already fulfilled its initial obligation to produce documents explaining how it arrived at the proposed rates.

The company also blames Epic for the delays, saying the Fortnite maker took weeks to submit additional document requests, and subsequently demanded extensive searches involving 27 individuals. Apple says it has agreed to those requests and expects to substantially complete its production by November 25.

In the document, Epic also disputes Apple’s assertions that only four senior executives were involved in determining the proposed commission rates, those four executives being Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Kevan Parekh, and Carson Oliver.

Epic argues that the decision was also informed by discussions and analyses conducted by other teams within Apple, including work on alternative commission structures in markets outside the United States. (And speaking of that, there is also a dispute over whether Epic should have access to documents concerning Apple’s international commission policies.)

Apple, in turn, maintains that the decision-making process was much narrower than the one behind its original 27% commission, and relied heavily on analyses conducted by outside experts rather than broader internal discussions.

Apple says it has already provided the business records and data that informed its proposal, and disputes Epic’s assertion that a larger group of employees must have been involved in determining the new rates.

Throughout its rebuttal of Epic’s accusations, Apple repeatedly emphasizes that it has agreed to Epic’s requests for additional documents and broader searches, arguing that the scope of those demands, and the time Epic took to make them, are responsible for the delays.

Apple also says Epic caught it by surprise by asking the court to impose a November 1 deadline for completing document production, rather than first discussing that deadline with Apple. The company makes a similar argument about Epic’s objections to the scope of the documents Apple agreed to produce, saying Epic should have raised those concerns directly before seeking court intervention.

Epic, on the other hand, says “Apple feigns surprise at every request Epic raises, as if the Parties, this Court, Magistrate Judge Hixson, and three Court-appointed special masters did not just recently complete a months-long process to extract from Apple documents Epic was clearly entitled to receive.”

For this reason, Epic asks the court to order Apple to:

“[I]mmediately begin rolling document productions and fully complete its productions on a reasonable timeline, and by no later than November 1, 2026”

“[P]roduce by said deadline all relevant documents, without regard to the artificial limitations Apple has placed on the scope of its production, as further detailed [in the document].”

title: MacBook Pro overhaul: entry-level model to gain new design sooner than expected
snippet: Earlier this year, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman revealed that Apple has a new M7-powered entry level MacBook Pro in the pipeline for spring 2027. This isn’t an ordinary MacBook Pro refresh though. It’ll bring the upcoming redesign down to the entry level, something that previously wasn’t expected. more…
fullText:
Earlier this year, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman revealed that Apple has a new M7-powered entry level MacBook Pro in the pipeline for spring 2027. This isn’t an ordinary MacBook Pro refresh though. It’ll bring the upcoming redesign down to the entry level, something that previously wasn’t expected.

Normally, when Apple introduces a new MacBook Pro design, it takes a while to trickle down. For instance, the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M1 Pro and M1 Max was introduced in 2021, but the base model MacBook Pro stuck with the 13-inch design until 2023, when it gained the 14-inch chassis with the M3 chip.

Similarly, when Apple redesigned the MacBook Pro in 2016, it wasn’t until 2019 that the entry level model gained the Touch Bar. There’s also a similar story for the 2012 retina MacBook Pro redesign.

This time around though, there’ll only be a roughly 6 month gap before the redesign comes to the entry level.

M7 entry-level with redesign

According to Bloomberg, Apple will be introducing the redesign to the entry level MacBook Pro in early 2027, shortly after debuting it in the high end MacBook Pros, rumored to be called MacBook Ultra. From the report:

Apple is also preparing a revamped entry-level MacBook Pro, code-named K104, for as early as the first half of next year. The 14-inch laptop will adopt a new design in line with what Apple is preparing for higher-end MacBooks with touch screens due between the end of this year and early next year.

It’s worth noting that there’ll also be another entry level MacBook Pro with the current design and the M6 chip, which is currently on track to debut this fall alongside the redesigned high-end MacBook Pros. 

To make things even weirder, those redesigned high-end MacBook Pros are also expected to debut with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, instead of M6 generation chips. Apple recently made a decision to abandon its plans for high end M6 chips to instead accelerate M7.

In short, it’ll look like this:

Fall 2026: Entry-level MacBook Pro with M6/old design, high-end with M5 Pro/Max and new design

Spring 2027: Entry-level MacBook Pro with M7 and new design

Fall 2027: High-end MacBook Pro refresh with M7 Pro/M7 Max

Of course, the redesign is expected to feature a slightly thinner chassis, OLED displays with touch support, and possibly even come with a Dynamic Island.

Wrap up

With the recent price hikes, this is excellent news for some people. I’m sure the redesigned 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro will likely cost over $2500, so if you’re looking to get something more in budget with the M7 chip and the redesign, you’ll only have to wait until the following spring.

	

It’s certainly unfortunate that the $1,999 price point of the entry level MacBook Pro today is what the Pro chip versions cost just under a year ago, but that’s the inevitable reality of this memory shortage.

title: Googlebook improving ‘Better Together’ Android sync features, Samsung support rolling out
snippet: The big selling point for Googlebook is that it’s a desktop platform that deeply integrates with your Android phone but, at launch, those “Better Together” sync features are in a messy place. Google is now rolling out updates, including the bafflingly-missing support for Samsung devices. more…
fullText:
The big selling point for Googlebook is that it’s a desktop platform that deeply integrates with your Android phone but, at launch, those “Better Together” sync features are in a messy place. Google is now rolling out updates, including the bafflingly-missing support for Samsung devices.

There are several core features that work between Android phones and Googlebook including app streaming, notification sync, “Continue On” for compatible apps, and more. But, at launch, not everything works as expected. Some features, like Instant Hotspot, seem to work widely, but others are either inconsistent, slow to activate, or simply unavailable. One of the problems is that it takes a bit of work to fully activate these features.

In a post on Reddit, Google explains that it has started rolling out “smoother first-time setup” for these features, reducing the needed steps to actually set up these cross-device features. A bug where the QR code used to pair your phone continues to show even after Googlebook pairing is complete is apparently also fixed with this update. Google Play Services 26.37 (on the phone) is the version you’re looking for. You can check for Play Services updates through the Play Store. Cross-device Services also needs to be updated to 1.0.1346, again through the Play Store. 

Apparently, these updates also seem to enable support for Samsung devices. 

	

Missing Galaxy smartphone support was perhaps the biggest gap in Googlebook at launch, at least in terms of compatibility. Google originally said this would arrive “in the coming weeks,” a phrase that continues to be incredibly vague.

Here’s Google’s full breakdown of everything you’re looking for:

Confirm your phone runs Android 17: Your Android phone must run Android 17. To check your version, open Settings > About phone > Android version (your phone’s settings may vary). Better Together features work with Pixel and compatible Android 17 phones including Xiaomi, Oppo, OnePlus, Motorola, Lenovo, Honor, Sharp, Sony, Samsung (One UI 9.0), and more.

Check your Bluetooth and Wi-Fi: Confirm your phone and Googlebook use the same personal Google Account with both Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on.

Use a private home Wi-Fi network: Hotel, cafe, office, and guest Wi-Fi networks frequently use client isolation, which blocks direct local connections between your phone and laptop. Pause any active VPNs or network DNS blockers and test on a standard home Wi-Fi network.

Update Google Play services: Google Play services must be at version 26.37 or higher. To ensure your phone has the latest version, select Settings > Apps (or Apps & notifications)> See all apps. If Google Play services doesn’t appear, select More and then Show system. Select Google Play services from the app list, then App details (or App details in store). If an update is available, select Update.

Update Cross-device services: Cross-device services must be at version 1.0.1346 or higher. To ensure your phone has the latest version, select Settings, then Apps (or Apps & notifications), then See all apps. Select Cross-device services from the app list, then App details (or App details in store). If an update is available, select Update.

Verify Continue activity sub-toggles: On your phone under Settings, search for Cross-device services > Continue activity, and confirm that Tasks, Apps, Notifications, Files & media sharing are all turned On. 

Restart both your phone and your Googlebook to ensure changes take effect.

Some Samsung Galaxy users have already confirmed that “Better Together” features are working on their Googlebooks following these updates.

Missing Samsung support was initially attributed to missing updates on Samsung’s end by some, but it sounds like everything is worked out at this point. You’ll still need One UI 9, though, which is only rolled out to a small portion of Samsung’s device catalog at this point.

Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17

Sound off in the comments below if you’ve been able to use any of these new Googlebook features, or if you even bought a Googlebook in the first place.

title: BF6 Lands on Xbox Game Pass While Clair Obscur Gets Gommaged in October
snippet: Bluey’s Happy Snaps is also coming to Game Pass soon to put a smile on your face.
fullText:
Xbox Game Pass subscribers can jump into huge battles now in Battlefield 6. That’s good because, in a few days, Microsoft will remove one of CNET’s best games of 2025, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, from the service. Maybe Battlefield 6 and the other games arriving this month will have what it takes to fill the Clair Obscur-sized hole in my heart.

Xbox Game Pass, a CNET Editors’ Choice award pick, offers a wide selection of games you can play on your Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, Xbox One and PC or mobile device for as little as $10 a month. With a subscription to the higher-tiered Game Pass Ultimate ($23 a month), you can access hundreds of games, including new ones the day they’re released, each month. 

Here are all the games Microsoft is adding to Xbox Game Pass in the first half of October 2026.

			

More from CNET

Battlefield 6

Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

CNET’s David Lumb called this installment in the popular Battlefield series a “riveting shooter.” It’s full of huge multiplayer battles, close-quarters combat and loads of gunfights and explosions. While most people will gravitate towards multiplayer, there is a single-player campaign if you want a break from the online mayhem.

Valor Mortis

Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play now.

In this first-person soulslike game, you’re a soldier in Napoleon’s army who dies. No worries, because you’re back from the dead with a handful of supernatural abilities that you wield in your left hand, like in the almost 20-year-old game BioShock. You’ll use these skills to battle monsters and uncover a conspiracy that could threaten all of humanity. 

Bluey’s Happy Snaps

Xbox Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass subscribers can play on Oct. 15.

Bluey’s Happy Snaps proves that not every game coming to Game Pass has to be full of action. You’ll unwind and explore Bluey’s world while taking photos in areas familiar to anyone who’s seen the popular children’s show – let’s be honest, this show’s also popular with adults. You can take photos on your own, or play with a partner, friend or your kid as you turn in-game moments into fun.

Other games coming to Game Pass soon

Those are a few of the games Microsoft is bringing to Game Pass in October. Here are the rest of the games you’ll see on the service soon.

title: Google starts rolling out its upgraded Pixel screen savers to the Pixel 9
snippet: When Google added Pixelsnap to the Pixel 10 series, it wasn’t just building in support for all kinds of magnetic accessories — it was also adding in some excellent software functionality, like upgraded screensavers for when your phone is docked and charging. After gaining some new styles and features alongside the launch of the Pixel 11, Google is finally bringing these upgraded styles to older hardware, despite the lack of magnets. more…
fullText:
When Google added Pixelsnap to the Pixel 10 series, it wasn’t just building in support for all kinds of magnetic accessories — it was also adding in some excellent software functionality, like upgraded screensavers for when your phone is docked and charging. After gaining some new styles and features alongside the launch of the Pixel 11, Google is finally bringing these upgraded styles to older hardware, despite the lack of magnets.

A select group of users are starting to spot these screensavers being added to older Pixels, beginning with the Pixel 9, as reported by Android Authority. Earlier Pixels did have support for a basic screensaver tool, but with this upgrade, every option available on Google’s latest releases have finally been backported to its 2024 hardware. The update appears to include a pop-up demo of these new options, along with everything currently available as of the Pixel 11’s launch. Clock, Charge, Weather, Photos, and Home Controls are all available, and can be swiped through at will. And speaking of Charge, it too seems to be headed to the Pixel 10 series, after having been exclusive to the Pixel 11 for the past two months.

Unfortunately, it does seem like this is one of Google’s classic slow rollouts. There aren’t a massive amount of reports from Pixel 9 users that these styles are live on their devices, implying it might take a few weeks before reaching everyone. The same goes for Charge on the Pixel 10, with plenty of Redditors confirming they have yet to see that specific style arrive.

title: ‘HomePad’ is coming next week, with three features I’ve long wanted
snippet: Apple’s long-rumored ‘HomePad’ product is finally set to be unveiled next Tuesday at the ‘Welcome home’ event. Here are three HomePad features I’ve been waiting a long time for. more…
fullText:
Apple’s long-rumored ‘HomePad’ product is finally set to be unveiled next Tuesday at the ‘Welcome home’ event. Here are three HomePad features I’ve been waiting a long time for.

#1: Apple Photos on a digital picture frame

Digital picture frames are nothing new. But I’ve never owned one, in large part for two reasons:

All my pictures live in Apple Photos

I don’t want to manually add pictures to the digital frame

There are currently zero digital picture frames with native Apple Photos integration for an effort-free experience. But with the HomePad, rumors indicate there’s a Photos face available that will automatically cycle through pictures from Apple Photos.

This is exactly what I’ve been wanting for years. I hope to put several HomePads throughout the house so they can surprise and delight me with memories at every turn (while providing other key features too).

#2: Apple Music in the home with lyrics onscreen

I own a few HomePods, and enjoy listening to music with them. But what I’ve really wanted for a long time is the chance to see lyrics while listening.

Thanks to AirPlay, I can do this with my iPhone while music plays through the HomePod. I rarely do this, though, because I try to avoid pulling my phone out as much as possible with family around.

With HomePad though, all signs point to the Music app letting you view lyrics onscreen while a song is playing. I’m terrible at picking up lyrics just by ear, so I’m excited for the chance to better learn songs while staying in the moment with family members when we’re listening together.

#3: Siri AI in a HomePod-like device with a display

	

Siri AI is a major improvement over the old Siri. Unlike the old Siri on my HomePods, Siri AI can handle basically any question you throw at it. And with the HomePad, not only will Siri’s intelligence get a boost—it will also be able to show visuals in its responses.

I ask Siri on my HomePods to do basic things like set reminders, or provide info on the weather. But with Siri AI on the HomePad, I imagine I’ll turn to Siri far more often than I ever have. That’s already been true with Siri AI on my iPhone.

Having Apple’s new AI assistant all throughout the house, and equipped with a display for showing visual results, should prove a big improvement from my current HomePod setup.

title: Googlebook’s hidden ‘Glowbar Disco’ turns your laptop’s lid into a light show — how to find it
snippet: Buried in the settings of Googlebook is a “Glowbar Disco” app that activates the LEDs on your laptop constantly, instead of leaving it blank. more…
fullText:
Buried in the settings of Googlebook is a “Glowbar Disco” app that activates the LEDs on your laptop constantly, instead of leaving it blank.

The Glowbar on Googlebook is a carryover from the iconic light bar on the original Chromebook Pixel. It doesn’t function quite the same, lacking the fun and useful “knock knock” gesture that Google’s original offered, but it still shows battery on plug-in, and serves as a nice accent too.

But, hidden behind the scenes is more control over the glowbar.

The “Glowbar Disco” app is an Easter egg buried deep within the OS, and even Google’s Alexander Kuscher admits it might be “too hard to find.” The app itself lets you set the Glowbar on a Googlebook to show a constant color, a preset animation, a gradient of colors, or even sync with music. It leaves the Glowbar active whenever the machine is turned on and the Disco app is open, and it’s a super fun little addition.

	

Finding the app, though, is not exactly an easy task. 

You’ll have to go to Settings > Apps then allow the search function to show system apps, then search for “Glowbar Disco.” From there you can launch the app, but you’ll need to repeat that process every time you want to access it. And, if you close the app, the effects stop.

If you ask me, this should be baked into the Settings because it is very fun. Hopefully that’ll change in time — Googlebooks certainly need a lot of updates.

title: The Ocarina of Time remake feels remarkably modern — and surprisingly terrifying
snippet: With its upcoming remake for the Switch 2, Nintendo might have nailed the best thing about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time: its timelessness. The 1998 3D action adventure game for the Nintendo 64 that pioneered so much - 3D graphics, movement, exploration, openness - has been reengineered with changes that make it feel more modern, and surprisingly terrifying at times. Based on my early hands-on time with the game, it's shaping up to be the best-looking, best-playing version of the game that addresses the most frustrating aspects of playing the original. More than just sanding off its roughest edges, Nintendo also fitted Ocarina of Tim … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
With its upcoming remake for the Switch 2, Nintendo might have nailed the best thing about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time: its timelessness. The 1998 3D action adventure game for the Nintendo 64 that pioneered so much — 3D graphics, movement, exploration, openness — has been reengineered with changes that make it feel more modern, and surprisingly terrifying at times. Based on my early hands-on time with the game, it’s shaping up to be the best-looking, best-playing version of the game that addresses the most frustrating aspects of playing the original.

More than just sanding off its roughest edges, Nintendo also fitted Ocarina of Time with modern trappings to make it more welcoming to those who were introduced to Zelda through more modern releases, like Breath of the Wild. The remake has a new progression marker, called Threads of Time, that’s viewable when you pause. It also has Zelda Notes integration within the Nintendo Switch app to let you view game maps and other info on your phone. Oh, it also has a dedicated jump button.

I spent around 90 minutes during a recent preview event in New York City playing through some chunks of the game, including when you first take control of Child Link, and later on after you yank the Master Sword in the Temple of Time to become Adult Link. Its story still makes it a standout Zelda title, and the improvements make it even easier to get immersed in.

In some ways, the remake feels similar to modern Zelda games. Link is snappy to control, and lock-on combat is engaging. Swapping between items and weapons no longer requires hopping into the pause menu, as it did in the original. Holding a shoulder button halts the action, and you can navigate with an analog stick to find what you want in near-realtime. However, it’s an adventure on a much smaller scale; the complexity of your quests, and the tools at your disposal for combat and getting around are simpler, but no less fun.

All of the sections I played were truncated, though I left feeling confident that Nintendo nailed this remake. My favorite section was the Forest Temple, which really shows off the more realistic art style. It can finally portray the game’s horror themes in ways that weren’t possible 28 years ago. For example, Link traverses rooms in the dungeon that have red stained glass windows, and as he passes through beams of light, he is cast in the color of blood. It really looks and feels like he’s on an adventure to stave off cataclysm, and the visual evolution frequently made me stop playing for a second while I took in the changes. Also, being able to use the right stick to control the camera lets you create cinematic moments on-the-fly, which is great if, like me, you like taking a lot of screenshots.

Ocarina of Time is one of Nintendo’s most influential games, and playing it is a rite of passage for any Zelda fan, but it can be tough to go back to the original. As accessible as it is considering it was one of Nintendo’s earliest fully-3D titles, the remake makes it so much easier to get into. And it’s launching at a time when the Zelda franchise is bigger than ever. Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom were big sellers, and they continue to attract new players years after launch, while fans will be able to dig into the live-action movie in April 2027. Even sooner, though, Switch 2 owners will get to feast on the best way to play through a defining Zelda classic.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches for the Nintendo Switch 2 on Thursday, November 5th.

title: Nintendo’s Zelda Remake Is Rewriting My Memories
snippet: After an hour of playing the new Ocarina of Time, I think I prefer it to the old one.
fullText:
I spent weeks of graduate school curled up in front of my TV playing The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on my N64. I remember the epic journey with fuzzy nostalgia that, when I load up the game on the Switch’s N64 app, doesn’t entirely pay dividends. It looks uglier now than it does in my head. As Bill Pullman said in Lost Highway, “I like to remember things my own way…how I remembered them. Not necessarily the way they happened.”

Nintendo’s $60 Ocarina of Time remake for the Switch 2 filled me with uncanniness when I saw the first trailers. It was lush, almost weirdly rich with detail. Hyrule Castle Town almost looked like a theme park. Everyone’s faces seemed so…shiny.

But after an hour of playing the remake in an early preview session, I came away from it in a happy haze. If someone had never played Ocarina of Time before, this would feel like a whole new game. And if you have…this might end up being your new memory of it.

			

More from CNET

A beautiful rebuild

It’s a freaky thing, the idea of game remakes. It’s the same way I feel about movies being updated or remade. I like to preserve the original artifact. Nintendo has been on a roll lately, working to reboot its classic catalog into fully new versions, starting with StarFox earlier this year and now continuing with Ocarina of Time. Both were Nintendo 64 games, and both, I think, feel so new in their remade versions that they almost feel original.

And yet Ocarina is a beat-for-beat return to the original, as far as I can tell. With a few new bits, and possibly other mysteries lurking, too.

Sometimes the graphics almost feel too lush.Nintendo

I played a bit of the beginning, where Link starts off in his Kakariko forest village. Link can jump now and also swim in the water (I dove for some rupees). I didn’t mind the new voice acting, and the character animations won me over. It almost felt like a more immersive version of the art style in Link’s Awakening or Echoes of Wisdom, blended with Breath of the Wild/Tears of the Kingdom.

The Great Deku Tree, with its dripping root mouth, now seems more sinister or overwhelming. Every part of the game’s visuals actually feels more ramped up than even Breath of the Wild or Tears of the Kingdom, but on a smaller scale. Less overwhelming vistas, more gorgeously detailed foliage and buildings.

Running across Hyrule Field and exploring Hyrule Castle Town, talking to villagers and exploring shops, I wondered if this many characters were here before. Was it this bustling? 

Everything feels atmospherically revamped.Nintendo

I played as Adult Link, too, exploring the Forest Temple and making my way through almost all its puzzles again. I played this temple long ago (and again on the Nintendo 3DS remaster), but everything is so graphically overhauled this time that some environments just feel totally new. The stained glass windows, the cathedral-like interiors…was I here before?

You can also play the Ocarina’s spell songs by actually singing them over the Switch 2’s microphone (or by tapping buttons the old school way). I tried and felt ridiculous, but it worked. Gimmicky, but fun.

Nintendo’s whole holiday lineup of Switch 2 game releases is throwbacks: Switch Sports Resort, then Ocarina of Time. I’d love some original games too, but those look like they’re on deck for 2027 (Metroid Ravenous, and the new Kirby and the World Beyond). In the meantime, is Nintendo testing the Switch 2’s graphics chops with remakes while it works out new games for the future…or biding time until more Switch owners hop aboard Switch 2? I like what I’ve tried so far, but will it make me want to play all of Ocarina all over again? We’ll find out soon.

title: Someone ported Pixel 11’s Rambler voice-to-text to other Android phones
snippet: One of the best new features of Google’s Pixel 11 (and Googlebook) is support for Rambler voice-to-text, and it’s now been ported to other devices – if you’re willing to take the risk, that is. more…
fullText:
One of the best new features of Google’s Pixel 11 (and Googlebook) is support for Rambler voice-to-text, and it’s now been ported to other devices – if you’re willing to take the risk, that is.

Rambler on the Pixel 11 series is essentially AI-enhanced voice-to-text. The feature takes what you say and runs it through AI, spitting out a result that includes grammar and formatting while taking out filler words and times you may have tripped over your words. It’s not perfect, as not being able to see a live preview or get word-for-word output can be a little unsettling, but it’s still a huge upgrade to traditional voice-to-text.

That’s why it can be a little annoying that it’s Pixel 11-only.

A developer, though, has managed to port the feature to any other Android phone. “PixelBoard” is a split off of the Gboard app that brings support for Rambler to essentially any other Android phone. 

	
	

In a post on Reddit (h/t Artem Russakovskii), the developer explains that the project is based on the official Gboard app, just modified to unlock Rambler and other new writing tools.

The app is available for sideloading via the project’s GitHub page, but as always that’s done at your own risk. That said, we installed the app on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 to a complete success. It runs just like Rambler on a Pixel 11. Your results may vary and, again, install at your own risk! The project has other install methods available, including patching the existing Gboard installation on your phone.

It’s still unclear if Google ever plans to bring Rambler to other devices, but third-party mods like this will be the only way to do so for the time being. For those wanting to stick with a Play Store install, Microsoft’s SwiftKey acts as a fine alternative.

title: Helix Carbon says it can make iron cheaper by recycling blast furnace pollution
snippet: The steel industry is a big polluter, but Helix Carbon can upcycle pollution from blast furnaces to drive down emissions and improve margins.
fullText:
The iron and steel industries are among the biggest polluters in the world. Plenty of startups have tried to cut the industry’s emissions, mostly by developing new ways to make the metals. Helix Carbon thinks those startups have been going about it all wrong.

“Any attempt to decarbonize the steel industry without dealing with the blast furnace is not going to work,” David Brown, Helix Carbon’s co-founder and CEO, told TechCrunch. A blast furnace is the giant furnace that turns iron ore into the iron used to make steel. Rather than replace blast furnaces, Helix wants to clean them up. Its approach promises to slash the steel industry’s carbon emissions while boosting profit margins for iron producers, a rare win-win for a dirty industrial process.

Blast furnaces have made iron for centuries, using coke, a processed form of coal, to help turn raw iron ore (iron bound up with oxygen) into metallic iron. The burning coke supplies heat for the reaction but doesn’t take part in it directly. Instead, carbon monoxide produced from the combustion does the work of reducing the iron, meaning stripping away its oxygen atoms.

The process releases tremendous amounts of carbon dioxide, or CO2, which is normally dumped straight into the atmosphere. But Helix Carbon has devised a way to turn that waste carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide and recycle it back into the blast furnace.

Helix Carbon’s process relies on an electrolyzer, a device that uses electricity and a catalyst to break off an oxygen atom from the carbon dioxide. Electrolyzers aren’t new, but Brown said the startup’s design can handle the entire exhaust stream from the blast furnace. Most electrolyzers are too delicate for raw exhaust like that. They work only on purified, concentrated carbon dioxide, so the exhaust typically has to be processed before they can use it.

By injecting carbon monoxide into a blast furnace, iron producers can use less coke. How much, exactly, is still debated, Brown said. Some scientific papers suggest as much as 90% of the coke can be eliminated, while other studies suggest it’s more like 30% to 40%. 

Helix Carbon is proposing that iron producers start by replacing 33% of their coke. The company says using its technology to do so would save them $14 per ton of iron. “That may not seem like a lot, but margins in the iron industry are famously thin,” Brown said.

The iron and steel industries are a combined $2 trillion market, according to Grand View Research, which makes the sector an appealing target for a young startup to chase. But it also moves slowly, in part because its equipment lasts so long. “There are blast furnaces that have lived for over 100 years,” Brown said.

To bring in revenue earlier, Helix Carbon plans to court the specialty chemicals industry first. “We don’t need to capture the CO2 first,” Brown said. “We just utilize it, and that opens up the door of making chemicals on-site right out of waste streams.”

title: Why did it take so long for someone to make a magnetic USB-C port? [Video]
snippet: In launching its new Surface Laptop Ultra this week, Microsoft showed off its magnetic USB-C port and I immediately want it on everything. more…
fullText:
In launching its new Surface Laptop Ultra this week, Microsoft showed off its magnetic USB-C port and I immediately want it on everything.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra is a full-on powerhouse with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chipset, up to 128GB of RAM, and plenty of ports. But it’s one of those ports that is the most unique new features.

“Magnetic Connect” is Microsoft’s name for “the world’s first built-in magnetic USB-C” charging port. The USB-C port itself functions as normal with any standard cable, but the included charger is specially designed to magnetically attach akin to Apple’s MagSafe or any other number of magnetic charging connectors.

I want it.

	

The “how” here is that the charging portion of the cable uses super-strong magnets to align and latch on the charger so the port connects properly, but the charger itself also tapers the edges of the USB-C port so it can more easily slide into place. As such, that end won’t securely connect to your phone or other devices, as it needs that magnet to hold itself in place. 

	

The Verge shows it in action in a video on YouTube:

Microsoft is apparently hoping this idea will catch on and show up on other laptops, and I sure hope that’s the case! As for phones, the size of the magnets implies it probably won’t be feasible in a standard smartphone, but I really hope this idea starts showing up everywhere! Certainly I hope it at least shows up on a laptop that doesn’t cost $2,600 — Surface Laptop Ultra pre-orders are open now.

What do you think?

title: iOS 27.2 beta 4 no longer includes Apple’s overhauled Health app
snippet: An overhauled Apple Health app is coming, but it looks like iOS 27.2 won’t include it. more…
fullText:
An overhauled Apple Health app is coming, but it looks like iOS 27.2 won’t include it.

Apple first announced the upgraded Health app in September. The company still says to expect it to launch later this year.

iOS 27.2 developer beta 1 was the first iPhone software update to include the new Health app.

Apple added it to iOS 27.2 public beta 1 and public beta 2 as well. It features new data points like health age while adding the ability to schedule lab work through Quest Diagnostics.

However, it appears Apple plans to take a bit more time to get the new Health app ready for release.

Today’s iOS 27.2 developer beta 4 release no longer includes the new Health app. Instead, the prior version is restored. The longevity section is replaced with the previous sharing section.

iOS 27.2 beta 4 notes that Health data added during the beta testing period will be retained and viewing in the Settings app. It also adds that the release is still planned for this year. 

This likely means that we’ll see iOS 27.3 beta in late October or early November with the Health app upgrade included.
